source_work: Heiser — Deuteronomy 32 and the OT Worldview (paper)
title: Deuteronomy 32:8-9 — The Foundation of the OT Worldview
content_summary: Deuteronomy 32:8 describes Yahweh's dispersal of the nations at Babel and his disinheriting of those nations, giving them over to other, lesser gods (elohim). Deuteronomy 32:9 states Israel belongs to Yahweh alone. The 'sons of God' reading comes from Dead Sea Scrolls manuscripts much older than the traditional 'received' text. The 'sons of Israel' reading was most likely changed sometime after the Jewish community — in response to the new Christian church and its use of the Septuagint — 'standardized' the Hebrew text in the second century AD.
content_detail: The Table of Nations (Genesis 10) catalogs 70 nations but does not include Israel, because Israel did not exist at the time of Babel. This makes 'sons of Israel' illogical and unsustainable. Deuteronomy 32:8-9 is fundamental for understanding the worldview of Old Testament Israel — these two verses explain both the existence of foreign pantheons and their inferiority to Yahweh. The parallel passage Deuteronomy 4:19-20 represents the other side of the same coin: in 32:8-9 God apportions the nations to the sons of God; in 4:19-20, God allots the gods to the nations. God, like a father dismissing disinheriting his children, judges all nations for their disobedience at Babel (Gen 11:1-9), then in the very next chapter calls Abraham (Gen 12:1-3), starting over in creating an earthly human family for Himself.

source_work: Heiser — Deuteronomy 32 and the OT Worldview (paper)
title: Cosmic Geography — Land, Worship, and the Deuteronomy 32 Worldview
content_summary: Israel, as Yahweh's inheritance, was holy ground. Other nations' territory belonged to other gods by Yahweh's decree. This explains why David (1 Samuel 26:19) was distressed about being driven from Israel — he linked being in Israel with the ability to worship Yahweh, because Israel was Yahweh's portion and all other territory was handed to other gods. Naaman (2 Kings 5:17) asked for two mules' loads of Israelite dirt to take back to Syria so he could worship Yahweh on holy ground. Circumcision reminded Israel they were Yahweh's portion. Israelite laws share features with other ANE cultures but the rationale — tied to an everlasting covenant with Yahweh as inheritance — is unique.
content_detail: The conquest of Canaan was a reclamation of holy ground from nations that worshiped other gods. The concept of cosmic geography means specific geographic locations had spiritual significance tied to which divine being had authority over that territory. Paul used geographical terminology to describe the heavenly host: principalities, rulers, thrones, authorities, powers, dominions (Ephesians 6:12).

source_work: Heiser — Deuteronomy 32 and the OT Worldview (paper)
title: Pentecost as Reversal of Babel — The Reclaiming of the Nations
content_summary: The most dramatic example of the Deuteronomy 32 worldview in the NT is the Pentecost event in Acts 2, where God begins to reclaim all the nations for Himself. God has not forever abandoned the nations. Israel was to be a kingdom of priests — mediators between the disinherited nations and the true God. Christ became the ultimate mediator, reconciling every nation to God. The Great Commission (Matthew 28:19) and Pentecost (Acts 2, with representatives from all nations hearing the gospel in their own languages) directly reverse the Babel event.
content_detail: Even in the Old Testament, Israel's laws, prophets, and Scriptures all convey knowledge of the true God to the nations. The idea that corrupt gods (sons of God) both populate and control certain geographical regions was still prevalent in the NT era.

source_work: Heiser — Deuteronomy 32:8 and the Sons of God (BibSac paper)
title: The Textual Variant in Deuteronomy 32:8 — Sons of God vs Sons of Israel
content_summary: The Masoretic Text of Deuteronomy 32:8 reads 'sons of Israel' (bny yśr'l), but the Septuagint reads 'angels of God' (angelōn theou) or 'sons of God' (huiōn theou), both presupposing a Hebrew Vorlage of either bny 'lhym or bny 'lym. Two Dead Sea Scrolls manuscripts (4QDeutj and 4QDeutq) confirm the 'sons of God' Hebrew reading. 4QDeutj clearly reads bny 'lwhym and 4QDeutq has spaces for additional letters after 'l, confirming this was not merely bny 'l.
content_detail: The Table of Nations in Genesis 10-11 catalogs 70 nations but does not include Israel. The same Hebrew root (prd) used in Genesis 10:5 for 'separation' of nations appears in Deuteronomy 32:8 for dividing humankind, confirming Genesis 10-11 as the backdrop. The logical problem with the MT reading: How could the number of pagan nations be determined in relation to Israel (70 family members per Gen 46:27/Exo 1:5) when Israel did not yet exist at the time of Babel? Ugaritic mythology states that El Elyon (the Most High — the same title used in Deut 32:8) fathered 70 sons (KTU 1.4:VI.46), providing an exact linguistic parallel with the Hebrew bny 'lym / bny 'lhym.

source_work: Heiser — Deuteronomy 32:8 and the Sons of God (BibSac paper)
title: Text-Critical Methodology: No A Priori MT Superiority
content_summary: No text tradition should be assigned a priori superiority. The MT rose to prominence not by intrinsic textual factors but by political and socioreligious developments. Evidence from Qumran testifies to certifiable textual plurality among Jews from the 3rd century BC to the 1st century AD. Three independent text traditions (proto-MT, LXX Vorlage, Samaritan Pentateuch) coexisted at Qumran without suppression. The LXX was abandoned by Jews only after Christianity adopted it, not because it was inferior.
content_detail: The MT of Samuel suffers significant haplography. Kings has extensive pluses, minuses, and transpositions. MT Ezekiel chapters 1 and 10 are riddled with textual corruptions. MT Jeremiah is one-sixth longer than LXX Jeremiah, demonstrating expansionistic tendencies. The Qumran fragments supporting the LXX 'sons of God' reading (4QDeutj,n) are among 'unaligned texts' that show equal agreement and disagreement with all three major textual traditions.

source_work: Heiser — Deuteronomy 32:8 and the Sons of God (BibSac paper)
title: Parablepsis Cannot Explain the Variant in Deuteronomy 32:8
content_summary: The proposal that a scribe accidentally omitted 'yśr'l' from 'bny yśr'l' by parablepsis (leaving 'bny 'l') fails because: (1) 4QDeutj clearly reads bny 'lwhym, not bny 'l — the extra consonants hwym cannot be explained by parablepsis; (2) 4QDeutq has spaces for additional letters after 'l, also ruling out a simple 'bny 'l' reading. Advocates would have to argue both parablepsis AND deliberate scribal insertion of extra letters — an extremely unlikely two-step corruption.
content_detail: More critically, there exists ANOTHER textual variant in Deuteronomy 32:43 where divine beings (sons of 'lhym/'lym) are also the focus. In Deut 32:43, the MT demonstrably lacks a complete bicolon — the missing colon is exactly the one referencing divine beings in the Qumran and LXX texts. This 'parallel corruption' means defenders of MT priority must argue for TWO accidental changes in the same chapter that both happen to eliminate references to divine beings. It is far more likely both texts were intentionally altered in MT to eliminate references to divine beings deemed polytheistic.

source_work: Heiser — Deuteronomy 32:8 and the Sons of God (BibSac paper)
title: The Divine Council in 1 Kings 22:19-23
content_summary: 1 Kings 22:19-23 depicts Yahweh enthroned among the members of His council ('all the host of heaven') who stand before Him — a technical term paralleled in Ugaritic council scenes. Yahweh asks a question in a form paralleled in Ugaritic literature. A spirit volunteers to be a lying spirit in the mouths of Ahab's prophets. Yahweh approves the course of action He knows will succeed, and the messenger is commissioned. The council does not exercise actual authority but serves to 'reemphasize and execute His decisions.'
content_detail: This scene resembles Ugaritic council scenes where the chief deity El sits enthroned and addresses the assembly. The prophet Micaiah was permitted to observe the deliberations of the divine 'boardroom meeting' and thus pronounce with certainty 'thus saith the LORD' as a messenger of the divine assembly. Visions of Yahweh's divine council authenticated the prophet's message — a sort of test of true 'propheticity.'

source_work: Heiser — Deuteronomy 32:8 and the Sons of God (BibSac paper)
title: Psalm 82 — Yahweh Judges the Divine Council Members
content_summary: Psalm 82 depicts God (Elohim) standing in the assembly of El (adat-'el) judging in the midst of the gods (elohim). The elohim of v.1b and 6a are divine beings, not human judges. Key evidence: (1) They are called 'sons of Elyon' (bny 'elyon) — Elyon is a completely transparent title for deity in both Hebrew and Ugaritic, used only of God/El, never of humans. (2) The chiastic structure of v.1 compels understanding the second elohim as divine. (3) The particle 'aken' in v.7 creates a strong antithetical contrast with v.6 — 'I had thought [you were gods]... but you shall die like Adam.' If they were already mortals, telling them they would die like mortals is nonsensical.
content_detail: Cyrus Gordon demonstrated that translating elohim as 'rulers' or 'judges' lacks validity and is an example of theologically 'protecting' God. The terms and themes are present in Ugaritic literature — Elyon, princes, gods all appear in the Ugaritic poem 'the Gracious Gods.' The notion of the elohim 'falling' like 'one of the Shining Ones' (ha-sarim) is found in Canaanite mythology about the fall of one of the 'bn srm' ('sons of the shining ones'). The Akkadian cognate saruru means 'shining' (used to describe Venus in astronomical texts). This connects to Isaiah 14:12-15 (Lucifer/Shining One) and Ezekiel 28:12-17 (the anointed guardian cherub). Psalm 82:7 says the divine beings will die like Adam and fall like the Shining One — stripped of immortality and cast from their high estate.

source_work: Heiser — Deuteronomy 32:8 and the Sons of God (BibSac paper)
title: Divine Council Terminology: Ugaritic and Hebrew Bible Comparison
content_summary: Precise linguistic parallels exist between Ugaritic divine council terminology and the Hebrew Bible. For the assembly: Ugaritic 'dt 'ilm ('assembly of the gods') = Hebrew 'adat 'el (Psalm 82:1). Ugaritic sd = Hebrew sod yhwh ('assembly of Yahweh', Jer 23:18) / sod 'eloah (Job 15:8). For members: Ugaritic 'ilm ('gods') = Hebrew elohim/elim. Ugaritic bn 'il ('sons of El') = Hebrew bene elim/bene elohim (Psalm 29:1; 89:6; Gen 6:2,4; Job 1:6; 2:1). Ugaritic phr kkbm ('congregation of stars') = Hebrew kokebe boqer ('morning stars', Job 38:7) / kokebe 'el ('stars of God', Isa 14:13). For meeting place: Ugaritic Mount Sapanu = Hebrew yarkete saphon ('heights of the north', Psalm 48:1-2); Ugaritic phr m'd ('assembled congregation') = Hebrew har mo'ed ('mount of assembly', Isa 14:13).
content_detail: Critically, the Hebrew Bible maintains a hierarchy within the council that parallels Ugaritic: the elohim/elim (gods/divine beings) are not the same as the mal'akim (messengers/angels). At no point are the mal'akim ever designated as elohim, elim, or bene elohim in the Hebrew text. English Bible translations that render all these terms as 'angels' blur the distinctions and obscure the divine council. The members of the council had higher status than the messenger beings. The 'hosts' of Yahweh (tseba'ot) is an umbrella term including all categories of nonhuman beings.

source_work: Heiser — Deuteronomy 32:8 and the Sons of God (BibSac paper)
title: Jesus' Use of Psalm 82:6 in John 10:34 — A Claim to Deity Via the Divine Council
content_summary: The traditional interpretation that Jesus quotes Psalm 82:6 to say 'even human judges were called gods, so I can call myself Son of God' actually WEAKENS Jesus' claim to deity. If the elohim were just humans with a title, then Jesus is merely claiming a non-ontological title. This is no more an argument for deity than calling Moses elohim in Exodus 4:16/7:1. Instead, Jesus was reminding his Jewish adversaries of the OTHER divine beings — the elohim — in Yahweh's divine council. Their own Scripture affirmed multiple elohim. Jesus was saying: 'My Father has many divine sons (Psalm 82:6 testifies to this), yet I am unique — I am the monogenes son of God, qualitatively different from all other divine beings.' Interpreting Psalm 82:6 as human judges ROBS Jesus of a very pointed claim to deity.
content_detail: The 'word of God' in John 10:35 is not a reference to receiving the Mosaic law (there is no reference to the law in all of Psalm 82). It refers to the judgment rendered against the divine beings by Yahweh in Psalm 82:7. Moses is called elohim in Exodus 4:16 and 7:1 not because he is a human 'judge' but because he functions as a member of God's council — he regularly spoke to Yahweh face to face and was a governing mediator ruling Israel at God's behest.

source_work: Heiser — Deuteronomy 32:8 and the Sons of God (BibSac paper)
title: The Nations Given to Fallen Divine Beings at Babel — Deuteronomy 32:8-9 Theology
content_summary: Deuteronomy 32:9 says 'the LORD's portion is his people, Jacob his allotted inheritance.' The parallelism requires that if Israel was TAKEN (hlq) as Yahweh's allotted inheritance (nhlh), then the nations of v.8 were also GIVEN as an inheritance — to the sons of God. After observing humanity's rebellion before the flood and again at Babel, God 'gave humanity up' (cf. Romans 1) to lesser divine beings and created Israel ex nihilo as His own nation, beginning with Abraham in the very next chapter (Genesis 12). Each pagan nation was overseen by a divine being inferior to Yahweh. Deuteronomy 4:19-20 confirms this was punitive — God allotted the gods (the host of heaven) to the nations as punishment.
content_detail: Tigay: 'These passages seem to reflect a biblical view that as punishment for man's repeated spurning of His authority in primordial times (Gen 3-11), God deprived mankind at large of true knowledge of Himself and ordained that it should worship idols and subordinate celestial beings. He selected Abraham and his descendants as the objects of His personal attention to create a model nation.' The verb hlq ('allotted') appears in both Deut 4:19 and 32:8, confirming the connection. This theology explains the entire biblical narrative: God disinherits the nations at Babel, gives them to the sons of God, takes Israel as his own, and the rest of Scripture traces the plan to reclaim the nations.

source_work: Heiser — Deuteronomy 32:8 and the Sons of God (BibSac paper)
title: Israelite Monotheism and the Reality of Plural Elohim
content_summary: If other divine beings do not actually exist, texts like Psalm 89:6-7 ('Who in the skies can compare with Yahweh? Who is like Yahweh among the sons of the gods? In the council of the holy ones God is greatly feared') and Psalm 29:1 ('Ascribe to Yahweh, O sons of the gods') would be eviscerated of meaning. The solution: Western Christians define 'GOD' as omnipotent, self-existent, omniscient, omnipresent — and assume any entity called elohim must have these attributes. But the ancient Semitic mind distinguished between Deity (God — possessing all these attributes uniquely) and divinity (god-likeness — sharing the category of 'divine being' without sharing the unique attributes). Yahweh is an elohim, but no other elohim is Yahweh.
content_detail: The Hebrew Bible's divine council differs from pagan pantheons in critical ways: (1) Yahweh alone is Creator, unassisted — no divine being helped; (2) There is NO theogony — Yahweh produced the elohim without a consort; (3) No genuine rivals — Yahweh need not battle divine beings to maintain leadership. Isaiah simultaneously affirmed the existence of other divine beings AND the one true deity (Isa 40:25-26 — 'To whom will you compare me?' then 'He brings out the starry host one by one and calls them by name' — He created the other elohim and they line up at His command). It would be nonsensical to have Yahweh claim to command entities that don't exist. Genesis 1:26 'let us make man in our image' is a decision announced to the council, but the following verb 'so God created' is singular — only Yahweh did the creating.

source_work: Heiser — The Divine Council (DOTWPW article)
title: The Council of the Gods — Textual Evidence for Israel's Divine Council
content_summary: The Ugaritic expression 'dt 'ilm ('assembly of El/the gods') corresponds exactly to Psalm 82:1's ba'adat 'el ('assembly of God/the divine council'). The second occurrence of elohim in Psalm 82:1 must be plural due to the preposition 'in the midst of.' The Trinity cannot explain this divine plurality since the psalm sentences these elohim to die 'like humankind.' Psalm 89:5-7 places God 'in the assembly of the holy ones' and asks 'who is like Yahweh among the sons of God (bene elim), a god greatly feared in the council of the holy ones (besod qedoshim)?' Psalm 29:1 commands the same sons of God to praise Yahweh. These heavenly sons of God (bene elohim or bene ha-elohim) appear in Genesis 6:2,4; Deuteronomy 32:8-9,43 (LXX, Qumran); Job 1:6; 2:1; 38:7.
content_detail: The Ugaritic council parallels are extensive: phr 'ilm ('assembly of El/the gods'), phr bn 'ilm ('assembly of the sons of El/the gods'), mprt bn 'il ('assembly of the sons of El'), dr bn 'il ('assembly/circle of the sons of El'), 'dt 'ilm ('assembly of El/the gods'). Phoenician texts also describe: wkl dr bn 'lm ('all the circle/group of the sons of the gods').

source_work: Heiser — The Divine Council (DOTWPW article)
title: The Abode and Meeting Place of the Divine Council — Cosmic Mountain Theology
content_summary: At Ugarit the divine council met on a cosmic mountain where heaven and earth intersected, at the 'source of the two rivers' in the 'midst of the fountains of the double-deep.' El dwelt in 'tents' and a 'tent shrine.' Baal held meetings in the 'heights' of Mount Sapanu, where there were 'paved bricks' making Baal's house 'a house of the clearness of lapis lazuli.' The same imagery appears in the Hebrew Bible: Yahweh dwells on mountains (Sinai/Zion), the Jerusalem temple is in the 'heights of the north' (yarkete saphon, Ps 48:1-2), Zion is the 'mount of assembly' (har mo'ed, Isa 14:13). Ezekiel 28:13-16 equates the 'holy mountain of God' with Eden, the 'garden of God.' Eden appears as the 'seat of the gods' (moshab elohim, Ezek 28:2). At Sinai, under God's feet was 'sapphire stone' (libnat hassappir, Ex 24:10) — just as with Baal's dwelling.
content_detail: The 'domed tent' imagery evokes the Tent of Meeting and the Tabernacle. Zion is Yahweh's tent ('ohel, Isa 33:20). Mount Zion is described as a watery habitation (Isa 33:20-22; Ezek 47:1-12; Joel 3:18; Zech 14:8). The description of Eden in Genesis 2:6-15 refers to the 'ground flow' that 'watered the entire face of the earth.' The cosmic mountain is where divine decrees are issued — the intersection of heaven and earth.

source_work: Heiser — The Divine Council (DOTWPW article)
title: The Structure and Bureaucracy of the Israelite Divine Council — Yahweh as Both Sovereign and Vicegerent
content_summary: The Ugaritic council had four tiers: (1) El and his wife Athirat at the top; (2) the royal family — 'sons of El,' 'princes' — with one member serving as vicegerent, given the title 'most high'; (3) craftsman deities; (4) messengers (ml'km). In the Israelite council, Yahweh was supreme authority over a bureaucracy with a second tier of lesser elohim (bene elim, bene elohim) and a third tier of mal'akim ('angels'). The CRITICAL DIFFERENCE: In Israelite religion, the vicegerent position was filled not by another god but by Yahweh himself in another form. This 'hypostasis' of Yahweh was the same essence as Yahweh but a distinct, second person. This is most plainly seen via the Name theology and the angel of Yahweh (for the angel's connection to the Name — the essence of Yahweh — see Exodus 23:20-33).
content_detail: This religious structure is the backdrop to the ancient Jewish acceptance of two powers in heaven (Segal). Since both powers were believed to be good, the belief does not reflect Zoroastrian influence. The belief in two powers in heaven was a contributing factor in the advent of 'binitarian monotheism' in Second Temple Judaism (Hurtado), which contextualizes the description of Jesus as the monogenes ('unique') son of God in the NT. Since the Hebrew Bible is clear that there are other sons of God (bene [ha]elohim), NT writers clarify that Jesus, as the same essence as the Father, is unique among all heavenly sons of God.

source_work: Heiser — The Divine Council (DOTWPW article)
title: Monotheism in the Hebrew Bible and the Divine Council — Yahweh's Qualitative Uniqueness
content_summary: Biblical writers refer exclusively to Yahweh as 'the God' (ha-elohim) and 'true God' (elohim emet). Although Yahweh was an elohim, he was qualitatively unique — preexistent and Creator of all things including the 'host of heaven' (Ps 33:6; 148:1-5; Neh 9:6). This is monotheism on ancient Semitic terms. The plural elohim of Psalms 82 and 89 CANNOT be human rulers — if they are humans, why are they sentenced to die 'like humans'? Israel's elders never had jurisdiction over all nations. The corrupt decisions of humans would not 'shake the foundations of the earth' (Ps 82:5). The 'sons of God' meet 'in the clouds' (basshahaq, Ps 89:6-7). The lesser elohim are not merely idols — Deuteronomy 32:17 calls them shedim (demons), whose existence cannot be denied. One psalmist demands the lesser elohim worship Yahweh (Ps 97:7) — puzzling if no such entities exist.
content_detail: Phrases like 'there is none beside Yahweh' (Deut 4:35,39; 32:12,39) appear IN PASSAGES that affirm the existence of other gods (Deut 4; 32). They express incomparability, not non-existence. Isaiah 47:8,10 proves this: Babylon claims 'I am, and there is none else beside me' — not claiming to be the only city, but that she has no rival. Isaiah 40:1-2 is a divine council text (via plural imperatives). Comparing Yahweh to imaginary beings cheapens the praise: David proclaims he will sing praise 'before the gods' (neged elohim, Ps 138:1). 185+ references to plural elohim/elim exist in the Qumran material alone.

source_work: Heiser — Two Powers in Heaven (article)
title: The Two Powers in Heaven — The Vice-Regent of the Divine Council
content_summary: The original model for the 'two powers in heaven' idea was the role of the vice-regent of the divine council. In Canaanite religion, the high sovereign El ruled through an appointed second god (Baal). In Israelite religion, this position was filled not by a separate deity but by Yahweh himself in another form — a second, visible Yahweh who was the same essence but a distinct person. Ancient Israelites understood Yahweh as occupying both sovereign and vice-regent positions simultaneously. The binitarian portrayal reflects knowledge of 'two Yahwehs' — one invisible/spiritual, one visible/human form. These figures sometimes appear together (Gen 19:24 — 'Yahweh rained fire from Yahweh out of heaven'), sometimes distinguished (Zech 3:1-2 — 'Yahweh said to Satan, may Yahweh rebuke you'), sometimes undifferentiated.
content_detail: Alan Segal's foundational 1977 work (Two Powers in Heaven: Early Rabbinic Reports about Christianity and Gnosticism) traced this concept to the Second Temple era (ca. 200 BCE), with biblical antecedents in Daniel 7:9ff (two thrones, the Ancient of Days and 'one like a son of man'), Exodus 23:20-23 (the angel in whom God's name dwells), and Exodus 15:3 (Yahweh as warrior). The two powers idea was not deemed heretical in Jewish theology until the second century CE — AFTER Christians identified Jesus as the incarnate second Yahweh. This belief in two powers was a contributing factor in the advent of 'binitarian monotheism' in Second Temple Judaism, which in turn contextualizes NT Christology. Both powers were believed to be good (not Zoroastrian dualism). The notion of two distinct deities at the top of the hierarchy was unthinkable to Israel — both were Yahweh.

source_work: Heiser — collected papers and articles
title: The Five Uses of Elohim in the Hebrew Bible
content_summary: The Hebrew word elohim lies behind 'God' in the OT. Several instances are plural, which may seem to indicate polytheism. Modern English translations often obscure the Hebrew text's references to plural elohim — e.g., the NASB renders the second elohim in Psalm 82:1 as 'rulers.' The Hebrew text refers to five different entities as elohim: (1) Yahweh, God of Israel (over 1000 times); (2) members of Yahweh's heavenly council (Psalm 82); (3) gods of foreign nations (1 Kings 11:33); (4) demons (Deuteronomy 32:17); (5) spirits of the human dead (1 Samuel 28:13); and possibly (6) angels (Genesis 35:7). This variety demonstrates elohim is NOT a synonym for God — the biblical writers do not qualitatively equate Yahweh with demons, angels, the dead, or other gods. All beings called elohim share one characteristic: they inhabit the non-human realm. Elohim indicates residence, not a set of attributes. Yahweh is an elohim, but no other elohim is Yahweh.
content_detail: Within the spiritual world, as in the human world, entities are differentiated by rank and power. The belief that Yahweh is utterly and eternally unique — that there is none like Him — is not contradicted by plural elohim in the OT.

source_work: Heiser — collected papers and articles
title: Proverbs 8 — Wisdom as a Co-Creator Figure Identified with Jesus
content_summary: Proverbs 8:22-31 describes the wisdom of God as a person/entity — a deity-level figure who assists God with creation. New Testament authors identify Jesus with this Wisdom figure. In Luke 11:49-51, Jesus quotes 'the Wisdom of God' as a separate speaker who says 'I will send them prophets and apostles.' But in the parallel passage Matthew 23:34, Jesus puts those same words into his OWN mouth — 'Therefore I send you prophets and wise men.' Luke and Matthew together identify Jesus as God's co-creator Wisdom, who was in turn identified as Yahweh, the God of Israel.
content_detail: The writer of Hebrews also identifies Jesus with Wisdom. In Hebrews 1:3, Jesus is called the 'radiance' (Greek: apaugasma) of the glory of God. This extremely rare word occurs in only one other place — Wisdom of Solomon 7:26, where Wisdom is 'a reflection (apaugasma) of eternal light.' The writer of Hebrews deliberately used this term to identify Jesus with the Wisdom figure. Colossians 1:15-17 and John 1:1-3 also identify Jesus as the pre-existent agent of creation — the Wisdom of Proverbs 8. This identification means Jesus is not merely a created being or first creation — He is the eternal Wisdom attribute of God personified.

source_work: Heiser — collected papers and articles
title: Deuteronomy 32:17 — Demons are Elohim, Not Merely Idols
content_summary: Deuteronomy 32:17 describes the gods (elohim) worshiped in disobedience as 'demons' (shedim) — low-ranking divine beings known in other ANE texts. They are not merely idols of wood and stone. Elsewhere in Deuteronomy, the writer describes these 'other gods' (acherim elohim) as the heavenly host (Deut 17:3). The same heavenly host terminology is used for actual spirit beings assembled in Yahweh's presence (1 Kings 22:19-23). Deuteronomy 4:19-20 and its explicit parallel Deut 32:8-9 together demonstrate that heavenly host terminology designates more than celestial objects — these celestial objects ARE the gods. In Deut 32:8-9, the writer calls them 'sons of God.'
content_detail: The starry host description of Deut 4:19-20 also occurs in Job 38:7, which refers to the presence of 'sons of God' at creation. 'Sons of God' is a common designation for divine beings (Job 1:6; 2:1), and in Psalm 82:6, the psalmist explicitly refers to the 'sons of the Most High' as gods (elohim). The Hebrew text uses elohim to refer to five different entities — though this distinction is rarely clear in English translations.

source_work: Heiser — collected papers and articles
title: Denial Statements Express Incomparability, Not Non-Existence of Other Gods
content_summary: Deuteronomy 4 and 32 affirm BOTH the existence of other gods AND their antagonism toward God — yet both chapters also use language presumed to deny the existence of other gods (Deut 4:35 'besides him there is no other'; Deut 4:39 'there is no other'; Deut 32:39 'there is no god beside me'). These 'denial phrases' do not assert nonexistence — they contend that no other gods COMPARE to Yahweh. The proof: the same denial statements occur in reference to Babylon (Isaiah 47:8,10 — 'I am, and there is none else beside me') and Nineveh (Zephaniah 2:15). Babylon is not claiming to be the only city in the world — she asserts she has no rival. The OT asserts the absolute and utterly incomparable uniqueness of Yahweh. No other god can claim to be uncreated or have His attributes.
content_detail: If the biblical writers could use elohim for entities besides Yahweh, they did not equate 'god' with only one entity. The modern term 'monotheism' does not accurately capture the beliefs of the biblical writers. This disconnect is caused by the desire of modern readers to reserve the word 'god' for one being, whereas the biblical writers did not share this desire. Biblical monotheism means: Yahweh is an elohim, but no other elohim is Yahweh. There is only one Yahweh. He is species unique.

source_work: Heiser — collected papers and articles
title: The Angel of Yahweh as the Visible Second Yahweh
content_summary: The OT writers deliberately make the Angel of Yahweh indistinguishable from Yahweh (e.g., Exodus 3:1-14). In Exodus 23:20-23, the Angel has Yahweh's 'Name' in him — reference to 'the Name' actually refers to Yahweh Himself (Name theology). Yahweh indicates He IS in the Angel. Yet in other passages, Yahweh and the Angel are simultaneously but separately present (Judges 6). Various passages attribute Israel's deliverance from Egypt to both God and the Angel (Judges 2:1-3; 1 Sam 8:8; Micah 6:4). Genesis 48:15-16 fuses God and the Angel: Jacob blesses Joseph's sons by invoking 'The God... the God... the Angel who has redeemed me from all evil, may HE bless the boys' — the verb 'bless' is grammatically SINGULAR, denoting a tight fusion of the two divine beings.
content_detail: The Angel that embodies Yahweh's presence parallels the role of Baal as co-regent who fights for El. In Joshua 5:13-15, the Angel leads Israel 'sword drawn in his hand' as captain of Yahweh's host. This description appears in only two other places, both referencing the Angel (Num 22:23; 1 Chr 21:16). Orthodox worship of Yahweh precluded cosmic rule by two separate deities, but COULD tolerate two personages of Yahweh. The Angel had the Presence (Name) of Yahweh in Him but was a distinct personage — He was Yahweh's presence, but not Him in His fullness.

source_work: Heiser — collected papers and articles
title: The Rider on the Clouds — Daniel 7:13 and the Second Yahweh
content_summary: The epithet 'Rider on the Clouds' was a well-known title for Baal in Canaanite religion. The Hebrew Bible consistently uses it and similar designations exclusively for Yahweh (Psalms 68:4; 68:33; 104:3; Deuteronomy 33:26; Isaiah 19:1) — with ONE exception: the 'son of man' in Daniel 7:13. This human figure is distinct from the Ancient of Days (the enthroned deity in Daniel 7) yet bears a title reserved exclusively for Yahweh in the OT. This is an unmistakable claim: the 'one like a son of man' IS a Yahweh figure — the second Yahweh, the visible one who comes in human form.
content_detail: Orthodox Yahwism replaced the co-regent slot that Baal occupied with a binitarian Godhead in which Yahweh occupied both slots. Within Israelite religion, Yahweh's occupation of both top tiers resulted conceptually in two Yahwehs — one invisible, the other visible. At times both speak as characters in the same scene, but more frequently they are virtually interchangeable.

source_work: Heiser — collected papers and articles
title: Yahweh Refers to Yahweh in the Third Person — Two Yahweh Figures
content_summary: In certain OT passages, Yahweh refers to Yahweh or 'God' in the third person: Genesis 19:24 — 'Then Yahweh rained on Sodom and Gomorrah sulfur and fire from Yahweh out of heaven' (one Yahweh on the ground, another Yahweh in heaven). Amos 4:11 — 'I overthrew some of you, as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah... declares Yahweh' (Yahweh speaks of 'God' as though referring to a distinct person). These passages directly support the two-powers-in-heaven theology.
content_detail: Jewish thinkers in the Second Temple period (516 BC-AD 70) were quite familiar with these patterns and did not consider them a violation of monotheism. Yahweh was alone at the top of the heavenly host, albeit in two forms. Jewish theologians devoted much speculation to identifying the second Yahweh — candidates included divinized humans (Adam, Abraham, Moses), exalted angels (Gabriel, Michael), and intermediate figures (Philo's 'the Word'). The early Christians altered these speculations by identifying the second power with Jesus. It wasn't until the second century AD that Jewish authorities declared the 'two powers' teaching heresy.

source_work: Heiser — collected papers and articles
title: Elohim as a 'Place of Residence' Term — The Key to Psalm 82
content_summary: Five different entities are referenced as elohim in the Hebrew Bible: (A) Yahweh (over 2000 times); (B) the elohim of Yahweh's heavenly council (Psalm 82, 89; Deut 32:8-9,43); (C) gods of foreign nations (1 Kings 11:33); (D) demons (Deut 32:17); (E) disembodied human dead (1 Sam 28:13); (F) angels (Gen 35:7). This variety means elohim is NOT identified with one particular set of attributes. It is a 'place of residence' term — it identifies the proper domain of the entity. All figures called elohim inhabit the non-human realm. Within the spiritual world there is ontological differentiation, rank, and power: Yahweh is an elohim, but no other elohim is Yahweh. The modern term 'monotheism' (17th century) is deficient for describing this, since it carries mental baggage of identifying 'god' with a single set of attributes held only by Yahweh.
content_detail: Elohim as a term does not refer to a set of attributes or ontology. Those issues are not explicated by a term; they are described in the Hebrew Bible. The biblical writers would not equate Yahweh in an ontological or qualitative sense with demons, angels, the dead, or other gods. We have nothing to fear from letting the text say what it says.

source_work: Heiser — collected papers and articles
title: Psalm 89:5-7 Rules Out Human Judges — The Council Is 'In the Clouds'
content_summary: Psalm 89:5-7 eliminates any ambiguity about whether the divine council elohim are human: 'Who in the CLOUDS (basshahaq) can be compared to Yahweh? Who among the sons of God (bene elim) is like Yahweh, a God greatly feared in the council (sod) of the holy ones?' Psalm 89 explicitly places the council 'in the clouds.' There is no text in the entirety of the Hebrew Bible that says or suggests there is a group of human judges in the heavens ruling with Yahweh over the nations. That position is offered only because of a perceived threat to monotheism, not because it has any textual merit.
content_detail: Rather than isolate Psalm 82, we should ask whether there are other passages with the same language of divine plurality in a council that rule out equating that language with human beings. Psalm 89:5-7 is exactly such a passage.

source_work: Heiser — collected papers and articles
title: Deuteronomy 32 as the Backdrop to Psalm 82 — The Judgment of the Gods of the Nations
content_summary: The council elohim in Psalm 82 are being judged for corrupt administration. The last verse implores God to 'inherit' (nahal) all the nations — the same lemma used for Yahweh's punitive judgment at Babel when He allotted the nations to the sons of God (Deut 32:8-9) and allotted those divine beings to the nations He was disinheriting (Deut 4:19-20). The psalmist is asking Yahweh to reverse the Babel judgment — to take back the nations from the corrupt divine beings. This is the cosmic geography worldview: each nation was under the dominion of a divine being assigned by Yahweh. These beings failed in their governance, and Psalm 82 records their sentencing. Psalm 82:8 is an eschatological cry for Yahweh to reclaim all nations — fulfilled in the Great Commission and Pentecost.
content_detail: The parallel between Psalm 82:8 (nahal — 'inherit' the nations) and Deuteronomy 32:8 (nahal — 'gave the nations their inheritance') creates a direct theological link. The nations were given as an inheritance to the sons of God at Babel; Psalm 82 pronounces judgment on those divine stewards; and the psalmist calls for Yahweh to take the inheritance back. No Israelite elder ever had jurisdiction over all the nations, but the divine beings of Deut 32:8-9 did.

source_work: Heiser — What Is an Elohim? and related articles
title: Elohim Describes a Plane of Existence, Not a Set of Attributes
content_summary: The Hebrew word elohim does not refer to a set of divine attributes (omnipotence, omniscience, etc.) but to a being's proper plane of existence — the spiritual realm. An elohim is a being whose proper habitation is the spirit world. This definition accounts for ALL biblical uses of elohim: (1) Yahweh, the God of Israel (over 1000 times); (2) the members of Yahweh's heavenly council (Psalm 82); (3) the gods of foreign nations (1 Kings 11:33); (4) demons (Deuteronomy 32:17); (5) spirits of the human dead (1 Samuel 28:13); (6) angels (Genesis 35:7). Yahweh is an elohim, but no other elohim is Yahweh — He is 'species unique' in possessing incommunicable attributes (omnipotence, self-existence, omniscience).
content_detail: The word elohim indicates residence, not a set of attributes; it identifies the proper domain of the entity it describes. All beings called elohim share one characteristic: they all inhabit the non-human realm. They may cross over into the human world, and certain humans may be transported to the non-human realm (prophets, Enoch), but the proper domains are separate. Within the spiritual world, entities are differentiated by rank and power. Yahweh shares 'communicable' attributes (love, mercy, intelligence) with lesser beings just as He does with humans, but His 'incommunicable' attributes (omnipotence, self-existence, omniscience) are His alone. By definition, only one being can be all-powerful.

source_work: Heiser — What Is an Elohim? and related articles
title: Demons as Elohim — Deuteronomy 32:17 and the Shedim
content_summary: In Deuteronomy 32:17, the Israelites 'sacrificed to demons (shedim), not God (eloah — singular), to gods (elohim) they had never known.' The demons who received sacrifices are explicitly called elohim. The singular eloah distinguishes the one true God from the plural elohim/demons. Some translations inaccurately render this as 'demons that were no gods' — but the Hebrew says the opposite. The demons ARE elohim (divine beings); they are just not eloah (the singular God, Yahweh).
content_detail: Heiser notes that the word 'God' in Deut 32:17 is the singular eloah — not the plural elohim. This is a critical distinction the text makes: the shedim are elohim (beings of the spiritual realm) but they are not eloah (Yahweh, the unique God). Translations that read 'demons that were no gods' are 'a misguided attempt at preserving monotheism by the translator.'

source_work: Heiser — What Is an Elohim? and related articles
title: The Spirits of the Human Dead as Elohim — 1 Samuel 28:13
content_summary: In 1 Samuel 28:13, the medium at Endor sees Samuel's spirit and says 'I see an elohim coming up out of the earth.' The spirit of the dead Samuel is called an elohim — a divine being. This is not the medium lying or faking; the text presents a genuine encounter with Samuel's spirit who delivers a true prophecy. The death penalty for consulting spirits of the dead (Lev 20:27) was not issued because such consultations didn't work — but because they DID. To commune with the dead was trespassing into the forbidden realm of the spirit world. The word ob ('spirit') refers to a spirit of a departed human being who could cross back over into the realm of the living.
content_detail: Everything in this narrative conforms to ancient Near Eastern parallels that refer to spirits of the human dead as divine beings (elohim), and that have such spirits crossing over to the realm of the living. In 1 Sam 28:7, the Hebrew literally reads 'Find me a woman, a mistress of the ob.' Saul specifically wanted a direct line to the spirit of Samuel — and the ob produced was also called an elohim. By nature, human beings are physical beings with an eternal spirit. When we die, our spirits go to the spirit world — and since that is the plane of the elohim, a disembodied human spirit is rightly called elohim.

source_work: Heiser — collected papers and articles
title: The Satan (Hassatan) in Job — An Adversary in the Divine Council, Not the Devil
content_summary: The hassatan in Job 1-2 is NOT a proper name — it has the Hebrew definite article prefixed (ha-satan = 'the Adversary'). This figure is therefore not the Devil as known in the New Testament. The Adversary's behavior in Job 1-2 is consistent with lesser deities in Ugaritic council scenes who report to a higher deity. He is the deity responsible for checking on human misbehavior. He is not 'talking back to God' but pointing out that humans behave well only when not under duress. Yahweh decides to test the Adversary's estimation, knowing Job will endure.
content_detail: Peggy Day's study 'An Adversary in Heaven' established that the hassatan is a functional role in the divine council, not a specific named entity. This is consistent with the Ugaritic parallel where lesser deities reported to El on the misbehavior of humans or other gods.

source_work: Heiser — collected papers and articles
title: Daniel 4 and 7 — The Watchers and the Divine Council Judgment Scene
content_summary: Daniel 4:17 describes Nebuchadnezzar's punishment as 'by the decree of the Watchers, the decision by the word of the holy ones' — but seven verses later (Dan 4:24), the same sentence is 'a decree of the Most High.' The Aramaic phrase shallitin shemay'a (Dan 4:26) can be translated either 'heaven rules' (corporate personification) or 'the heavenly ones rule' (council authority). The decree is from the Watchers, yet it is the singular Most High who rules — the council's decrees are Yahweh's decrees. Daniel 7:9-12 describes a divine council meeting: plural 'thrones' are set up, the Ancient of Days is seated, the 'court' (council) is seated, books of judgment are opened, and the fourth beast is killed. The 'holy ones of the Most High' (Dan 7:25) who receive the kingdom are probably divine beings (not humans) — humans enter later: 'the people of the holy ones' (Dan 7:27).
content_detail: In Daniel 7, the Son of Man bears the title 'rider on the clouds' — a title reserved exclusively for Yahweh in the OT, with this one exception. This character is distinct from the Ancient of Days (the enthroned deity) yet bears a divine title. Along with the Angel of YHWH as 'man of war,' this passage formed the basis for Judaism's doctrine of two powers in heaven, a point of orthodoxy until the second century AD.

source_work: Heiser — collected papers and articles
title: Deuteronomy 32:17 — Demons, Gods, Idols, and the Host of Heaven Are the Same Beings
content_summary: Deuteronomy 32:17 reads: 'They sacrificed to demons (shedim) who are not God (eloah — SINGULAR), to gods (elohim) they did not know.' The singular eloah means the demons are NOT Yahweh — but they ARE elohim (gods/divine beings). Translations rendering this as 'demons that were no gods' are inaccurate — eloah is never plural or collective in the Hebrew Bible. The lesser elohim are not merely idols: ancient idolaters knew statues were not identical to the deities they represented. A deity's non-corporeal essence was unlimited by time and space and could manifest in all its 'bodies' simultaneously. The shedim, the 'other gods' (elohim acherim), and the 'host of heaven' are all the same entities — the sons of God to whom the nations were allotted at Babel (Deut 32:8-9 / 4:19-20).
content_detail: The chain of identification across Deuteronomy: host of heaven (4:19) = other gods/acherim elohim (17:3; 29:25) = sons of God/bene elohim (32:8 DSS) = shedim/demons (32:17). These are real spiritual entities, not merely idols. Passages like Deut 4:28 and 7:25 link these beings to the statues that represented them, but the beings themselves are real. Psalm 97:7 demands that the lesser elohim worship Yahweh — a puzzling command if no such entities exist.

source_work: Heiser — collected papers and articles
title: Genesis 48:15-16 — Jacob Fuses God and the Angel with a Singular Verb
content_summary: Genesis 48:15-16 is a key binitarian text. Jacob blesses Joseph's sons by invoking three entities with a SINGULAR verb: 'The God (ha-elohim) before whom my fathers walked, the God (ha-elohim) who has been my shepherd all my life, the Angel (ha-mal'akh) who has redeemed me from all evil — may HE bless (yevarekh — SINGULAR) the boys.' If two separate persons were in view, the verb would be plural. The singular verb denotes a tight fusion of the two divine beings — God and the Angel are one. The Angel that embodies Yahweh's presence parallels Baal's role as co-regent warrior for El.
content_detail: This is complicated by the biblical teaching that God is eternal while angels are created beings. The explicit parallel of 'God' and 'Angel' does not imply God is an angel. Rather, it affirms that this Angel IS God. Joshua 5:13-15 has the Angel lead Israel 'sword drawn in his hand' as captain of Yahweh's host — this precise description occurs in only two other places, both describing the Angel (Num 22:23; 1 Chr 21:16).

source_work: Heiser — collected papers and articles
title: The Consensus View of Monotheistic Evolution Is Circular and Fails
content_summary: The dominant critical consensus since the 19th century holds that Israel's faith evolved from polytheism/henotheism to monotheism. This view is marred by circular reasoning — it assumes what it seeks to prove. Evidence: (1) Psalm 82, with its clear reference to a pantheon over which Yahweh presides, is supposedly 'late' — but if there was a campaign to stamp out polytheism, why was it 'missed'? Because there are approximately 185 occurrences of elohim, ha-elohim, bene elohim, bene ha-elohim, elim, bene elim in divine council contexts in the Qumran material ALONE. Second Temple Jews, willing to die rather than worship other gods, did not consider these texts a threat to monotheism. (2) The rhetorical use argument (Psalm 82 uses polytheistic language to promote monotheism) ignores pre-exilic texts like Psalms 24 and 29 that contain the same divine council language.
content_detail: The alternative view — that plural elohim are merely humans or idols — also fails. Making the elohim of Psalm 82 human requires ignoring: Psalm 89:5-7 which places the council 'in the clouds'; the Deut 32:8-9 backdrop where divine beings (not humans) administer the nations; the death sentence 'you shall die like humans' which is nonsensical if addressed to humans. The modern term 'monotheism' (coined in the 17th century) does not accurately capture the beliefs of the biblical writers. Both the evolutionary view and the traditional protective view bring theology to the text rather than deriving it from the text.

source_work: Heiser — collected papers and articles
title: Denial Statements in Deuteronomy Are Incomparability Claims, Not Denials of Existence
content_summary: The phrases 'there is no other' (Deut 4:35,39) and 'there is no god beside me' (Deut 32:39) occur IN THE SAME CHAPTERS that assume and affirm the existence of other gods (Deut 4:19-20; 32:8-9,17). Four proofs that these are incomparability claims: (1) The same constructions occur for Babylon (Isa 47:8,10) and Nineveh (Zeph 2:15) — 'I am, and there is none else beside me' — obviously not claiming to be the only city. (2) The Hebrew levaddo ('alone/beside') need not mean exclusive isolation — in 1 Kings 18:1-6, Ahab goes levaddo but obviously has servants; in Psalm 51:4, David sins 'against you alone' though he also sinned against Bathsheba and Uriah. (3) The negative particle 'eyn + 'od can express incomparability rather than nonexistence. (4) Deuteronomy 32:8-9,17 in the same chapter explicitly assumes the existence of other elohim (sons of God, shedim/demons).
content_detail: Hans Rechenmacher's linguistic study argued the denial phrases point to exclusivistic monotheism, but as Nathan MacDonald showed, his methodology is flawed — he assumes what he seeks to prove and fails to explain why the construction cannot describe incomparability. MacDonald observes that in every case where 'eyn + 'od occurs in questions/answers, 'what is being questioned is not the absolute existence of an object, but only if there is an object in a person's immediate domain.'

source_work: Heiser — collected papers and articles
title: The Mortal View of Psalm 82:6 Undermines Jesus' Claim to Deity in John 10
content_summary: Three problems with the standard 'mortal view' that Psalm 82:6 refers to human beings: (1) How is it a coherent defense of John's high Christology to have Jesus say 'I can call myself the son of God because every Jew can too'? The mortal view does nothing to advance John's strategic goal of portraying Jesus as the incarnate Logos and monogenes son of God — it casts Jesus as just another mortal. (2) If Jesus cites a text any Jew could cite, why would his audience react with outrage and call for stoning (John 10:30-31,39)? (3) The mortal interpretation of Psalm 82:6 would be utterly foreign to any Hebrew Bible scholar focused on Israelite religion — the divine council context makes the divine beings reading transparently obvious.
content_detail: The mortal view options include: (a) Israel's judges in view — but nowhere in the Hebrew Bible are Moses' appointed judges called elohim; (b) Israelites at Sinai — a midrashic fabrication with no textual basis (the Angel of Death at Sinai is nowhere in the text, 'law' in John 10:34 cannot refer to the Psalms given at Sinai); (c) humans who received divine revelation — but this doesn't explain the audience's rage, since every prophet claimed divine commission without being charged with blasphemy.

source_work: Heiser — collected papers and articles
title: Jesus Claims Divine Council Membership and Co-Regency — The Alternative Reading of John 10:34
content_summary: Heiser proposes that John understood the elohim of Psalm 82 as divine beings and has Jesus presuming the same. Jesus' quotation serves TWO purposes: (1) He reminds his detractors that there are other non-human divine beings (elohim) in their Scriptures who are also sons of God — the phrase 'sons of God' is used in the Hebrew Bible only of non-human divine beings. By linking his statements (10:30,38) to Psalm 82, Jesus claims his own divinity and membership in the divine council. (2) But John 10:30 and 10:38 go even further — when Jesus says 'the Father is in me, and I in him' and 'I and the Father are one,' he connects himself to the council co-regency. In effect, he equates himself as co-regent to the lord of the council, Yahweh himself. THIS is why the blasphemy charge makes sense — Jesus is not claiming to be just another son of God, but the unique co-regent, the second Yahweh.
content_detail: The 'word of God that came' in John 10:35 refers NOT to the law at Sinai but to the utterance itself in Psalm 82:6 — the pronouncement from God in the divine council scene. 'To whom the word of God came' = the gods (elohim) of the divine council in 82:1b. Compare Exodus 23:20-23 where the Name (the presence/essence of Yahweh, cf. Deut 4:37) is IN the Angel, who is therefore Yahweh in human form. Jesus is making the same claim: the Father is in him. He is lord of the council. This interpretation is consistent with: (1) Psalm 82 in its original ANE context; (2) other instances of 'sons of God' being divine in the Hebrew Bible; (3) John's portrayal of Jesus as God. No other view meets all three criteria.

source_work: Heiser — Naked Bible Podcast
title: The Watchers' Sin as the Origin of Evil — Not Adam's Fall Alone
content_summary: Paul says the Law was 'added because of transgressions' (Galatians 3:19). The common assumption is that this refers to Adam's sin. But nearly every Second Temple Jewish text that comments on human depravity attributes the proliferation of evil not to Adam but to the sin of the Watchers in Genesis 6:1-4. The Watchers (divine beings who transgressed by taking human wives) produced the Nephilim, whose deaths released disembodied spirits — called 'bastard spirits,' 'Watchers,' and 'demons' in Enochian literature. Some Second Temple writers considered the Watchers' transgression more significant than Adam's disobedience as the origin of widespread human evil. Paul, writing in this intellectual milieu, may have had the Watchers tradition in view when he wrote about the Law being added 'because of transgressions.'
content_detail: Tyler Stewart's SBL paper ('Fallen Angels, Bastard Spirits, and the Birth of God's Son: An Enochic Etiology of Evil in Galatians 3:19-4:11') argued Paul's discussion of the Law's purpose reflects the Watchers tradition. The Watchers taught forbidden knowledge (metalwork for weapons, cosmetics, sorcery — 1 Enoch 8:1-3) that corrupted humanity. Irenaeus and other early church fathers recognized the Watchers tradition as lurking behind discussions of human depravity. The 'elements of the world' (stoicheia tou kosmou) in Galatians 4:3,9 may refer to the rebellious divine beings (the Watchers/gods of the nations) under whose authority the Gentile nations were placed at Babel (Deut 32:8-9).

source_work: Heiser — Naked Bible Podcast
title: Demons as Disembodied Spirits of Dead Nephilim — The Second Temple Understanding
content_summary: In Second Temple Judaism (1 Enoch, Jubilees, Book of Giants), the Nephilim were the hybrid offspring of the Watchers (divine beings) and human women. When the Nephilim died (in the Flood and afterward), their spirits became disembodied — these are the demons (shedim) of the biblical text. They are called 'bastard spirits' because they are neither fully divine nor fully human. This understanding distinguishes demons from the fallen divine council members (the gods of the nations in Deuteronomy 32) and from Satan/the nachash. There are thus THREE categories of evil spiritual beings in the biblical framework: (1) the nachash/Satan — the original rebel from Eden; (2) the rebellious gods of the nations — divine council members who became corrupt (Psalm 82); (3) demons — disembodied Nephilim spirits.
content_detail: The term 'Watchers' (irin in Aramaic) comes from Daniel 4:17 where divine council members are called Watchers. In 1 Enoch, the same term is applied to the divine beings who transgressed in Genesis 6. The Watchers are distinct from the gods of the nations (Deut 32:8-9) — the Watchers transgressed by leaving their proper domain (their 'first estate' per Jude 6) to cohabit with humans, while the gods of the nations were legitimately assigned to govern nations but became corrupt in their governance.

source_work: Heiser — Naked Bible Podcast
title: The Nephilim Were Giants — Offspring of the Divine-Human Union
content_summary: The Nephilim (H5303) in Genesis 6:4 were the offspring of the sons of God (divine beings) and human women. The word is related to the Aramaic root nphl ('to fall') — 'the fallen ones.' They are explicitly called giants in the LXX translation (gigantes). Numbers 13:33 confirms the Nephilim survived as the Anakim clan encountered during the conquest. The giant clans of Canaan (Anakim, Rephaim, Emim, Zamzummim) are all connected to the Nephilim lineage. Deuteronomy 2-3 catalogs these giant clans and their territories. The cherem warfare (total devotion/destruction) during the conquest specifically targeted these Nephilim-infested regions — it was the elimination of the corrupt divine-human hybrid lineage.
content_detail: The Hebrew gibborim ('mighty warriors') in Gen 6:4 describes the Nephilim's warrior nature. The phrase 'men of the name' (anshei ha-shem) means 'men of renown.' The 'and also afterward' clause in Gen 6:4 indicates the Nephilim lineage continued after the Flood — explaining the giant clans in Canaan. Og king of Bashan (Deut 3:11) had a bed of iron 9 cubits long (~13.5 feet). Bashan is significant in cosmic geography — it is the region associated with Mount Hermon, where the Watchers descended according to 1 Enoch 6:6. The word 'Rephaim' means both 'giants' and 'shades/dead' — connecting the giant clans to the realm of the dead.

source_work: Heiser — Naked Bible Podcast
title: Jude 6 — The Angels Who Left Their Proper Domain Are the Watchers of Genesis 6
content_summary: Jude 6: 'And the angels who did not stay within their own domain (arche) but left their proper dwelling (oiketerion), he has kept in eternal chains under gloomy darkness until the judgment of the great day.' This is a direct reference to the Watchers tradition — the divine beings of Genesis 6:1-4 who transgressed by leaving the heavenly realm to cohabit with human women. The word arche ('domain/position') refers to their assigned sphere of authority in the divine council. The word oiketerion ('dwelling place') is used only here and in 2 Corinthians 5:2 (of the resurrection body) — it refers to their proper spiritual habitation. Jude 7 then compares their sin to Sodom and Gomorrah, which 'in a similar way to these (angels)' pursued 'other flesh' (sarkos heteras) — just as the angels pursued flesh not their own (human women), the Sodomites pursued flesh not their own.
content_detail: 2 Peter 2:4-5 parallels Jude 6: 'God did not spare the angels who sinned but cast them into Tartarus (tartaroo — a Greek term for the prison of the Titans, used only here in the NT) and committed them to chains of gloomy darkness.' The word Tartarus is significant — it is the Greek mythological prison for divine beings who transgressed, a precise parallel to 1 Enoch's account of the Watchers being imprisoned. Peter then immediately references Noah and the Flood, connecting the angelic sin to the pre-Flood era of Genesis 6. Jude's citation of 1 Enoch 1:9 in Jude 14-15 confirms his familiarity with and acceptance of the Watchers tradition as interpretive context for Genesis 6.

source_work: Heiser — Naked Bible Podcast
title: The Azazel/Scapegoat Connection — Leviticus 16 and the Watchers Tradition
content_summary: The scapegoat ritual of Leviticus 16:8 sends one goat 'for Azazel' (la-azazel) into the wilderness. In 1 Enoch 10:4-8, Azazel is the leader of the Watchers who is bound and cast into a pit in the wilderness as punishment. The Day of Atonement ritual symbolically returns the sins of the people to the Watcher who originated the corruption. The wilderness/desert is the domain of Azazel — a hostile, spiritually dangerous territory outside the sacred space of Yahweh's land. This is cosmic geography: Israel (Yahweh's territory) vs. the wilderness (Azazel's prison/domain). The scapegoat ritual makes no sense without the Watchers tradition as background.
content_detail: Most English translations render la-azazel as 'for the scapegoat' or 'as a scapegoat,' obscuring the proper name Azazel. The Hebrew text has two destinations: one goat 'for Yahweh' (la-YHWH) and one 'for Azazel' (la-azazel) — parallel constructions with proper names. The goat for Azazel is not sacrificed; it is sent alive into the wilderness bearing the sins of the people. This parallels 1 Enoch's account of Azazel being bound in the wilderness. The connection between the Day of Atonement and the Watchers was recognized in Second Temple Judaism and the Dead Sea Scrolls.

source_work: Heiser — What Is an Elohim? and related articles
title: The Nachash of Eden — A Shining Divine Being, Not a Talking Snake
content_summary: The Hebrew nachash (H5175) in Genesis 3:1 has three semantic ranges: (1) as a noun: serpent/snake; (2) as a verb root: to practice divination/enchantment (Gen 30:27; 44:5,15; Lev 19:26; Deut 18:10; 1 Kings 20:33; 2 Kings 17:17; 21:6); (3) as an adjective: shining/bronze (cognate with nechoshet/copper/bronze). The Eden figure should be understood as a luminous divine being — a 'shining one.' Ezekiel 28:12-17 describes this being as: 'the signet of perfection, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty,' who was 'in Eden, the garden of God,' covered with precious stones, 'an anointed guardian cherub' on 'the holy mountain of God,' who 'walked among the stones of fire,' and was 'blameless from the day you were created, until unrighteousness was found in you.' Isaiah 14:12 describes this figure as 'Helel ben Shachar' (Shining One, son of the Dawn). The nachash was not a common animal but a high-ranking divine being — a member of the divine council who rebelled against Yahweh.
content_detail: The word arum ('crafty/shrewd') in Gen 3:1 is not inherently negative — it is used positively for prudence in Proverbs (12:16; 13:16; 14:8; 22:3). The nachash's shrewdness is that of a divine being, not an animal. Eden was the divine council meeting place — Ezekiel 28:2 calls it the 'seat of the gods' (moshav elohim), and 28:13-16 equates the 'garden of God' with the 'holy mountain of God' where the divine council met. The nachash was 'among the stones of fire' — the council members (cf. the fiery seraphim of Isaiah 6). His punishment in Genesis 3:14 ('on your belly you shall go') is a demotion from his exalted status, not a biological transformation of a literal snake. The enmity between the nachash's 'seed' and the woman's 'seed' (Gen 3:15) is the protoevangelium — the first prophecy of the cosmic conflict resolved by Christ.

source_work: Heiser — What Is an Elohim? and related articles
title: The Eden Rebellion — The First of Three Supernatural Rebellions
content_summary: The primeval history (Genesis 1-11) contains three supernatural rebellions that escalate the cosmic conflict: (1) The nachash's rebellion in Eden (Genesis 3) — a divine council member tempts humanity to disobey, resulting in exile from the divine abode and the protoevangelium (Gen 3:15); (2) The sons of God/Watchers transgression (Genesis 6:1-4) — divine beings cross the boundary between the heavenly and earthly realms by taking human wives, producing the Nephilim, and unleashing a corruption so severe it provokes the Flood; (3) The Babel event (Genesis 11) — humanity's united rebellion prompts Yahweh to disinherit all nations, assigning them to lesser divine beings (Deuteronomy 32:8-9), and starting over with Abraham (Genesis 12:1-3). Each rebellion provokes a divine response that advances the cosmic conflict narrative toward its resolution in Christ.
content_detail: Eden was the divine council's meeting place (Ezek 28:13-16) — the cosmic mountain where heaven and earth intersect. Adam was God's first human representative, walking with God in the garden (the divine abode). Job 15:7-8 alludes to this: 'Are you the first man who was born? Have you listened in the council (sod) of God?' Adam was created to do on earth what the council does in heaven — to image God's rule over creation. The nachash disrupted this vocation. The curse on the nachash ('enmity between your seed and her seed') sets up the entire biblical metanarrative — the conflict between the seed of the woman (ultimately Christ) and the seed of the serpent (the forces of evil). The three rebellions together explain why the world is broken: Eden explains the human condition, the Watchers explain the proliferation of evil and the giant clans, and Babel explains the existence of hostile pagan nations under corrupt divine authorities.

source_work: Heiser — What Is an Elohim? and related articles
title: The Image of God — Humans as Yahweh's Earthly Imagers
content_summary: Genesis 1:26-27 has God announcing to His divine council ('let US make man in OUR image') His decision to create humanity as His earthly representatives. The 'image' (tselem) and 'likeness' (demut) are functional and vocational — humans are God's imagers, tasked with extending Eden's sacred space over all creation. They do on earth what the divine council does in heaven: govern, steward, and represent God's authority. The council witnesses the announcement (plural 'us/our') but only Yahweh creates (singular verb 'so God created' in v.27). The 'image of God' concept means humans were designed to be the earthly counterpart to the heavenly council — vice-regents of the visible world under Yahweh's authority, just as the divine beings are vice-regents of the unseen world.
content_detail: In the ancient Near East, kings placed images (statues) of themselves in territories they conquered to represent their rule. Humans are God's living 'statues' — His representative images placed on earth to rule on His behalf. This is why attacking the image of God (murder) is treated as an attack on God Himself (Gen 9:6). The image concept also explains the Great Commission: God's original intent was for His image-bearers to fill the earth with His presence. After the three rebellions fractured this plan, God calls Abraham to restart it (Gen 12:1-3), and ultimately Christ — the perfect image of God (Col 1:15; Heb 1:3) — completes what Adam failed to do. Believers are being 'conformed to the image of His Son' (Rom 8:29) — the restoration of the imager vocation. In the new creation, redeemed humans will take the place of the corrupt divine council members who failed in their governance of the nations (1 Cor 6:3 — 'we will judge angels').

source_work: Bradley — Two Fathers Only (paper)
title: Two Fathers, Two Families: The Canon's Own Ontological Binary
content_summary: Every recorded ancient society organized reality around a single structural unit: the family under its pater familias. Scripture establishes two fathers heading two families by explicit ontological chains: YHWH's chain consists of three IS-statements without origin (God IS life, God IS love, God IS truth); the rival's chain consists of three interlocking nodes (sin constitutes ek-belonging to Satan, sin produces death, Satan holds the power of death). Jesus, John, and Paul each name the rival's status from independent angles using the same category: family membership. The ek (out of) preposition IS the ontological claim.
content_detail: The Father's Chain: God IS life ('The Son has life in himself,' John 5:26; 'I AM the resurrection and the life,' John 11:25). God IS love ('God IS love,' 1 John 4:8, 4:16). God IS truth ('I am the way, the truth, and the life,' John 14:6; 'Your word is truth,' John 17:17). The Rival's Chain: Sin constitutes ek-belonging to Satan ('Whoever makes a practice of sinning IS of the devil,' 1 John 3:8; 'You ARE OF your father the devil,' John 8:44). Sin produces death ('The wages of sin IS death,' Rom 6:23). Satan holds the power of death ('The one who has the power of death, THAT IS, the devil,' Heb 2:14). The three chains interlock: to sin is to belong to the one who holds the power of what sin earns.

source_work: Bradley — Two Fathers Only (paper)
title: Both Chains Confirmed across Independent Canonical Registers
content_summary: The risen Christ's commission to Paul (Acts 26:17-18) states the structure of salvation in compressed form: 'from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God.' Every term maps onto the chains. The Lord's Prayer assumes the same structure at the level of daily existence. The same binary operates in Jesus' Temple dispute (John 8:38-44), his exorcism controversy (Matt 12:25-29), Paul's table-fellowship ruling (1 Cor 10:21), and the transfer formula (Col 1:13). Each text arrives from a different context; all assume the same two-household structure.
content_detail: John 8:38-44: Jesus names two fathers and two kinship-lines in a single exchange. He does not say 'your god the devil' or 'your master the devil' — he says 'your father,' the pater familias category deliberately and precisely. Matt 12:25-29: Jesus collapses kingdom, city, and house into one another, then defines cosmic conflict as one household head entering another's domain. He moves from kingdom language DOWN to household language, treating them as the same category. 1 Cor 10:21: 'You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons' — two tables are categorically incompatible because they belong to two incompatible households. Col 1:13: methistemi (population deportation) — the image is not individual conversion but relocation of a people from one pater familias's territory to another's.

source_work: Bradley — Two Fathers Only (paper)
title: Life and Death as Scripture's Primary Definitions
content_summary: The ontological chains are not proof texts; they are the definitional act. Life is what God IS, not a condition members enter — members have life because they belong to the one who IS it (1 John 5:12). Death is what the rival holds the power of, not the condition of being spatially distant from God. 'Separation from God' as primary definition imports a spatial frame the chains do not use. The question is not spatial proximity but domain membership. Romans 5:12 states the sequence without argument: sin precedes death because God IS life; to sin is to depart from the Life-giver.
content_detail: Life: 'The Son has life in himself' (John 5:26) — life resides in him as his own nature. 'This is eternal life, that they know you' (John 17:3) — eternal life IS the relational union with the Father. 'Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life' (1 John 5:12) — the possession is household membership. 'Eternal life' is not a different kind of life; it is the same life, named by its duration because it belongs to the one for whom duration is not a limit. Death: Sin's wages ARE death (opsonia, Rom 6:23) — not a penalty imposed from outside but the natural yield of sin's labor. 'He was a murderer from the beginning' (John 8:44) — death is constitutive of what the rival IS. The second death (Rev 20:14) is the maximally realized form of what death always was.

source_work: Bradley — Two Fathers Only (paper)
title: The Binary Pairs Are Hierarchically Organized, Not Coordinate
content_summary: The two household heads have incompatible natures. The three primary pairs describe three dimensions of the same ontological reality: Life/Death (dimension of being), Righteousness/Sin (dimension of character), Love/Pride (dimension of posture). Light/Darkness is the perceptual derivative — how the three primaries manifest visibly (John 1:4: 'the life was the light of men'). Structural derivatives include Kingdom, Holy/Profane, Blessing/Curse, Inside/Outside, Near/Far. Consequent analogies include Sheep/Goats, Flesh/Spirit, Wise/Foolish, Slave/Free. The hierarchy is testable: remove a primary pair and derivatives collapse; remove a derivative and primaries stand.
content_detail: The hierarchy table spans four tiers. Foundation: YHWH's 'I AM WHO I AM' (Ex 3:14) vs. the rival's 'You were blameless until iniquity was found in you' (Ezek 28:15) — IS vs. WAS. Primary: Life/Death, Truth-Righteousness/Sin, Love/Pride. Perceptual Derivative: Light/Darkness. Structural Derivatives: Kingdom of God/kingdom of this world; Good age/evil age (the age is poneros because its lord is ho poneros, Gal 1:4); Holy/Profane; Blessing/Curse; Inside/Outside; Near/Far. Consequent Analogies: Sheep/Goats (Matt 25:31-46); Children of God/children of the devil (1 John 3:10); Found/Lost (Luke 15); Flesh/Spirit (Rom 8:5-9); Gathered/Scattered (John 11:52); Wise/Foolish (Prov 9); Slave/Free (Rom 6:16-22). Control texts where Scripture performs the hierarchy: 2 Cor 6:14-18 (stacked binaries resolved into pater familias language); John 1:4-12 (life/light resolved into household transfer); Eph 2:1-19 (death, darkness, disobedience resolved into 'members of the household of God').

source_work: Bradley — Two Fathers Only (paper)
title: Sin, Death, Satan, Darkness as Explicitly Connected Nodes
content_summary: The four terms are not assembled by inference; every link is connected by a direct equation text. Sin's wages IS death (Rom 6:23). The one who holds the power of death, THAT IS (touto estin), the devil (Heb 2:14). Darkness and the power of Satan are equated by syntactic parallelism (Acts 26:18). The chain closes without a gap: Sin, Death, Satan, Darkness are one reality at four levels — the mechanism (sin), the condition (death), the lord (Satan), the perceptual domain (darkness). Satan's first recorded speech ('You will not surely die,' Gen 3:4) is specifically a denial of the Sin-to-Death link.
content_detail: Eden is where the chain was installed and simultaneously denied. God names the consequence: 'in the day you eat of it you shall surely die' (Gen 2:17). Satan's first recorded speech is a direct negation of the Sin-Death link: 'You will not surely die' (Gen 3:4). The Lie targets the Sin-Death link specifically. Romans 7:11: 'Sin, seizing the opportunity, deceived me and through the commandment put me to death' — Paul speaks as Adam, and personified Sin deceives and kills, the same two operations of the one John 8:44 names as liar and murderer from the beginning. The explicit link-by-link connections: Sin to Death (Rom 6:23; Rom 5:12), Sin to Satan (1 John 3:8; John 8:44), Death to Satan (Heb 2:14), Satan to Darkness (Acts 26:18; Col 1:13), Darkness to Sin (1 John 1:6), Darkness to Death (Matt 4:16/Isa 9:2, tsalmaveth: shadow of death).

source_work: Bradley — Two Fathers Only (paper)
title: The Divine Council Is a Household Administration
content_summary: Scripture presents the divine council as the cosmic form of the pater familias structure. YHWH presides over created heavenly beings who are members and servants of his cosmic household administration — 'ministering spirits sent out to serve' (Heb 1:14). The council is a household staff, not a military command. Deuteronomy 32:8-9 establishes cosmic geography: the nations were allotted to 'sons of God' while YHWH kept Israel as his own nahalah (inheritance/estate). Psalm 82 documents the failure: the allotted gods judged unjustly and are sentenced to die. The rival household exists as rebellion within the created order — parasitic, not primordial.
content_detail: Jeremiah 23:18, 22 presupposes the council as a real deliberative body. The allotment texts (Deut 32:8-9, DSS reading 4QDeutj: 'sons of God') establish a pater familias cosmic geography: the household head distributes administrative responsibility over his estate, reserving a portion as his own. Practical geography confirms this: Naaman's request for Israelite soil (2 Kgs 5:17), David's complaint that exile means 'Go, serve other gods' (1 Sam 26:19), Ben-Hadad's assumption 'their gods are gods of the hills' (1 Kgs 20:23). The binary is real but radically asymmetric — not dualism. God's incommunicable attributes (aseity, omniscience) are not part of the binary. The rival's 'fatherhood' is a corruption of the creaturely form of something God made good.

source_work: Bradley — Two Fathers Only (paper)
title: The Rival Household: Defected Insider with Full Pater Familias Structure but No Generative Capacity
content_summary: Ezekiel 28 and Isaiah 14 describe a created being — the throne guardian who sought to replace the household head. His names are job descriptions: ha-satan (the accuser, attacking from below) and diabolos (the slanderer, attacking from above). His method is rekullah (trafficking, Ezek 28:16) — infiltration, not frontal assault. The rival household has full household structure — head, domain, administration, subjects, table, destiny — but every feature is corrupted or counterfeited. Satan mimics light (2 Cor 11:14), sonship (Gen 6), a table (1 Cor 10:21), a kingdom (Matt 12:26), a throne (Rev 2:13), a temple (2 Thess 2:4). Every counterfeit confirms the original belongs to YHWH.
content_detail: The counterfeit column is structural evidence: a creature with no I AM has no capacity to originate; he can only corrupt and counterfeit. The rival household's features: Head — Satan, 'god of this age,' 'your father the devil' (John 8:44; 2 Cor 4:4). Domain — Darkness, 'the power of the air,' 'the whole world' (Col 1:13; Eph 2:2; 1 John 5:19). Administration — 'Rulers and authorities,' 'cosmic powers over this present darkness' (Eph 6:12). Table — 'The table of demons' (1 Cor 10:21). Subjects — 'Sons of disobedience,' 'the whole world lies in the power of the evil one' (1 John 5:19; Eph 2:2). Destiny — Second death, destruction, the lake of fire (Rev 20:14-15). The triad of Satan, Sin, and Death functions as the rival household's internal structure: Satan is the lord, Sin is the mechanism of conscription, Death is the domain's condition.

source_work: Bradley — Two Fathers Only (paper)
title: The Nested Household: Adam as Captured Head, Not Rebel
content_summary: Western soteriology often centers Adam's transgression as the controlling problem, producing a two-party drama (God vs. humanity). Scripture consistently identifies the serpent/Satan as the rebel and Adam as the captured household head. Paul's vocabulary in Romans 5:14-20 uses paraptoma (trespass) and parabasis (transgression) seven times — never the language of cosmic rebellion. Adam is a covenant-breaker, not an insurrectionist. The nested structure: Satan (cosmic head) over Adam (creaturely head) over individual households. Christ addresses both levels simultaneously — as the last Adam replacing the creaturely head, and as the Son of God defeating the cosmic head.
content_detail: The exegetical case: Gen 3:1-5 — the serpent initiates, this is a household-capture bid. Gen 3:14-15 — God's sentence falls on the serpent first; the two-seed structure is installed as consequence of the serpent's action. Rev 12:9; 20:2 — the serpent is identified as 'the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world'; Adam receives no such identification. The nesting has estate consequences: Creation is Adam's estate by commission (Gen 1:28). When Adam's household was captured, creation entered Satan's domain as the estate of a captured lord. Paul: creation was 'subjected to futility' (Rom 8:20) and 'groans together' (Rom 8:22). Creation's liberation depends on the household transfer completing: 'creation waits with eager longing for the revealing of the sons of God' (Rom 8:19). Christ's incarnation is the structural intersection: fully human (entering Adam's household) and fully divine (entering Satan's domain with authority to dismantle it). 'The ruler of this world is coming. He has no claim on me' (John 14:30).

source_work: Bradley — Two Fathers Only (paper)
title: Acts 26:17-18: The Risen Lord's Compressed Definition of Salvation as Pater Familias Transfer
content_summary: Acts 26:17-18 is the risen Christ's own framing of salvation as pater familias transfer, delivered as a binding commission. It is categorically distinct from any apostolic doctrinal summary — it is the dominical thesis statement that Paul's letters systematically explicate.
