The efficacy of the priestly work is measured by the majesty of the one who performs it; a divine person gives infinite value to the purgation of sin.
content_detail:
Owen treats verse 3 as the seedbed of the entire epistle. Two phrases fix the Son's deity. 'Brightness of his glory' means the Son is to the Father as the shining radiance is to the light itself -- distinct in person yet inseparable and co-essential, eternally proceeding without division of the divine nature. 'The express image of his person' presses the same truth: the Son is the exact impress or stamp of the Father's subsistence, so that to see him is to see the Father's own glory exhibited. Against every Socinian lowering of Christ, Owen insists these titles ascribe true and proper deity.

To this he joins a work of omnipotence: the Son 'upholds all things by the word of his power.' Owen notes the participle is continuous -- a present, ceaseless sustaining of the universe in being and order, carried not by labour but by a bare word of command. Creation-holding is a divine prerogative; the Son exercises it. Thus the same person who governs all worlds is the one who stooped to the office of a priest.

Owen's pastoral and doctrinal payoff comes in the clause 'when he had by himself purged our sins.' 'By himself' excludes all other means: he was at once the priest and the sacrifice, purging sin by the offering of himself. And because the person offering is the infinite, all-upholding Son, the purgation is of infinite value and full efficacy -- not needing repetition, as the following chapters will argue. The 'sitting down at the right hand of the Majesty on high' is the sign that the work is finished and accepted. Owen thus reads verse 3 as a compressed Christology and soteriology together: the glory of Christ's person is not an abstract speculation but the very ground of the believer's confidence, since so great a person has purged our sins and now reigns.

source_work: Owen — Exposition of Hebrews (1668-84)
title: Tasting Death, Destroying the Devil Through Death (Hebrews 2:9, 2:14)
content_summary: Owen expounds the deep necessity and the triumphant end of Christ's humiliation. The Son was 'made a little lower than the angels' precisely 'for the suffering of death' -- his abasement was ordered toward dying. He 'tasted death,' Owen insists, in its full bitterness and curse, not a token but the real thing, and did so 'by the grace of God' for the many sons being brought to glory. Verse 14 gives the strategy: because the children share flesh and blood, the Son took the same nature, so that 'through death' he might destroy the devil, who held the power of death, and free those enslaved by the fear of it. Owen marvels that death is conquered by dying: the Redeemer enters the enemy's own domain and, from within, breaks his tyranny over God's people.
content_detail:
Two things govern Owen's reading. First, the incarnation is purposive. The Son was made 'lower than the angels' not as a bare fact but 'for the suffering of death': his taking of a lower, mortal nature was the necessary means to a death he could not otherwise have died. Owen dwells on 'taste death' -- to taste is to experience really and inwardly; Christ drank death down to its dregs, bearing its penal bitterness as the wages of sin, though for himself he owed nothing. The 'grace of God' is the fountain of the whole transaction, and Owen, a defender of particular redemption, reads the scope in step with the context: the death is 'for' the 'many sons' whom God is 'bringing to glory' in verse 10, the 'brethren' and 'children' God gave him.

Second, verse 14 supplies the divine strategy of redemption. Owen stresses the kinship: 'the children are partakers of flesh and blood,' therefore the Son 'likewise took part of the same.' Only by sharing their nature could he act as their representative and die in their room. The astonishing means is stated as 'through death he might destroy him that had the power of death.' Owen notes the word rendered 'destroy' means to annul, unstring, render powerless -- not to annihilate the devil but to strip him of his usurped dominion. Satan's 'power of death' was the power of accusation and execution over guilty sinners; by satisfying the law and bearing the curse, Christ removes the ground of that power, so death can no longer condemn his people.

Owen's wonder is that the victory is won by submission: the Captain of salvation defeats death by dying, spoiling the strong man in his own house. The fruit is deliverance -- those who 'through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage' are set free, their consciences released from the terror of the grave because the sting of death, which is sin, has been drawn.

source_work: Owen — Exposition of Hebrews (1668-84)
title: A Merciful and Faithful High Priest to Make Propitiation (Hebrews 2:17)
content_summary: Here Owen grounds the incarnation in the requirements of the priestly office. It 'behoved' Christ -- there lay a moral necessity -- to be 'made like unto his brethren' in all things, sin excepted, so that he might be a 'merciful and faithful high priest' and 'make reconciliation for the sins of the people.' Owen weighs the two adjectives: 'merciful' looks toward us, a compassion learned by sharing our nature and sufferings; 'faithful' looks toward God, a fidelity in discharging every part of the office committed to him. The end of the priesthood is propitiation -- to expiate sin and turn away wrath. A priest must be taken from among those he represents; therefore the Son truly became man, that a real human high priest might offer a real sacrifice for real sins.
content_detail:
Owen reads 'it behoved him' as marking a necessity arising not from compulsion but from the nature of the office he undertook. A high priest, by the law of the office, must be one with those for whom he acts; he is 'taken from among men' to appear before God on their behalf. Hence the Son was 'in all things' made like his brethren -- sharing a true body and reasonable soul, our infirmities and temptations -- with the single, necessary exception of sin, which Owen guards carefully, for the priest must himself be spotless.

Owen makes much of the paired qualifications. As 'merciful,' Christ is inclined with tender compassion toward the tempted and the guilty; having taken our nature and passed through suffering, his mercy is not abstract but experiential, fitting him to succour those he represents. As 'faithful,' he is entirely trustworthy toward God who appointed him, exact in the whole discharge of his mediation, so that nothing needful to the reconciling of his people is left undone. The one qualification secures our confidence; the other secures the office's integrity.

The office terminates in 'making reconciliation for the sins of the people' -- Owen understands the verb as propitiation: the expiation of sin by sacrifice and thereby the appeasing of the divine displeasure it provoked. This is priestly and sacrificial language: sin is covered or done away by the offering, and God's justice, satisfied, is turned from wrath to favour. Owen is careful that this is 'for the sins of the people' -- a definite people, the 'brethren' and 'children' of the preceding verses -- not an indefinite gesture toward all without exception. The whole verse, then, joins the reality of the incarnation to the necessity of the atonement: because our salvation required a propitiatory sacrifice offered by a genuine and sympathetic human priest, the Son became like us in all things, that he might stand for us in things pertaining to God.

source_work: Owen — Exposition of Hebrews (1668-84)
title: Consider the Apostle and High Priest, Greater Than Moses (Hebrews 3:1)
content_summary: Owen turns from the person of Christ to a direct exhortation: 'consider' him. The word bids the mind fix itself attentively on Jesus as the 'Apostle and High Priest of our profession.' Owen sees the two offices as complementary directions of one mediation: as Apostle, Christ is God's supreme envoy sent to us, the final revealer surpassing all prophets; as High Priest, he is our representative sent from us to God. In the verses following, Owen presses the comparison with Moses that governs this section. Moses was faithful, but 'as a servant in the house'; Christ is faithful 'as a Son over his own house,' and so counted worthy of more glory, as the builder has more honour than the house. The Hebrews are urged to prize and hold fast this greater Mediator.
content_detail:
Owen makes the imperative 'consider' the hinge of the passage: it calls for a deliberate, fixed, believing contemplation of Christ, not a passing glance. The readers, 'holy brethren, partakers of the heavenly calling,' are summoned to turn the whole attention of faith upon Jesus, that they might not drift from him.

Owen finds in the double title a compact statement of Christ's mediatorial work. As 'Apostle,' Christ is the one sent from God to men -- the great ambassador and revealer who declares the mind of God fully and finally, in whom the prophetic line and Moses himself are surpassed, for he speaks not as a servant relaying another's word but as the Son who is himself the Word. As 'High Priest,' he goes the other way, from men to God, to represent his people and present their cause; the offices of revealing and reconciling meet in the single person of Christ Jesus. Under the old economy these were divided -- Moses the lawgiver, Aaron the priest; in Christ they are united.

The comparison with Moses, which Owen expounds at length from the following verses, is the point of the exhortation. Moses was indeed 'faithful in all his house,' and Owen will not diminish that honour; but he was faithful 'as a servant,' and his faithfulness had the character of testimony to things that were to be spoken after -- it pointed forward. Christ is faithful 'as a Son over his own house,' the house being the church, which is his by right of building and ownership. As the one who built the house has more honour than the house, so Christ is counted worthy of more glory than Moses. Owen's pastoral aim is plain: since the Mediator now set before them so far exceeds the greatest servant of the old covenant, the Hebrews have every reason to hold their profession fast and none to fall back to the shadows Moses served.

source_work: Owen — Exposition of Hebrews (1668-84)
title: There Remains a Sabbath Rest for the People of God (Hebrews 4:9)
content_summary: On the promise that 'there remaineth a rest to the people of God,' Owen builds his great meditation on gospel rest. He distinguishes several rests in Scripture: God's own rest after creation, sealed in the Sabbath; the rest of Canaan into which Joshua led Israel; and a further, better rest that still 'remains.' Owen's argument, drawn from Psalm 95, is that if the Canaan rest had been the final one, David would not, long afterward, still speak of a rest to be entered 'today.' Therefore a Sabbath-keeping abides for God's people: the spiritual rest found now in Christ by faith, in which we cease from our own works as God did from his, and the consummate rest of glory to come. Faith is the way in; unbelief shuts men out.
content_detail:
Owen's exposition of this verse anchors one of his longest discussions, on the nature and perpetuity of a day of rest. The reasoning is exegetical. The writer to the Hebrews argues from Psalm 95, where God, speaking through David, still warns a later generation not to harden their hearts lest they fail to 'enter into my rest.' Owen presses the chronology: Israel under Joshua had already entered Canaan; yet centuries afterward God still holds out a rest to be entered 'today.' It follows that the Canaan rest, real as it was, was typical and not final; a greater rest was still in prospect. Hence 'there remaineth a rest' -- Owen notes the distinctive word chosen here, a Sabbath-keeping or Sabbath-rest, which links this remaining rest to God's own primeval rest.

Owen unfolds the rest in stages. There is God's rest at creation, when he ceased from his works and blessed the seventh day. There is the rest of the land, a shadow. And there is the gospel rest -- the rest of the soul that comes to Christ and finds relief from the burden of sin and the toil of self-justification. Verse 10 gives its inward character: 'he that is entered into his rest, he also hath ceased from his own works, as God did from his.' Owen reads this as ceasing from all confidence in one's own works for acceptance, resting instead upon the finished work of Christ -- the very posture of justifying faith.

This rest has a present and a future dimension. Believers enter it now, by faith, in peace of conscience and communion with God; they enter it fully hereafter, in the eternal rest of glory. Correspondingly, Owen argues from the passage that a stated day of rest continues under the gospel, now transferred to the Lord's Day, the first day, commemorating the finished work of the risen Christ. Throughout, the warning stands as the counterpart of the promise: it is unbelief, and the hardening of heart it breeds, that shuts men out of God's rest, and faith alone that enters in.

source_work: Owen — Exposition of Hebrews (1668-84)
title: The Sympathizing High Priest and the Throne of Grace (Hebrews 4:15, 4:16)
content_summary: Owen draws the epistle's practical centre out of these verses: because our high priest can be 'touched with the feeling of our infirmities,' believers may 'come boldly unto the throne of grace.' Christ was 'in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin,' and from that real experience there springs a genuine, tender fellow-feeling for the tempted and afflicted. This sympathy, Owen stresses, is no mere pity from a distance but the compassion of one who has himself passed through our trials. It is the ground of the exhortation that follows. The mercy-seat has become for us a 'throne of grace,' and to it we are invited to draw near with confidence -- not presumption -- to 'obtain mercy' for our guilt and 'find grace to help' in every season of need.
content_detail:
Owen treats these two verses as promise and inference. The promise is the sympathy of Christ: 'we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities.' The double negative, Owen observes, is emphatic -- far from being unable to sympathize, our priest is fully able and ready. The ground is his own experience: he 'was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin.' Owen is careful with the exception. Christ knew temptation from without -- hunger, weariness, grief, Satan's assaults, the pressures that beset our nature -- and felt their force truly; but there was in him no inward corruption, no consenting to sin, for temptation found nothing in him. His sinlessness does not lessen his sympathy but perfects it, for sin in us dulls compassion, while his unstained nature feels our sorrows purely.

Owen distinguishes this compassion from mere divine pity. As God, the Son always regarded his people; but by taking our nature and suffering in it, he acquired an experiential, human fellow-feeling, so that he is inwardly moved toward the tempted as one who has been there. This is a spring of unspeakable comfort to weak and assaulted believers.

From this Owen draws the exhortation of verse 16: 'Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace.' The 'therefore' rests the whole invitation on the priest's sympathy. Owen notes that what was the 'mercy-seat' -- the place of atonement, once approached only by the high priest, once a year, with blood -- is now for believers a 'throne of grace,' freely open. 'Boldly' means with holy freedom and confidence of acceptance, the opposite of the bondage and terror of the old approach, yet never with irreverence. The double aim answers our double need: 'mercy' for the guilt of sins past, and 'grace to help in time of need' -- seasonable, sufficient supply for present weakness and future trial. Assurance, for Owen, is thus not a feeling worked up in us but a confidence grounded in the person and office of our sympathizing priest.

source_work: Owen — Exposition of Hebrews (1668-84)
title: A Priest Forever After Melchizedek, Saving to the Uttermost (Hebrews 5:6, 7:17, 7:25)
content_summary: Owen gathers the argument of the middle chapters: Christ is 'a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek,' and therefore 'able to save to the uttermost.' The Melchizedek order, Owen shows, is superior to the Aaronic -- royal as well as priestly, without recorded beginning or succession, and established by God's own oath. Above all it is unchangeable and everlasting: this priest does not die and hand on his office, but 'ever liveth.' From that perpetuity Owen draws the great conclusion of 7:25. Because Christ continues a priest forever, he can save 'to the uttermost' -- completely and to the very end -- all who come to God by him, for he 'ever liveth to make intercession for them.' His endless life guarantees the finishing of their salvation; the priest who never dies cannot fail those he represents.
content_detail:
Owen reads Psalm 110:4, cited at 5:6 and again at 7:17, as the divine charter of Christ's priesthood: 'Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek.' Two things follow. First, Christ's priesthood is not of the order of Aaron but of Melchizedek, and Owen expounds from chapter 7 the marks of its superiority. Melchizedek was king as well as priest -- king of righteousness and of peace -- uniting the two offices that Aaron never held; he appears in the record without genealogy, 'without father, without mother,' without registered beginning or end of days, so that he stands as a type of a priesthood that does not depend on descent or succession; and Abraham, with Levi in his loins, paid tithes to him and was blessed by him, the lesser by the greater. Second, this priesthood is confirmed by an oath of God, where the Levitical was not, marking it as unchangeable and the covenant it serves as better.

The crown of the argument, for Owen, is the perpetuity stated in 7:24-25: 'he continueth ever' and has 'an unchangeable priesthood.' Because he does not die and pass the office to another, but abides a living priest forever, his saving work is never interrupted or left unfinished. Hence the conclusion: 'he is able to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him.' Owen unpacks 'to the uttermost' as completeness both in extent and in duration -- a full salvation carried through to its very end, lacking nothing and failing at no point.

The ground is his unceasing intercession: 'seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them.' Owen understands Christ's heavenly intercession not as fresh suffering or repeated sacrifice, but as the continual, authoritative presentation of himself and his once-offered sacrifice before the Father, pleading its virtue for his people and securing the application of all its benefits. Because this living advocacy never ceases, the perseverance and final salvation of those who come to God by Christ is made certain. The endlessness of the priest is the guarantee of the endlessness of the salvation.

source_work: Owen — Exposition of Hebrews (1668-84)
title: The Warning Against Apostasy and the Perseverance of the Saints (Hebrews 6:4, 6:6)
content_summary: Owen handles the sternest of the warning passages with characteristic care. The people described are 'once enlightened,' having 'tasted the heavenly gift' and been made 'partakers of the Holy Ghost,' yet if they 'fall away' it is 'impossible' to renew them to repentance. Owen argues that these are common, not saving, operations of the Spirit -- illumination, gifts, and experiences that may be had short of justifying faith and true union with Christ. The apostasy in view is total, deliberate, and malicious: a renouncing of Christ that 'crucifies him afresh.' It is irremediable, not because grace runs short, but because such apostates reject the only remedy. Owen insists this does not overthrow the perseverance of true saints, who are kept by God and never so finally fall; the passage describes hypocrites and temporary believers, not the regenerate elect.
content_detail:
Owen's exposition here is a model of careful distinction, for the passage has long troubled those who hold the perseverance of the saints. He fixes first on the description of the persons. They were 'enlightened' -- granted a real illumination of the mind in the knowledge of gospel truth. They 'tasted of the heavenly gift' and 'the good word of God' and 'the powers of the world to come' -- they had genuine, affecting experiences of gospel realities and perhaps of miraculous gifts. They were 'made partakers of the Holy Ghost' -- sharers, Owen argues, in the Spirit's common gifts and operations. But Owen presses the point that nothing here names the saving graces: justifying faith, adoption, union with Christ, sanctifying renewal, the love of God shed abroad in the heart. All that is said may be found in men who are enlightened and gifted yet never truly regenerate -- the stony-ground hearers who receive the word with joy but have no root.

On this basis Owen reads the 'falling away' as the total and final apostasy of such persons: not a lapse into sin from which believers may be recovered, but a deliberate, wilful, and malicious renunciation of the gospel once professed, against knowledge and conviction. Verse 6 gives its character -- they 'crucify to themselves the Son of God afresh, and put him to an open shame,' taking their old place among Christ's crucifiers.

The 'impossibility' of renewing them, Owen argues, lies not in any deficiency of God's power or grace but in the nature of their sin: having knowingly cast off the only sacrifice for sin, they leave themselves no remedy, for there remains no other Christ to be preached to them. Owen is emphatic that this in no way endangers the true believer. The elect, born of God and united to Christ, are kept by his power and preserved by his unfailing intercession; they may fall grievously, but not totally and finally. The warning is real, and is one of the means God uses to preserve his own, but the apostates it describes were never savingly Christ's.

source_work: Owen — Exposition of Hebrews (1668-84)
title: Mediator of a Better Covenant on Better Promises (Hebrews 8:6, 8:10)
content_summary: On these verses Owen sets out his covenant theology. Christ has obtained a 'more excellent ministry' because he is 'the mediator of a better covenant, established upon better promises.' The new covenant is better than the old (Sinai) both in its mediator and in what it secures. Owen highlights the promises quoted from Jeremiah: God will 'put my laws into their mind, and write them in their hearts,' will be their God, and 'their sins and iniquities will I remember no more.' These are promises of efficacious grace -- inward renewal, saving knowledge of God, and free and final forgiveness -- not merely of an outward, conditional arrangement. Where the old covenant demanded and could not give, the new covenant bestows what it requires. Its blessings are secured in Christ's blood and infallibly applied to all its members.
content_detail:
Owen reads 8:6 as the transition from the priesthood to the covenant it administers. Christ's ministry is 'more excellent' in exact proportion as the covenant he mediates is better than the old; the dignity of the mediator and the excellency of the covenant rise and fall together. Owen takes the 'better covenant' to be the new covenant, formally established and confirmed in the blood of Christ, over against the covenant God made with Israel at Sinai, which is now removed as 'old' and 'ready to vanish away.'

The superiority lies chiefly in the 'better promises' on which the new covenant is 'established' -- Owen notes the word means enacted as a law, given the force of a settled constitution. He expounds the promises cited from Jeremiah 31. First, 'I will put my laws into their mind, and write them in their hearts' -- an internal, effectual work of regeneration and sanctification, whereby God gives the obedience the law demands, writing his will upon the renewed heart instead of only upon tables of stone. Second, 'I will be to them a God, and they shall be to me a people' -- the covenant bond of communion, God giving himself as the portion of his people. Third, all shall 'know the Lord, from the least to the greatest' -- a saving, experiential knowledge diffused among all covenant members. Fourth, 'their sins and iniquities will I remember no more' -- full, free, and final forgiveness, grounded in the one sacrifice of Christ.

Owen's decisive point is that these are promises of grace that God himself works, not conditions left to human strength. The old covenant at Sinai demanded righteousness but did not communicate the power to perform it, and so, considered as a covenant of works for life, it left its subjects under its curse. The new covenant is unilateral in its efficacy: God undertakes to do in his people what he requires of them. Therefore its blessings are not merely offered but infallibly conveyed to those it embraces, for the same blood that ratifies the covenant secures the application of all its promises.

source_work: Owen — Exposition of Hebrews (1668-84)
title: Eternal Redemption by His Own Blood, One Offering Perfecting Forever (Hebrews 9:12, 9:14, 10:10, 10:14)
content_summary: Owen brings together the heart of Christ's priestly work: by his own blood he 'entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption,' and 'by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.' Owen weighs the contrasts. Not the blood of goats and calves but his own blood; not the earthly sanctuary but heaven itself; not yearly repetition but 'once' for all. Because the sacrifice is of infinite worth, its redemption is 'eternal' -- accomplished, not merely offered, and never to be repeated. Verse 9:14 adds that Christ 'through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot,' and that his blood 'purges the conscience from dead works,' reaching the inward guilt the old rites never touched. And its effect is final: the one offering has 'perfected for ever' those it sanctifies, leaving no more offering for sin.
content_detail:
Owen expounds the sacrifice of Christ under the two great emphases of these chapters: its efficacy and its finality. From 9:12 he draws the contrast between type and reality. The Levitical high priest entered the earthly holy place year by year with the blood of animals; Christ entered 'the holy place' -- heaven itself, the true sanctuary -- 'by his own blood,' and 'once.' The single entrance corresponds to a single, all-sufficient sacrifice. And the fruit is stated as accomplished, not merely attempted: 'having obtained eternal redemption for us.' Owen stresses the verb -- Christ found and procured redemption as a thing actually secured, and it is 'eternal' both because its price is of infinite value and because its effect abides forever, needing no repetition.

Verse 9:14 carries the argument inward. Christ 'through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God' -- the offering was voluntary, of his whole spotless person, sustained by his own divine Spirit, and directed Godward as a true sacrifice. Its effect answers the deepest need: his blood 'purges the conscience from dead works to serve the living God.' Owen observes that the ceremonial sacrifices could cleanse only outwardly, sanctifying to the purifying of the flesh; the blood of Christ reaches the conscience itself, removing the real guilt of sin that no legal rite could take away, and freeing the worshipper for living service.

From chapter 10 Owen presses the finality. 'By the which will we are sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all' (10:10): the single offering, done according to the Father's will, sets his people apart as holy to God. 'By one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified' (10:14): Owen reads 'perfected for ever' as a completed and permanent perfection -- a full expiation and acceptance that cannot be added to or repeated, so that, as verse 18 concludes, 'there is no more offering for sin.' The very singleness of the sacrifice is Owen's proof of its perfection, for what is repeated confesses itself insufficient. And 'them that are sanctified' marks the definite compass of its effect: the offering actually perfects a particular people, securing their standing before God once and for all.

source_work: Owen — Exposition of Hebrews (1668-84)
title: Looking to Jesus, the Author and Finisher of Faith (Hebrews 12:2)
content_summary: Owen closes the running theme of faith and perseverance with the command to look 'unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith.' The word means to look away -- from every distraction, weight, and fear -- and to fix the eye of faith on Christ alone. He is faith's 'author,' the one who begins it in us and ran its course perfectly before us, and its 'finisher,' who carries it through to completion. Owen sets before believers his pattern: 'for the joy that was set before him he endured the cross, despising the shame,' and is now 'set down at the right hand of the throne of God.' The exalted, once-suffering Christ is thus both the object that draws faith and the example that sustains it, so that weary believers may run their race with endurance.
content_detail:
Owen reads this verse as the climax of the exhortation begun with the cloud of witnesses: having named the saints who lived by faith, the writer now directs the eye to the one supreme example and object, Jesus himself. The participle 'looking' means, Owen notes, a looking away -- turning the eye off from all other things, the weights and the besetting sin, the discouragements and the fear of suffering, in order to fix it steadily upon Christ. This fixed regard of faith is the secret of endurance.

Owen weighs the double title. Christ is the 'author' of faith -- its beginner and leader, the one who both works faith in his people by his Spirit and himself went before them as the great pattern of a believing life, the captain who leads the way. He is also its 'finisher' -- the one who perfects and consummates what he begins, carrying his people's faith through to its appointed end, so that the grace he authors he also completes. Faith thus depends on Christ from first to last.

The pattern Owen holds up is Christ's own endurance: 'for the joy that was set before him he endured the cross, despising the shame.' The joy set before him -- his glory and the salvation of his people -- sustained him through the utmost suffering and disgrace, which he despised, counting the shame as nothing beside the end in view. And the outcome is his session: he 'is set down at the right hand of the throne of God,' the reward of his endurance and the pledge of his people's. Owen's application is direct. Believers, wearied in the race and tempted by present affliction, are to consider him -- how he suffered and where he now sits -- that they may 'not be wearied and faint in their minds,' but run with patience, assured that the one who authored their faith will also finish it.

source_work: Owen — The Doctrine of Justification by Faith (1677)
title: Justification Is a Forensic Sentence: God Justifies the Ungodly (Romans 4:5, 8:33)
content_summary: Owen insists that justification is a forensic, judicial act -- a term drawn from the law-court, where God as judge pronounces a sentence upon the sinner. To justify is not to make a person inherently good but to declare him righteous and to accept him as such, absolving him from guilt and its penalty. The proof Owen presses is Paul's startling phrase: God 'justifieth the ungodly' (Rom 4:5). If justification were an infusing of righteousness that made the person actually holy, God could not be said to justify the ungodly, for they would no longer be ungodly. The word describes a change of state and standing before God's tribunal, not yet a change of nature. 'It is God that justifieth' -- the sentence is his, complete and irreversible, grounded outside the sinner.
content_detail:
Owen's whole doctrine turns on the meaning of the word 'justify,' and he labours to show that its sense throughout Scripture is forensic, not physical or moral. To justify is a judicial act, the opposite of to condemn; as a judge does not make a man righteous by acquitting him but declares and treats him as righteous in the eye of the law, so God in justifying pronounces the believing sinner righteous and accepts him accordingly. Owen marshals the courtroom language that surrounds the doctrine -- accusation, charge, sentence, absolution -- to fix this legal frame. 'Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God's elect? It is God that justifieth' (Rom 8:33): the setting is a tribunal, and justification is the verdict of acquittal.

The decisive text for Owen is Romans 4:5, 'to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness.' He draws out its force against every notion of justification as an infused, inherent righteousness. God justifies the person while yet ungodly -- at the moment of justification the sinner is not yet subjectively transformed into a holy man; if he were, the description 'ungodly' could not stand. Therefore justification cannot be the making of a person actually righteous in himself; that is the work of sanctification, which Owen carefully distinguishes as a real and gradual change wrought by the Spirit. Justification is instantaneous, complete, and equal in all believers, terminating on their state and relation before God.

Owen guards the distinction pastorally as well as polemically. To confound justification with sanctification is to unsettle assurance, for it makes acceptance rest partly on the believer's own inherent condition, which is always imperfect. By holding justification to be a declarative sentence, grounded in a righteousness not our own and pronounced by God the judge, Owen secures both the freeness of grace and the peace of the conscience: the ungodly, believing, are pronounced righteous, and the verdict stands because it is God's.

source_work: Owen — The Doctrine of Justification by Faith (1677)
title: The Great Exchange: The Imputation of Christ's Righteousness (2 Corinthians 5:21, Romans 5:19)
content_summary: At the material heart of Owen's doctrine stands the imputation of Christ's righteousness. Justification is grounded not in anything wrought in us but in a righteousness reckoned to us -- Christ's own, put to our account. Owen finds the blessed exchange in 2 Corinthians 5:21: God 'made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin, that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.' Our sins were imputed to the sinless Christ, who bore their penalty; his righteousness is imputed to us, so that we stand accepted in him. Romans 5:19 states the ground: 'by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous.' Owen defends the imputation of Christ's whole obedience -- his suffering of the penalty and his perfect keeping of the law -- as the one righteousness on which the believer's acceptance rests.
content_detail:
For Owen the question 'on what ground does God justify?' is answered by the imputation of the righteousness of Christ. Imputation is the reckoning or accounting of something to a person's account that is not inherently his own -- here, the righteousness of another set to the believer's reckoning as if it were his. Owen's governing text is 2 Corinthians 5:21, which he treats as a description of the great commutation or exchange: 'he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin, that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.' There is a double imputation. Christ 'knew no sin,' yet was 'made sin' -- not made a sinner inherently, but charged with our sins by imputation and dealt with accordingly, bearing their curse. Correspondingly we, who have no righteousness of our own, are 'made the righteousness of God in him' -- not made inherently righteous, but accounted righteous with his righteousness imputed to us.

Owen grounds the exchange in Romans 5:19: 'by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous.' As Adam's one disobedience constituted the many under him sinners, so Christ's obedience constitutes the many under him righteous -- a representative, imputed transaction. Owen defends against objectors that this obedience includes both parts of Christ's righteousness: his passive obedience, in suffering the whole penalty due to sin, and his active obedience, in perfectly fulfilling the law's precepts in our stead. Both are imputed, for the law requires both a penalty paid for transgression and a perfect righteousness performed; Christ supplies both, and both are reckoned to the believer.

Owen roots imputation in union with Christ. The righteousness of Christ is imputed to none but those who are united to him by faith and the Spirit; it is 'in him' that we are made the righteousness of God. The exchange is not a legal fiction floating free of any real bond, but the fruit of a genuine union, whereby what is Christ's becomes ours in law because he and his people are one. On this imputed righteousness, and on no inherent worth of ours, the whole weight of justification rests.

source_work: Owen — The Doctrine of Justification by Faith (1677)
title: Faith the Instrument, Not the Ground, of Justification (Galatians 2:16, Romans 3:28)
content_summary: Owen is precise about how faith justifies: instrumentally, not meritoriously. Faith is the means by which the believer receives and rests upon Christ and his righteousness -- the hand that takes hold, not the price that pays. It does not justify as a work, a virtue, or a righteousness of its own; that would be to make faith itself our righteousness and so overthrow grace. Owen reads Galatians 2:16 -- 'a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ' -- as setting faith over against all works precisely because faith looks away from self to another. Its whole value in justification lies in what it lays hold of. So Owen guards against turning faith into a subtle work, insisting the righteousness that justifies is entirely Christ's, only received by believing.
content_detail:
Owen devotes careful attention to the role of faith, for here many errors lodge. He denies that faith justifies as a work or an inherent virtue, and equally denies that the act of believing is itself imputed to us as our righteousness. Faith justifies instrumentally: it is the appointed means or instrument by which we receive Christ and his righteousness. Owen's favoured images are of a receiving or apprehending -- faith is the hand that takes the gift, the empty vessel that receives the treasure. Its dignity in justification is wholly derivative, lying not in itself but in its object; a weak faith that truly lays hold of Christ justifies as surely as a strong one, because the righteousness is in Christ, not in the believing.

Galatians 2:16 governs Owen's argument: 'a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ.' Paul sets faith and works in flat opposition as ways of being justified, and Owen presses that the opposition makes sense only if faith justifies in a manner utterly unlike works -- that is, not by doing or meriting, but by receiving what another has done. Were faith itself our justifying righteousness, it would be a work of our own after all, and the boasting Paul excludes would return.

Owen distinguishes his position from two errors. Against Rome and the moralists, he denies that faith justifies as the beginning of an inherent righteousness or as formed and made meritorious by love. Against the Socinians, he denies that God graciously accepts the act of faith in the room of a perfect righteousness we cannot render; that too would make believing our righteousness. In both, faith is made the ground rather than the instrument. Owen holds instead that the sole ground is Christ's imputed righteousness, and faith is only the God-given means of receiving it. This safeguards assurance, for it directs the anxious conscience away from the quality of its own believing to the sufficiency of the object believed on; peace is found not by examining faith but by resting, through faith, on Christ.

source_work: Owen — The Doctrine of Justification by Faith (1677)
title: Abraham the Pattern: Faith Counted for Righteousness (Genesis 15:6, Romans 4:3)
content_summary: Owen finds the pattern of all justification in Abraham: 'Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness' (Gen 15:6; Rom 4:3). The key word is 'counted' or 'reckoned' (imputed) -- an accounting term that Owen weighs closely. Righteousness was not found in Abraham and then acknowledged; it was reckoned to him, put to his account, in connection with his faith. And that faith looked away from himself to the promise of God, ultimately to the promised Seed, Christ. Paul underlines that this reckoning was to one 'that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly' (Rom 4:5), and that David describes the same blessedness as God 'imputing righteousness without works' (Rom 4:6). Abraham is thus the standing proof that justification is by imputation, apart from works, received through faith alone.
content_detail:
Owen makes Genesis 15:6, as expounded by Paul in Romans 4, the great scriptural demonstration of justification by imputed righteousness. Everything hangs on the word Moses uses and Paul repeats: Abraham's faith 'was counted unto him for righteousness.' The term is, Owen argues, an accounting or reckoning word -- to put to one's account, to impute. It does not describe the recognition of a righteousness already inherent in Abraham; it describes righteousness being set to his account in the sight of God. Owen notes that Paul's argument requires this sense, for he immediately contrasts reckoning 'of grace' with reckoning 'of debt' (Rom 4:4), and reward reckoned by debt belongs to the worker, while righteousness reckoned by grace belongs to the believer who works not.

Owen is careful about what exactly was imputed. He does not hold that the bare act of Abraham's believing was accepted as, or counted to be, his righteousness in itself; that would make faith a work. Rather, faith is named because faith was the means by which Abraham received the promise, and the promise had Christ for its substance -- the Seed in whom all nations would be blessed. Faith laid hold of Christ, and God imputed righteousness to Abraham accordingly. The expression 'counted for righteousness' thus stands, by Owen's reading, for the imputing of the righteousness apprehended by faith.

Paul reinforces the point with two further strokes that Owen follows closely. In Romans 4:5 the reckoning is made to 'him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly' -- proof that the righteousness is not earned but received, and received by one still ungodly. And in Romans 4:6 David is brought as a second witness, describing 'the blessedness of the man unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works.' Two witnesses, Abraham and David, from the law and the Psalms, establish that God's way of justifying has always been by imputation, apart from works, and through faith alone -- so that the gospel Paul preaches is no novelty but the ancient method of grace.

source_work: Owen — The Doctrine of Justification by Faith (1677)
title: Not My Own but a Righteousness from God: Imputed, Not Infused (Philippians 3:9, Romans 10:3)
content_summary: The sharpest edge of Owen's treatise is aimed at the Roman doctrine of infused righteousness. Rome holds that a man is justified by a righteousness wrought within him -- grace infused, renewing his nature -- so that he is accepted for what he becomes. Owen answers with Philippians 3:9, where Paul renounces 'mine own righteousness, which is of the law,' desiring instead 'the righteousness which is of God by faith.' The justifying righteousness is not our own and not inherent in us; it is a righteousness 'of God,' external, imputed, received by faith. Romans 10:3 exposes the error at its root: Israel, 'ignorant of God's righteousness,' went about 'to establish their own righteousness,' and so 'did not submit to the righteousness of God.' For Owen this is the dividing line: an alien, imputed righteousness versus one's own, however graciously infused.
content_detail:
Owen frames the great controversy with Rome as a question about the nature and location of the righteousness by which we are justified. The Roman doctrine, as defined at Trent, holds that justification is the infusion of an inherent righteousness -- a renewing grace poured into the soul -- so that a man is made truly righteous within and is accepted by God on the ground of that inherent, though God-given, righteousness, which may afterward be increased by works. Owen's objection is not that God fails to renew his people; he strongly affirms an inward, Spirit-wrought holiness. His objection is that this inherent righteousness is made the ground of acceptance, when Scripture assigns that place to a righteousness that is not our own.

Owen's leading text is Philippians 3:9, where Paul states his own desire 'to be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith.' Owen presses every clause. The righteousness that justifies is set in flat opposition to 'mine own' -- it is not a quality inhering in the believer, even one graciously infused, but a righteousness that remains Christ's, imputed and received by faith. It is 'of God,' both as its author and as answering to his justice, and it comes 'through the faith of Christ,' not through inward renovation.

Romans 10:3 supplies the diagnosis of the opposite error. Israel, 'being ignorant of God's righteousness, and going about to establish their own righteousness, have not submitted themselves unto the righteousness of God.' Owen finds here the very anatomy of every scheme of self-justification, including the Roman: not knowing that God provides a complete righteousness to be received, men labour to erect a righteousness of their own, whether by works of law or by inherent grace, and in so doing they refuse the righteousness God gives. To submit to God's righteousness is to renounce all confidence in what is wrought in or by us and to rest wholly on the imputed righteousness of Christ. On this hinge, for Owen, the whole difference between the gospel and its counterfeits turns.

source_work: Owen — The Doctrine of Justification by Faith (1677)
title: Justified Freely by Grace, Apart from the Works of the Law (Romans 3:24, 3:28)
content_summary: Owen sets out the exclusion of works and the freeness of grace from Romans 3. Believers are 'justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus' (v.24), and the conclusion of the apostle's argument is that 'a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law' (v.28). Owen distinguishes the causes: the moving cause of justification is God's free grace; the procuring or meritorious cause is the redemption accomplished by Christ; the instrumental cause on our part is faith. Works of the law -- of whatever kind, done by us -- are wholly shut out from the ground of acceptance. Not that the justified are left without good works, but that their works contribute nothing to the sentence by which God pronounces them righteous. Justification is 'freely,' as a gift, or it is not of grace at all.
content_detail:
Owen reads Romans 3:24-28 as Paul's compact statement of the grounds and manner of justification, and he uses it to order the several 'causes' the doctrine involves. 'Being justified freely by his grace' names the moving or original cause: justification springs from the free, undeserved favour of God, and the word 'freely' (Owen notes it is the same term rendered 'without a cause' elsewhere) excludes any procuring worth in us. 'Through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus' names the meritorious or procuring cause: the price Christ paid, his blood-bought redemption, is that for the sake of which God justifies, so that grace reigns 'through righteousness' and not against justice. And, as the following verses show, faith is the instrument by which this redemption is received.

Verse 28 draws the polemical conclusion Owen builds upon: 'we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.' Owen insists the exclusion is comprehensive. 'The deeds of the law' are not merely the ceremonial observances, as some would limit them, but all works of obedience whatsoever, moral as well as ritual, considered as a ground of acceptance; for Paul's argument is that by the law is the knowledge of sin, and that no flesh shall be justified in God's sight by law-keeping. Whatever is our own doing is shut out from the office of justifying.

Owen is quick to add the safeguard against antinomian abuse. To deny works any place in the ground of justification is not to deny them their proper place in the life of the justified. Faith that justifies is never alone in the person justified, but is ever accompanied by repentance and productive of good works; these are the necessary fruits and evidences of justifying faith, though they are no part of the righteousness for which we are accepted. The distinction Owen presses is between the cause of justification and its consequents: works follow from justification as fruit, but contribute nothing to the sentence itself. So the freeness of grace is preserved whole, and the redemption of Christ is honoured as the sole procuring cause of the sinner's acceptance.

source_work: Owen — Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers (1656)
title: Be Killing Sin or It Will Be Killing You: The Charter of Romans 8:13
content_summary: Owen builds his whole treatise on Romans 8:13, "if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live." He dissects the verse into its parts: a conditional ("if"), a duty ("mortify the deeds of the body"), a means ("through the Spirit"), the persons addressed (believers, the "ye" who are in Christ), and a promise ("ye shall live"). From it he draws his famous rule: "Do you mortify; do you make it your daily work; be always at it whilst you live; cease not a day from this work; be killing sin or it will be killing you." Mortification is not optional maintenance but the believer's ceaseless, life-or-death occupation. The verse ties life to the ongoing killing of sin, yet grounds that killing in the Spirit, so that duty and grace are joined, not opposed.
content_detail:
Owen treats Romans 8:13 as a compact charter and unfolds each clause. The persons are believers: Paul writes to those with "no condemnation" (8:1) who are "in the Spirit" (8:9); mortification is therefore a duty laid on the justified, not a means by which the unconverted earn acceptance. The conditional "if... ye shall live" does not make life the wages of mortification but marks mortification as the certain path and evidence of life: the living mortify sin, and only they. Owen is careful that this not be read as legal; the life is promised in the gospel, and mortifying is the way in which those who have that life walk toward its full possession.

The duty is "to mortify the deeds of the body," to put to death, to kill, the workings of indwelling sin, here called "the body" or "the flesh" as the seat of corruption. Owen insists the object is not the physical body (as ascetics suppose) but the sinful principle expressing itself through the whole person. The means is decisive: "through the Spirit." The same Spirit who gives life supplies the power to kill sin; mortification is neither self-generated nor mechanical but the believer acting in the Spirit's strength.

From this analysis comes the treatise's governing maxim: "Be killing sin or it will be killing you." Because indwelling sin is always active, never dormant, never neutral, the believer who ceases to oppose it does not hold ground but loses it. There is no truce. Owen therefore presses mortification as constant, daily, lifelong labor, as native to the Christian as breathing. The verse thus sets the terms for everything that follows: a real duty, resting on a real promise, performed by a real power, on pain of real loss. Life and death hang on whether sin is being put to death.

source_work: Owen — Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers (1656)
title: The Spirit Kills Sin: Mortification as the Spirit's Work Through Union with Christ
content_summary: Owen's most insistent point is that mortification is the Holy Spirit's work, not the achievement of the natural will. "They that are Christ's have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts" (Gal 5:24); the crucifying happens by virtue of union with the crucified Christ and by his Spirit, not by unaided resolve. The Spirit works it by causing the fruit of the Spirit to abound, by real efficacy upon the heart, and by bringing the cross of Christ into the sinner's soul. Owen warns that "mortification from a self-strength, carried on by ways of self-invention, unto the end of a self-righteousness, is the soul and substance of all false religion." Because it is God who works in us "both to will and to do" (Phil 2:13), the believer works, really and actively, yet always in dependence on a power not his own.
content_detail:
Having located mortification's power in the Spirit (Rom 8:13, "through the Spirit"), Owen presses home that no other agent can accomplish it. He surveys and rejects the natural resources men trust: sheer willpower, temperamental restraint, remorse after sin, or the exchange of one lust for a quieter one. None of these reach the root, and some merely relocate corruption. True mortification is a supernatural work, wrought by the Spirit alone.

Galatians 5:24 is his key text: "they that are Christ's have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts." Owen reads the crucifying as flowing from union with Christ: because the believer is joined to the crucified Lord, the flesh is judicially crucified with him (cf. Rom 6:6) and is progressively put to death by the Spirit who applies that death. The believer does not crucify the flesh by an independent act of self-mastery; he does it "in Christ" and by the Spirit's power. Owen names the Spirit's ways: he convinces the soul of the evil of sin, weakens its root and habit, causes the heart to abound in contrary graces, and reveals the fulness and cross of Christ to the soul.

This does not make the believer passive. Owen guards both sides: the Spirit works in us and by us; the work is not done without us. Philippians 2:13, "it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure," grounds the very energy of human striving in God's prior working, so that the more the Spirit works, the more the believer actually acts. What Owen forbids is self-strength directed to self-righteousness, which he brands the substance of all false religion. The believer's activity is real; its source is not himself. Thus mortification is duty and gift at once, commanded of us, yet performed only in the strength that God supplies through the indwelling Spirit.

source_work: Owen — Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers (1656)
title: Not by Self-Made Severity: Why Asceticism and Will-Worship Cannot Kill Sin
content_summary: Owen sharply separates gospel mortification from the counterfeit taught, he says, by Rome: vows, penances, fastings, disciplines, and bodily austerities imposed on men as the way to subdue sin. Paul had already exposed such "will-worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body" as being "not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh" (Col 2:23). These outward severities may afflict the body while leaving the sinful heart untouched, and they can even breed spiritual pride, the deepest corruption of all. Mortification is not the maceration of the body but the killing of indwelling lust by the Spirit; a man may weaken his flesh with disciplines and never mortify a single sin. Owen grants the right use of fasting and watching as helps, but denies that any self-invented rigor, apart from faith in Christ and the Spirit's power, can put sin to death.
content_detail:
One of Owen's aims is to rescue "mortification" from a grievous misunderstanding. He charges the Roman church with mistaking its nature and use, directing troubled consciences to a battery of self-imposed rigors (vows of abstinence, set penances, corporal disciplines, retirements, and fastings) as the appointed means of killing sin. Owen's verdict is that such practices, taken as mortification itself, are at best beside the point and at worst dangerous.

His scriptural warrant is Colossians 2:20-23, where Paul dismisses ordinances like "Touch not; taste not; handle not" (2:21) and the whole apparatus of "will-worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body" as having "a shew of wisdom" but being "not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh" (2:23), of no real value against fleshly indulgence. Owen's point is that these disciplines operate on the outer man while indwelling sin has its seat in the heart and mind. A man may fast until his body is worn and never touch the pride, unbelief, or sensuality lodged within; indeed the very rigor may feed a self-righteous conceit, so that in "mortifying" one sin he nourishes a worse one.

Owen does not despise fasting, watching, and self-denial in their place; he commends them as helps and as ways of humbling the soul. What he denies is that any self-invented severity, pursued in one's own strength and toward one's own righteousness, can kill sin. That is the false religion he elsewhere condemns. Real mortification strikes at the love of and delight in sin by the Spirit and through faith in Christ's cross (cf. Gal 6:14, the believer "crucified unto the world" by that cross). The test is not how much the body is chastened but whether the heart's cleaving to sin is being weakened. Bodily austerity apart from the Spirit is, at most, the reforming of the outside of the cup; it is not the death of sin.

source_work: Owen — Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers (1656)
title: A Lifelong War: Mortification Is the Constant Duty of Every Believer
content_summary: Owen argues that mortification is not for advanced saints only, nor for a season of life, but is the abiding duty of every believer to the end. Because "fleshly lusts... war against the soul" (1 Pet 2:11) without ceasing, the believer must be always resisting; sin left alone does not stay quiet but grows. Paul makes the duty perpetual and comprehensive: "having therefore these promises, dearly beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God" (2 Cor 7:1). Flesh and Spirit are locked in continual conflict (Gal 5:17), so there is no point at which a Christian may lay down his weapons. To neglect the work even briefly is to let sin regather strength. Mortification is thus the settled, daily posture of the whole Christian life.
content_detail:
Owen answers the natural wish to be done with the fight. Some suppose mortification belongs to conversion's first struggles, or to old age, or to unusually holy people. Owen replies that Scripture lays it on all believers, at all times, as long as sin indwells, which is all their days. The premise is that indwelling sin is never eradicated in this life and never idle; it is a standing enemy within.

First Peter 2:11 frames the Christian's whole earthly existence as a campaign: "abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul." The lusts are combatants; they do not negotiate or retire. Galatians 5:17 states the standing opposition: "the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh... so that ye cannot do the things that ye would," a conflict that persists as long as both principles remain. Since the flesh will not cease its war, the believer cannot cease his resistance without loss.

Second Corinthians 7:1 supplies the positive duty and its horizon: "let us cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God." Owen notes the sweep ("all filthiness," of body and mind alike) and the direction ("perfecting holiness," a work never finished this side of glory). The cleansing is ongoing and total in its aim. From these texts Owen concludes that mortification is a duty of constancy, to be pursued daily, in prosperity and adversity, in youth and age, in the strongest as in the weakest saint. He warns that vigor abandoned is quickly regained by sin; a lust unopposed for a day gathers force. There is no discharge in this war until death; the believer who would live must be, without intermission, putting sin to death.

source_work: Owen — Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers (1656)
title: The Law of Sin: The Nature and Seat of Indwelling Corruption (Romans 7)
content_summary: In his companion treatise Owen examines the "indwelling sin" that mortification opposes. Paul calls it "a law in my members, warring against the law of my mind" (Rom 7:23), sin as a law, an inward principle with the force of a rule, constantly inclining and impelling toward evil. It "dwelleth" in the believer (7:20), a settled resident, not an occasional visitor; "in me (that is, in my flesh) dwelleth no good thing" (7:18). Its seat is the whole soul, but chiefly the heart and mind, so that even the renewed man finds "evil is present with me" when he "would do good" (7:21). Owen's point is that sin remaining in believers is not weak or dormant but an active, effectual power with real strength and inclination. Understanding sin as an indwelling law explains why the conflict is so constant and why mortification must be pursued with such seriousness.
content_detail:
Owen's second treatise anatomizes the enemy. Its title text is Romans 7, where Paul, describing the believer's experience, speaks of "sin that dwelleth in me" (7:17, 20) and "another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind, and bringing me into captivity to the law of sin which is in my members" (7:23). Owen builds his doctrine on the word "law." Sin remaining in the regenerate is not a mere privation or a spent force; it has the nature of a law, an inward principle that habitually inclines, directs, and urges the soul toward evil, with a kind of authority and constancy, as a law commands.

He stresses its indwelling permanence: it "dwelleth" in the believer, a fixed inhabitant with a claim upon the house, not a passing intruder. Hence Paul's "when I would do good, evil is present with me" (7:21) and "in me (that is, in my flesh) dwelleth no good thing" (7:18): the good is willed, yet corruption is always at hand, resident and ready. Owen locates sin's seat not in the body alone but in the whole soul, and chiefly in the heart, the seat of the affections and the spring of action, and in the mind, which sin darkens and bends.

The pastoral force is realism. Owen writes to disabuse believers of the notion that indwelling sin, once subdued at conversion, becomes a slight or sleeping thing. It is, he insists, a powerful, living, effectual principle, with strength and readiness always disproportionate to what the careless suppose. Recognizing sin as an indwelling law (permanent, active, and forceful) is the necessary foundation for taking mortification as seriously as Owen does. A man who underestimates the enemy will never watch or fight as he must. The captivity Paul confesses (7:23) is not the last word for the believer, but it measures the strength of the foe that grace must daily overcome.

source_work: Owen — Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers (1656)
title: Deceit and the Cry of the Wretched Man (Romans 7:24)
content_summary: Owen gives close attention to sin's deceitfulness, its way of working by stealth rather than open assault. It "beguiles," drawing the mind off watch, filling it with reasonings and pretenses until the affections are entangled and consent is gained: "sin... deceived me, and by it slew me" (Rom 7:11). Because a man may be hardened "through the deceitfulness of sin" (Heb 3:13), the believer must suspect its subtlety and not merely its strength. This deep, resident corruption wrings from Paul the anguished cry, "O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?" (Rom 7:24), the honest groan of a saint who feels sin's weight. Yet the cry does not end in despair: "I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord" (7:25). Deliverance is real, but it comes through Christ, and the very sense of wretchedness is a mark of spiritual life, not its absence.
content_detail:
Alongside sin's power, Owen dwells on its deceit, which he thinks even more dangerous because it works unseen. Romans 7:11 gives the pattern: "sin, taking occasion by the commandment, deceived me, and by it slew me." Sin rarely wins by frontal assault on a watchful conscience; it wins by beguiling, drawing the mind off duty, engrossing it with other things, presenting sin under fair pretenses, plying the affections with reasonings until consent is quietly secured and the act follows almost before it is resolved. Owen traces this deceit especially through the mind and the affections: the mind is diverted and darkened, the affections are entangled, and the will is at last drawn along.

Hebrews 3:13 supplies the warning Owen presses on every believer: exhort one another daily, "lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin." Sin's aim is not merely a single fall but the gradual hardening of the heart, and it reaches that end by a thousand small deceptions. Therefore the Christian must distrust indwelling sin's subtlety as much as its force, keeping conscience tender and the heart on guard.

The felt result of living with such a residing, deceiving enemy is the cry of Romans 7:24: "O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?" Owen reads this as the genuine voice of a believer, not a lament of despair but the honest groan of one who feels the burden of remaining corruption and longs to be free of it. Crucially, it is a mark of spiritual life: only the regenerate feel sin as this kind of wretchedness. And it does not terminate in the groan. The very next words turn to relief and hope: "I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord" (7:25). Deliverance is certain, but it is Christ's gift, not the fruit of the sinner's own strength, which is exactly why mortification must be carried on in dependence upon him.

source_work: Owen — Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers (1656)
title: Set Faith on Christ: Owen's Directions for Mortifying a Particular Lust
content_summary: Owen closes with concrete counsel for the believer battling a specific besetting sin. He calls first for radical dealing, the spirit of Christ's "if thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out" (Matt 5:29): spare nothing that feeds the lust. He directs the sinner to load his conscience with the guilt, danger, and evil of the sin until it is truly felt; to cut off its occasions and provisions; to rise against its first motions; and to long and pray for deliverance. But the decisive direction is evangelical: "set faith at work on Christ for the killing of thy sin." No preparatory work of humbling can itself slay a lust; that comes only by faith drawing power from the crucified and risen Christ, "mortify... your members" (Col 3:5) being accomplished "through the Spirit" (Rom 8:13). Duty and directions prepare the ground; Christ alone gives the deathblow.
content_detail:
Having laid the foundations, Owen turns intensely practical, addressing the believer troubled by some particular lust that keeps its hold. His directions move in two stages: preparatory work that brings the soul to a right frame, and the decisive act of faith that actually kills.

The preparatory directions are searching. Take the radical stance of Matthew 5:29, "if thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out, and cast it from thee," sparing nothing, however dear, that gives the sin strength. Get a clear and abiding sense of the guilt, danger, and evil of the sin, loading the conscience with it so that it is felt, not merely acknowledged. Consider the sin's particular symptoms and inroads. Cut off its occasions, advantages, and provisions (cf. Rom 13:14, "make not provision for the flesh"). Rise with speed against its first stirrings, before they gather force. Meditate on God's greatness and one's own vileness until the heart is humbled, and stir up longing and prayer for deliverance. These, Owen says, bring the soul to the ground on which sin may be slain, but they do not of themselves slay it.

The decisive direction is evangelical, and Owen is emphatic that all the foregoing is preparatory to it: "set faith at work on Christ for the killing of thy sin. His blood is the great sovereign remedy for sin-sick souls. Live in this, and thou wilt die a conqueror." Faith looks to the crucified Christ for the guilt of the sin and to the risen Christ for power against it, expecting from him, by his Spirit, the actual mortifying stroke. Thus Colossians 3:5, "mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth," is obeyed only as Romans 8:13's "through the Spirit" is honored, and only as Galatians 6:14's being "crucified unto the world" by the cross of Christ is made experiential. Owen's whole practical method refuses both presumption and despair: the believer must labor with all diligence in the directions, yet the deathblow to sin is Christ's, received by faith.

source_work: Stott on the person and claims of Christ
title: The Claims of Christ: His Self-Witness and Implicit Deity
content_summary: Basic Christianity begins with the person of Christ, and Stott argues that the central issue is Jesus' own self-witness. Though Jesus seldom stated his deity in bald propositions, his words and bearing are saturated with implicit and explicit claims that only God could rightly make. He set himself at the center of his message, forgave sins as one wronged by every sin (Mrk.2.5), and made himself the sole way to the Father: 'I am the way, and the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me' (Jhn.14.6). Most startling are his claims to eternal, divine existence — 'before Abraham was, I am' (Jhn.8.58) — and to unity with the Father: 'I and the Father are one' (Jhn.10.30). Both provoked attempts to stone him for blasphemy. Stott presses the reader to weigh these claims honestly, for they force a verdict.
content_detail:
Stott opens his case for Christianity not with argument about God in the abstract but with the concrete figure of Jesus, and specifically with his self-understanding. The reader, he says, must begin by facing what Jesus claimed. Some of the claims are explicit; many are implicit in the way he spoke and acted, which is in some ways more compelling because less self-conscious.

Jesus placed himself at the center of everything. He called people to himself, promising rest to the weary and making allegiance to him the hinge of human destiny. He assumed the authority to forgive sins — not merely sins committed against himself, but sins as such, as when he told the paralytic, 'Son, your sins are forgiven' (Mrk.2.5), prompting the scribes rightly to ask who but God can forgive sins. He claimed to be humanity's only mediator with God: 'no one comes to the Father except through me' (Jhn.14.6).

Most direct of all are his claims to a divine nature. To hostile questioners he said, 'before Abraham was, I am' (Jhn.8.58), applying to himself the timeless self-designation of God and provoking them to pick up stones. He declared, 'I and the Father are one' (Jhn.10.30), and again they moved to stone him for making himself God. Stott's point is that these claims cannot be filed away as the sayings of a great moral teacher. A merely good teacher does not talk this way about himself. The claims force the classic alternative that Stott, like others, presses: a man who says such things is either deceiving us, or deluded, or telling the truth — a liar, a lunatic, or the Lord he claimed to be. The comfortable option of 'great teacher and nothing more' is precisely the one Jesus' own words rule out, and the rest of the book unfolds from how the reader answers this question.

source_work: Stott on the person and claims of Christ
title: The Character and Resurrection of Christ as Evidence
content_summary: Claims alone prove nothing; Stott asks whether Jesus' claims are corroborated. He points to two lines of evidence: Jesus' character and his resurrection. The character of Jesus is startlingly consistent with his claims — a life of such moral perfection that he could challenge his enemies, 'which one of you convicts me of sin?' (Jhn.8.46), and those closest to him testified he 'committed no sin' (1Pe.2.22). A deluded or dishonest man does not display such humility, integrity, and love. The decisive corroboration is the resurrection. Stott treats it as a historical event on which everything turns: 'if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain' (1Co.15.14). The empty tomb, the transformed disciples, and the birth of the church are, he argues, best explained by the fact that God raised Jesus from the dead.
content_detail:
Having set out Christ's claims, Stott turns to the question of their credibility. Anyone can make grand assertions; the issue is whether the evidence supports them. He offers two principal witnesses: the character of Jesus and his resurrection from the dead.

First, character. Stott argues that the moral portrait of Jesus in the Gospels is impossible to reconcile with the theory that he was either a liar or a deluded fanatic. His teaching set the highest ethical standard the world has known, and he embodied it. He combined qualities rarely found together — strength and gentleness, authority and humility. Above all, he displayed no consciousness of personal sin, no confession, no sense of needing forgiveness, even while calling everyone else to repent. He could openly challenge his opponents, 'which one of you convicts me of sin?' (Jhn.8.46), and those who lived beside him concluded that he 'committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth' (1Pe.2.22). Such sinless self-possession fits the claims of one who is more than a man.

Second, and decisively, the resurrection. Stott presents it as a matter of historical evidence, not mere piety, and stakes the whole of Christianity upon it. Paul himself did so: 'if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain' (1Co.15.14). Stott weighs the data — the sealed and guarded tomb found empty, the failure of anyone to produce the body, the many appearances to witnesses who could be cross-examined, and the sudden transformation of demoralized disciples into fearless heralds willing to die for their testimony. The birth and explosive growth of the church, centered from the first on the claim that God 'raised him up' (Act.2.24), demand an adequate cause. Stott concludes that the resurrection is the best explanation of the facts, and that in raising Jesus God set his seal on his Son's astonishing claims.

source_work: Stott on the person and claims of Christ
title: The Fact and Nature of Sin: Self-Centredness That Separates from God
content_summary: Having established who Christ is, Stott turns to human need, for the gospel is good news only to those who know their plight. He treats sin as a universal fact and a personal condition, not merely a catalog of misdeeds. Every person is implicated: 'all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God' (Rom.3.23). Sin's essence is self-centredness — the dethroning of God and the enthroning of self — and its root is the heart, from which come evil thoughts and deeds (Mrk.7.21). The heart itself is 'deceitful above all things' (Jer.17.9), so we habitually underestimate our condition. The gravest consequence is relational: sin separates us from God. 'Your iniquities have made a separation between you and your God' (Isa.59.2). Stott insists this diagnosis is not pessimism but realism, and that only those who feel the disease will seek the cure.
content_detail:
The second main section of Basic Christianity moves from Christ's person to humanity's need. Stott argues that we cannot appreciate the remedy until we have felt the disease, and so he presses an honest diagnosis of sin. He resists both the modern denial that sin exists and the reduction of sin to isolated bad deeds. Sin is first a universal fact: Scripture's verdict falls on everyone without exception — 'all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God' (Rom.3.23). No one may exempt themselves; the standard is God's own glory, and all fall short of it.

More importantly, Stott probes the nature of sin. Its essence is not merely breaking rules but self-centredness — the reversal of the created order in which God should be at the center and self in orbit around him. In sin, self usurps the throne that belongs to God. This is why Jesus located sin in the heart rather than in circumstances: 'from within, out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts' — and he lists a grim catalog of what the heart produces (Mrk.7.21). The problem is internal, not external; we are not basically good people spoiled by a bad environment but people whose very inclinations are disordered. Jeremiah's diagnosis stands: 'the heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick' (Jer.17.9) — so deceitful that it hides its own condition from us, and we consistently think better of ourselves than the truth warrants.

The most serious consequence of sin, in Stott's account, is neither guilt-feelings nor social harm but separation from God. 'Your iniquities have made a separation between you and your God, and your sins have hidden his face from you' (Isa.59.2). Sin ruptures the relationship for which we were made, leaving us estranged and under judgment. This, Stott says, is the predicament the gospel addresses. His purpose is not to depress the reader but to be truthful, for only those who recognize their lost condition will seek and value a Savior.

source_work: Stott on the person and claims of Christ
title: The Work of Christ: Bearing Our Sin in Our Place
content_summary: How does Christ's death meet our need? Stott's answer is substitution: Christ bore our sins in our place. He came not merely as teacher or example but as Savior, and the Savior deals with sin by taking it upon himself. Peter states it plainly: Christ 'himself bore our sins in his body on the tree' (1Pe.2.24) and 'suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God' (1Pe.3.18). Paul reaches the same center: 'for our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God' (2Co.5.21). The sinless one was identified with our sin so that we might be identified with his righteousness. This great exchange, foreshadowed in Isaiah's Suffering Servant on whom the LORD laid our iniquity (Isa.53.6), is for Stott the heart of what the cross accomplished.
content_detail:
At the heart of Basic Christianity stands the cross, and Stott interprets it in terms of substitution: Christ died in our place, bearing the sin and its consequences that were ours.
