He is emphatic that Jesus did not come merely to teach or to inspire but to save, and that salvation required him to deal with the sin that separates us from God. The only way to remove that barrier was for Christ to bear it himself.

Stott gathers the New Testament's witness. Peter writes that Christ 'himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness' (1Pe.2.24) — a deliberate echo of Isaiah 53, presenting Christ as the sin-bearer. Again Peter says he 'suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God' (1Pe.3.18): the innocent in the place of the guilty, with reconciliation as the goal. Most striking is Paul's formulation of the exchange: 'for our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God' (2Co.5.21). Stott handles this carefully. Christ was personally sinless — he 'knew no sin' — yet God treated him as sin for us, identifying him with our guilt so completely that its penalty fell on him; and in return the righteousness of God becomes ours in him.

Stott traces this pattern back to Isaiah's Suffering Servant, on whom 'the LORD has laid the iniquity of us all' (Isa.53.6), showing that the New Testament reads the cross through that prophecy. The result is a divine exchange at the center of the gospel: our sin transferred to Christ, his righteousness credited to us. This, Stott insists, is not an arbitrary arrangement but the costly means by which a holy God can justly forgive. What we could never do — remove our own guilt — Christ did on the cross, in our place. Only against this dark background of sin borne does the summons to respond make sense.

source_work: Stott on the person and claims of Christ
title: Counting the Cost: Repentance and Faith
content_summary: For Stott, the gospel demands a response, and that response is costly. He warns against a cheap Christianity that wants the benefits of Christ without submission to his lordship. To become a Christian is to repent and believe — to turn decisively from sin and self-rule and to trust and follow Christ as Lord. Jesus never concealed the cost: 'if anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me' (Mrk.8.34). Discipleship means the abdication of self and the enthronement of Christ. Faith is not mere intellectual assent but wholehearted commitment, confessed openly: 'if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved' (Rom.10.9). Stott urges the seeker to count the cost honestly, for Christ asks for nothing less than everything.
content_detail:
In the final section, Basic Christianity turns from information to decision. Stott insists that Christianity is not a set of ideas to be admired but a Person to be received, and that receiving him carries a real cost that must be weighed in advance. He is sharply critical of any presentation that offers forgiveness and heaven while quietly omitting repentance and the lordship of Christ. To respond to the gospel is to repent and to believe — the two are inseparable.

Repentance, Stott explains, is more than regret; it is a deliberate turning away from everything known to be wrong — from sins, from self-centredness, and from the right to run one's own life. It touches the will, not merely the emotions. Faith is its positive counterpart: a personal trust in Christ that commits the whole person to him. Stott is careful to distinguish saving faith from bare intellectual assent; even the demons believe that God exists. Real faith surrenders and follows.

Jesus himself set the terms without softening them: 'if anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me' (Mrk.8.34). Stott reads self-denial as the dethroning of self and cross-bearing as a daily readiness to die to one's own will in order to obey Christ. Following is the ongoing obedience that flows from that surrender. Because Christ is Lord, the response he requires is nothing partial; he claims the whole of life. Faith must also be public: Paul makes open confession part of the response — 'if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved' (Rom.10.9). Stott therefore urges the reader to face the cost soberly, not to be deterred by it but to embrace it clear-eyed, since what Christ offers infinitely outweighs what he asks us to surrender.

source_work: Stott on the person and claims of Christ
title: Reaching a Decision: Opening the Door and Receiving Christ
content_summary: Stott closes with the summons to a definite decision. Christianity, he argues, cannot remain a matter of drifting interest; at some point the seeker must actively receive Christ. He fastens on the image of Christ standing at the door: 'behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in' (Rev.3.20). Christ will not force an entrance; the handle is on the inside. Salvation becomes personal when the individual opens the door and welcomes him. John states the same truth as receiving: 'to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God' (Jhn.1.12). Stott stresses that this step, though it may be quiet, is decisive, can be made in a prayer of surrender, and issues in a new relationship and the assurance of belonging to Christ.
content_detail:
Stott ends Basic Christianity by pressing for an actual decision, since a book about Christ that produced only admiration would have failed. Faith, he argues, must become personal and definite; the seeker must move from considering Christ to receiving him. He grants that the manner may vary — for some a memorable crisis, for others a quiet and gradual step — but a real transaction of the will is required either way.

His governing image is drawn from the risen Christ's words to the church at Laodicea: 'behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me' (Rev.3.20). Stott draws out its logic with care. Christ has come and taken the initiative; he stands, he knocks, he speaks. But he does not break the door down. The decision to open lies with the individual, and the handle, so to speak, is on the inside. To become a Christian is consciously to open the door and welcome Christ as Savior and Lord into the center of one's life.

The Gospel of John describes the same act as receiving: 'to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God' (Jhn.1.12). Believing and receiving are two sides of one response, and the outcome is a new status — adoption into God's family. Stott suggests that the seeker may make this response through a simple prayer of penitence and surrender, inviting Christ in. He is realistic about the cost already counted, and equally clear about the result: a personal relationship with the living Christ and the beginnings of assurance, grounded not on shifting feelings but on Christ's own promise to come in to all who open the door. The book thus ends not with an argument but with an appeal to decide, echoing the summons to confess Jesus as Lord (Rom.10.9).

source_work: Stott on Acts and the work of the Spirit
title: The Spirit and the Worldwide Witness: Acts 1:8 as the Programme of the Church
content_summary: Stott takes Acts 1:8 as the key that unlocks the whole book. The apostles' question about restoring the kingdom to Israel is redirected: they are not to speculate about dates or a nationalist kingdom but to receive power from the Holy Spirit and become witnesses. The verse is at once a promise and a table of contents -- 'Jerusalem, all Judea and Samaria, and the ends of the earth' maps the very expansion Luke will narrate. Stott underlines that the Spirit is given primarily for mission, not private enrichment: the power promised is power to witness to Christ. The church is thus, by definition, a Spirit-empowered missionary community, and the same commission still defines its task. Pentecost, when it comes, will be the equipping for exactly this worldwide testimony.
content_detail:
Stott gives Acts 1:8 a pivotal place, calling it in effect the text of which the rest of Acts is the exposition. The setting is the risen Christ's final conversation with the apostles, and it opens with their question about whether he will now 'restore the kingdom to Israel' (1:6). Stott reads Jesus' reply as a gentle but firm correction of three assumptions embedded in that question. Their preoccupation with the timing of the end is set aside: it is not for them to know 'times or seasons.' Their nationalist and political conception of the kingdom is quietly redirected toward a spiritual, worldwide reign advanced by witness. And their passivity as mere spectators of a restored Israel is replaced by an active commission.

The positive content is the promise of power and the definition of a task. 'You will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you.' Stott is careful about the purpose of this power: it is not primarily for personal ecstasy, moral transformation, or private blessing, but for witness -- 'you will be my witnesses.' The Spirit and mission are bound together; the church receives the Spirit in order to testify to Christ.

Stott also reads the geography of the verse as the deliberate outline of the book. The gospel will move out in widening circles: 'in Jerusalem' (chapters 1-7), 'in all Judea and Samaria' (chapters 8-12), and 'to the end of the earth' (chapters 13-28), reaching at last to Rome, the empire's centre. The programme is centrifugal and universal, breaking every barrier of race and region.

From this Stott draws his large thesis about Acts and about the church: the people of God are essentially a missionary people, constituted and empowered by the Spirit for the task of world evangelization. The command was given to the apostles first, but Stott insists the underlying mandate continues; the church that stops witnessing has forgotten why the Spirit was given. Pentecost, narrated in the next chapter, is precisely the fulfilment of this promise -- the equipping of the church for its worldwide witness.

source_work: Stott on Acts and the work of the Spirit
title: Pentecost: The Spirit Poured Out and the Last Days Begun
content_summary: Stott presents Pentecost as a unique, unrepeatable event in salvation history, comparable to the incarnation and resurrection: the once-for-all inauguration of the age of the Spirit. When the disciples are 'filled with the Holy Spirit' and speak in other tongues (2:4), the many languages are a sign that the gospel is for every nation -- a reversal of Babel's scattering. In his sermon Peter interprets the outpouring by Joel: this is the promised deluge of the Spirit 'in the last days,' now poured out not on a chosen few but on all flesh -- sons and daughters, young and old, slave and free (2:17). Stott thus reads Pentecost christologically and eschatologically: the exalted Jesus has poured out the Spirit, and the new age has dawned, though the event itself belongs to the foundation of the church, not to normal repeated experience.
content_detail:
Stott interprets the day of Pentecost as a landmark event in the history of salvation, and he insists on its uniqueness. Just as the incarnation and the resurrection happened once and cannot be repeated, so Pentecost was the once-for-all inauguration of the era of the Spirit -- the moment the ascended Christ poured out on his church the Spirit he had promised. The dramatic phenomena, the sound like a rushing wind and the tongues as of fire, are signs marking this decisive beginning.

Of the speaking 'in other tongues' (2:4), Stott takes the plain sense of the narrative: the disciples spoke real, recognizable human languages, so that the international crowd each heard the mighty works of God in their own tongue. He draws out the theological symbolism: whereas at Babel human languages were confused and the nations scattered, at Pentecost the language barrier is momentarily overcome, signalling that the gospel is for all peoples and that God is gathering a worldwide church. The gift is a sign of the universality of the good news.

The heart of Stott's exposition is Peter's interpretation of the event through the prophecy of Joel (2:16-21). Peter declares, 'this is what was uttered through the prophet Joel' -- the promised outpouring of the Spirit 'in the last days.' Stott stresses two things about this. First, the phrase 'the last days' means the new age has actually begun; the church lives in the era of fulfilment inaugurated by the Spirit's coming. Second, the outpouring is strikingly democratic and universal: no longer reserved for prophets, priests, and kings, the Spirit now comes upon 'all flesh' -- sons and daughters, young and old, male and female, slave and free (2:17-18). What in the Old Testament was occasional and selective becomes, in the new age, the common possession of the whole people of God.

Stott also notes the christological climax of Peter's sermon: it is the crucified, risen, and exalted Jesus who, having received the Spirit from the Father, has 'poured out this that you yourselves see and hear' (2:33). Pentecost is thus Christ's own act. For Stott it stands as the foundational, non-repeatable birth of the Spirit-filled church, even as the fullness it inaugurates remains the church's continuing possession.

source_work: Stott on Acts and the work of the Spirit
title: Repent, Be Baptized, Receive the Spirit: The Norm of Christian Initiation
content_summary: When the convicted crowd asks what to do, Peter's reply (2:38) gives Stott the normal pattern of Christian beginnings: repentance and faith, expressed in baptism, issuing in the forgiveness of sins and the gift of the Holy Spirit. Crucially, Stott insists these belong together as facets of one initiation, not as a first and then a separate, later second blessing. The gift of the Spirit is promised to every penitent believer, not to a spiritual elite. And the promise is expansive: 'for you and for your children and for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself' (2:39) -- reaching across generations and, Stott notes, already hinting at the Gentiles. This text, not the exceptional cases later in Acts, is Stott's baseline for what conversion normally includes.
content_detail:
For Stott, Peter's answer to the Pentecost crowd is the theological centre of gravity for the doctrine of Christian initiation, and he returns to it repeatedly. Cut to the heart, the hearers ask, 'What shall we do?' Peter replies, 'Repent and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit' (2:38). Stott reads this as setting out the normal ingredients of becoming a Christian, bound together as parts of one whole rather than strung out as separate stages. Repentance and the faith it implies are the inward turning; baptism is its outward expression and seal; forgiveness of sins is the blessing received; and the gift of the Holy Spirit is the crowning endowment. All four belong to Christian beginnings.

Stott makes two points he regards as decisive against a 'second-blessing' theology. First, the gift of the Spirit here is promised to all who repent and are baptized, not to a special class of Christians who go on to some further experience. It is the birthright of every believer, integral to conversion-initiation itself. Second, there is no interval or second condition interposed between believing and receiving the Spirit; the Spirit is part of the initial package, not a later supplement to be sought by those already converted.

The reach of the promise is, for Stott, equally striking. 'The promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself' (2:39). Stott notes the widening scope: it spans generations ('your children'), and it extends to 'all who are far off' -- a phrase that, in the light of the rest of Acts, already anticipates the inclusion of the Gentiles. And the whole rests on divine initiative: it is granted to 'everyone whom the Lord our God calls,' so that the gift is grounded in God's own summoning grace, not in human attainment.

Stott therefore treats Acts 2:38-39, rather than the irregular episodes that follow in Samaria, Caesarea, and Ephesus, as the norm. Those later cases are, in his reading, exceptional and transitional; this is the pattern -- repentance, baptism, forgiveness, and the gift of the Spirit received together by everyone God calls.

source_work: Stott on Acts and the work of the Spirit
title: The Samaritan Delay: Why the Spirit Came Through the Apostles
content_summary: The Samaritan believers present the famous anomaly: they believe Philip's preaching and are baptized, yet the Spirit does not fall on them until Peter and John come down and lay hands on them (8:15-17). Stott resists using this as a proof text for a routine two-stage Christian experience. He reads it instead as a deliberate, exceptional act of God suited to a unique moment in the mission's advance. Given the old, bitter Jew-Samaritan schism, God withheld the Spirit until the Jerusalem apostles could be present, so that the birth of the Samaritan church would be visibly one with the mother church and no rival, schismatic Christianity could arise. The delay, Stott argues, concerns church unity at a hinge point in Acts, not a template requiring every believer to seek the Spirit as a distinct second step.
content_detail:
The conversion of the Samaritans in Acts 8 poses what Stott frankly acknowledges is a genuine difficulty for any tidy doctrine of initiation. Philip preaches Christ in Samaria; the people believe and are baptized; and yet, unusually, the Holy Spirit does not come upon them at that point. Only when the apostles Peter and John travel down from Jerusalem, pray, and lay hands on them do the Samaritans receive the Spirit (8:15-17). The narrative openly notes that 'the Spirit had not yet fallen on any of them' (8:16).

Stott's chief concern is to interpret this rightly rather than to let it overturn the norm of Acts 2:38. He rejects the use of the episode as a proof text for the doctrine that Spirit-reception is normally a distinct second stage following conversion. Two features tell against generalizing from it: it is presented as an exception, precisely because it is out of the ordinary; and it belongs to a strategic moment in the geographical advance charted in Acts 1:8, the gospel's first crossing of a major ethnic boundary from Jews to Samaritans.

The explanation Stott favours turns on the long and bitter hostility between Jews and Samaritans. Had the Samaritan believers received the Spirit independently, through Philip alone and apart from the Jerusalem apostles, there was a real danger that a separate, rival Samaritan church would spring up, perpetuating the old schism inside the body of Christ. So, on Stott's reading, God sovereignly delayed the gift until the leaders of the mother church could be present, lay on hands, and thereby visibly incorporate the new Samaritan believers into the one apostolic church. The withholding served the unity of the church at a decisive turning point; it demonstrated that there is one people of God, not two.

The strange episode with Simon the sorcerer, who tries to buy the power to confer the Spirit (8:18-24), fits this reading: it shows how easily spiritual gifts could be misunderstood and abused, and it underscores that the Spirit is God's gift, not a commodity. For Stott, then, Acts 8 is a transitional, unrepeatable event about the unity of the expanding church, not a paradigm requiring ordinary Christians to pursue a second blessing after conversion.

source_work: Stott on Acts and the work of the Spirit
title: The Gentile Pentecost: The Spirit Falls at Cornelius' House
content_summary: At Cornelius' house the Spirit interrupts Peter mid-sermon and falls on the Gentile listeners (10:44), and the circumcised believers who came with him are 'astonished' that the gift is poured out even on Gentiles (10:45). Stott calls this the Gentile Pentecost: God's own dramatic verdict that the uncircumcised are accepted on precisely the same terms as Jews. The sequence is striking -- the Spirit comes before baptism and without any laying on of hands -- because God is settling a disputed question by sovereign action, overturning Peter's inherited scruples and pre-empting any demand that Gentiles first become Jews. For Stott the point is not a paradigm of how individuals today receive the Spirit, but a turning point in redemptive history: the door of faith is thrown open to the nations, and the church must recognize what God has done.
content_detail:
Stott regards the Cornelius episode as one of the great watersheds of Acts, the moment the gospel decisively breaks the barrier between Jew and Gentile. The build-up is elaborate and deliberate: the double vision given to Cornelius and to Peter, Peter's rooftop lesson that he must call no person common or unclean, and his arrival at a Gentile household with the confession that 'God shows no partiality' (10:34). All of this prepares for the climactic act.

While Peter is still preaching, before he can even finish, 'the Holy Spirit fell on all who heard the word' (10:44). Stott highlights the reaction of 'the believers from among the circumcised' who had come with Peter: they were 'amazed' -- astonished, even scandalized -- that the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out 'even on the Gentiles' (10:45), for they heard them speaking in tongues and extolling God, just as had happened at the original Pentecost. Stott stresses this parallel, which is why he calls the event a 'Gentile Pentecost': God gave to these uncircumcised believers the identical gift he had given to the Jewish disciples at the beginning.

The order of events is, for Stott, the theological heart of the passage. The Spirit is given before baptism and without the laying on of hands -- an order different again from both Acts 2 and Acts 8. Stott's explanation is that God deliberately took the initiative out of human hands to settle a contested question by his own unmistakable action. By pouring out the Spirit on Gentiles as Gentiles, before any ritual and without their first becoming Jews, God demonstrated that he accepts them on exactly the same terms as Jewish believers -- by grace, through faith. This overturned Peter's own deep-seated scruples and left him only one conclusion: 'Can anyone withhold water for baptizing these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?' (10:47).

Stott notes that Peter later appeals to precisely this event to justify himself in Jerusalem, arguing that since 'God gave the same gift to them as he gave to us' (11:17), it was not for him to stand in God's way. So for Stott the episode is not a template for individual Spirit-reception today, with its unusual sequence, but a unique, epoch-making act in redemptive history: God himself flinging open the door of faith to the nations, and the church learning to recognize and accept what God has done.

source_work: Stott on Acts and the work of the Spirit
title: The Ephesian Twelve: Disciples of John Brought Up to Date
content_summary: Paul finds about twelve 'disciples' at Ephesus and asks whether they received the Spirit when they believed (19:2); they have not so much as heard that there is a Holy Spirit, and prove to know only John's baptism. Stott argues they were not yet Christians in the full new-covenant sense at all, but followers of John the Baptist stranded before Pentecost -- believers in the promise who had never received its fulfilment. Paul instructs them, baptizes them into the name of Jesus, lays hands on them, and the Spirit comes with tongues and prophecy (19:6). Stott therefore denies this supports a two-stage doctrine for ordinary Christians; it is the unique case of pre-Christian disciples being completed, their deficient initiation made good, so that they pass from Old-Covenant anticipation into full Christian faith and the gift of the Spirit.
content_detail:
The dozen 'disciples' Paul meets at Ephesus (Acts 19:1-7) are, for Stott, another case regularly pressed into service for a second-blessing theology, and again he argues the text will not bear that weight. Paul's opening question, 'Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?' (19:2), is sometimes read as though it distinguished receiving the Spirit from believing, as two separate steps. Stott counters that the more natural sense is coincident: did you receive the Spirit when (that is, at the point at which) you believed? The question expects that faith and the Spirit belong together, and Paul asks it precisely because something about these men seemed defective.

The defect quickly emerges. They reply that they have not even heard 'that there is a Holy Spirit,' and under questioning it appears they had received only 'John's baptism' (19:3). Stott concludes that they were not Christians in the full sense at all. They were, at best, disciples of John the Baptist -- people who had responded to John's call to repentance and his announcement of the coming One, but who had never come through into the new-covenant reality inaugurated at Pentecost. They stood, spiritually, on the far side of the great divide, holding to the promise without its fulfilment. The word 'disciples' here, Stott notes, need not mean Christian disciples; it describes their attachment to John.

Paul's response confirms this diagnosis. He does not treat them as believers seeking a second blessing; he completes their deficient initiation. He explains that John's was a baptism of repentance pointing forward to Jesus; on hearing this, they are baptized 'in the name of the Lord Jesus' -- Christian baptism proper -- and when Paul lays his hands on them, the Holy Spirit comes upon them and they speak in tongues and prophesy (19:5-6). In other words, they are brought at last from Old-Covenant anticipation into full Christian experience.

For Stott the lesson is the opposite of the two-stage reading. This is not a Christian's later reception of the Spirit; it is the belated, once-only regularizing of men who had never been properly Christian at all. Like the other 'irregular' episodes in Acts, it is transitional and exceptional, and it leaves untouched the norm of Acts 2:38, in which repentance, baptism, and the gift of the Spirit belong together at the very outset.

source_work: Stott on Acts and the work of the Spirit
title: One Baptism, Many Fillings: Spirit-Baptism as Initiation, Fullness as the Norm
content_summary: This cell states the central thesis of Stott's Baptism and Fullness. The 'baptism of the Spirit,' he argues, is not a second blessing for advanced Christians but the initial gift bestowed on every believer at conversion -- the one act by which, as Paul says, 'we were all baptized into one body' (1Co.12.13). It is therefore universal among Christians and, in that sense, unrepeatable. What Scripture then commands repeatedly is something different: 'be filled with the Spirit' (Eph.5.18), a present-tense, continuous imperative addressed to all. Stott's conclusion reframes the whole Pentecostal debate: the New Testament norm is not to seek a subsequent baptism one may still lack, but to go on being filled with the Spirit one has already received. Fullness, not a second baptism, is the abiding call, and it may be enjoyed and renewed many times.
content_detail:
This entry gathers the constructive argument of Stott's book Baptism and Fullness, which sets out to distinguish two things the popular teaching of a 'second blessing' had run together. Stott's central contention is a careful separation of terms: the baptism of the Spirit on one hand, and the fullness of the Spirit on the other.

Regarding the baptism of the Spirit, Stott argues from the New Testament usage that it is initiatory and universal, not a later, higher experience reserved for some Christians. His decisive text is 1 Corinthians 12:13: 'in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body.' He stresses every part of it. It is 'all' -- so Spirit-baptism is the common possession of every believer, not the privilege of an elite; the Corinthians, whom Paul is rebuking for their immaturity, are included. It is past tense, 'we were baptized' -- so it is something already true of them, tied to their conversion and incorporation into Christ's body, not a blessing still to be sought. On this reading, Spirit-baptism is simply another way of describing entry into new life in Christ; and if a person is in Christ at all, that person has the Spirit (Romans 8:9). It is therefore, like conversion, unrepeatable.

Regarding the fullness of the Spirit, Stott points to a different and repeated note in the New Testament. The great command is Ephesians 5:18: 'be filled with the Spirit.' He draws attention to the grammar. The verb is a plural imperative addressed to all Christians, so it is a command, not merely a privilege for the few. It is passive, 'be filled' -- fullness is God's work, to be received, not self-generated. And it is present continuous in force -- 'go on being filled' -- describing not a single crisis but an ongoing, renewable condition. Where baptism is once-for-all, filling is meant to be repeated and habitual; a Christian may be filled, and filled again.

Stott's pastoral conclusion reframes the whole 'second blessing' debate. The mistake, he argues, is to make baptism the ongoing quest and to divide the church into the Spirit-baptized 'haves' and the un-baptized 'have-nots.' The New Testament pattern is the reverse: the baptism is presupposed as belonging to all believers already, while the filling is the perpetual command and the proper ambition. Christians are not to seek a second baptism they supposedly lack, but continually to be filled with the Spirit they have received -- fullness, not a further baptism, being the abiding norm of the Christian life.

source_work: Stott on Acts and the work of the Spirit
title: The Fruit of the Spirit: Christlike Character as the Primary Evidence
content_summary: For Stott the true and primary evidence of the Spirit's fullness is not spectacular gifts but Christlike character -- the fruit of the Spirit (Gal.5.22). Paul sets this ninefold fruit against the works of the flesh, and Stott notes that it is singular ('fruit,' not 'fruits'): a single cluster of graces, headed by love, that the Spirit grows in everyone he indwells. Gifts can be counterfeited and can coexist with immaturity, but the fruit cannot be faked; it is the Spirit reproducing the likeness of Jesus. So when people ask how to tell whether someone is filled with the Spirit, Stott points not to tongues or ecstasy but to love, joy, peace, and self-control. This keeps the doctrine of the Spirit tethered to sanctification and to the imitation of Christ, guarding it against a merely sensational spirituality.
content_detail:
Having argued that fullness is the true norm of Spirit-filled living, Stott turns to the question of evidence: how is the fullness of the Spirit actually recognized? Much popular teaching answered by pointing to the more dramatic gifts, above all speaking in tongues, as the decisive sign. Stott's reply, developed in Baptism and Fullness, is to relocate the primary evidence from gifts to fruit, and his key text is Galatians 5:22-23.

Paul there contrasts two harvests. On one side stand 'the works of the flesh' -- a list of sins of sex, religion, society, and drink that betray unregenerate human nature. On the other stands 'the fruit of the Spirit': love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control. Stott makes a grammatical observation he regards as significant: Paul speaks of 'fruit' in the singular, not 'fruits.' The nine graces are not a menu from which the Spirit-filled select a few, but a single ripening cluster, an organic whole that the Spirit grows together in the believer -- and it is headed, deliberately, by love, which for Stott (as in 1 Corinthians 13) is the supreme and comprehensive Christian grace.

The force of preferring fruit to gifts, Stott argues, lies in what each can and cannot prove. Spiritual gifts, including tongues, can be counterfeited or imitated, and, as the Corinthian church painfully showed, they can coexist with carnality, jealousy, and immaturity; a person may be highly gifted and yet spiritually shallow. The fruit of the Spirit cannot be faked in the same way, because it is nothing less than the character of Christ himself being reproduced in the disciple. Love, joy, peace, and self-control are the Spirit's own likeness formed within, and they grow only where the Spirit is genuinely at work.

Stott's conclusion is therefore both a corrective and a pastoral reassurance. When someone asks how to tell whether a person -- or oneself -- is filled with the Spirit, the answer is not to look first for the sensational but to look for Christlikeness: is love growing? Is there joy, patience, gentleness, self-mastery? By tying the evidence of the Spirit's fullness to sanctification and the imitation of Christ, Stott guards the doctrine against a spirituality that prizes experience and power over holiness, and he restores the fruit of the Spirit to its place as the surest mark that the Spirit is filling a life.

source_work: Stott on Ephesians
title: Every Spiritual Blessing: Chosen in Christ Before Creation
content_summary: Stott opens his exposition with Paul's great outburst of praise to the God who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places. Stott notes that these blessings are already ours in Christ, not future prizes to be won but present possessions to be enjoyed. The first of them is election: God chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him. Stott handles this reverently, insisting that election is God's free and gracious choice, made before we existed and so owing nothing to our merit, and that its declared purpose is holiness, not licence. He traces the trinitarian structure of the passage, in which the Father chooses and predestines to adoption, the Son redeems by his blood, and the Spirit seals and guarantees the inheritance, all to the praise of God's glorious grace.
content_detail:
Stott treats the long opening sentence of Ephesians, a single sustained doxology in the Greek, as the fountainhead of the letter. Paul blesses God because God has first blessed us, and Stott draws out the sweep of the phrase every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ. He insists on three things about these blessings: they are comprehensive, embracing every spiritual good; they are located in Christ, so that to be joined to Christ is to possess them all; and they are already given, so that the Christian life is not a matter of acquiring blessings we lack but of grasping and enjoying what is already ours.

Stott then expounds election as the first and most foundational of these blessings. God chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world. He approaches the doctrine with care, aware of its difficulty, but refuses to explain it away. Election is God's own sovereign and gracious choice, made in eternity before we had done anything good or bad, and therefore resting entirely on his grace and not on any merit or foreseen worth in us. Stott stresses two guardrails Paul himself supplies. First, election is in Christ, never apart from him, so it is not a cold decree but a choice bound up with the Beloved. Second, its purpose is moral: God chose us that we should be holy and blameless before him. Far from encouraging carelessness, election summons to holiness, and any doctrine of election that leaves a person indifferent to sin has misunderstood it.

Stott then follows the trinitarian movement that structures the whole passage, noting how it falls into three stanzas, each closing on the refrain of praise to God's glory. The Father is the source, who chose us, predestined us to adoption as sons through Jesus Christ, and made known to us the mystery of his will. The Son is the sphere and agent of redemption; in him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of God's grace. The Spirit is the seal and guarantee; having believed, we were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, who is the down payment of our inheritance until we acquire full possession of it. Stott underlines that the recurring goal of the whole saving work is doxological, to the praise of the glory of God's grace. So the passage is not cold speculation about predestination but warm worship, tracing every blessing back to the free grace of the triune God and forward to his eternal praise.

source_work: Stott on Ephesians
title: From Death to Life: Saved by Grace Through Faith for Good Works
content_summary: Stott expounds this passage as one of the fullest statements of the gospel in Scripture, moving from the depth of our ruin to the height of God's grace. By nature we were dead in trespasses and sins, enslaved to the world, the flesh, and the devil, and by nature children of wrath. Against this dark background stands Paul's great 'but God,' rich in mercy, who made us alive together with Christ, raised us up, and seated us with him. Stott insists that salvation is by grace from first to last: it is by grace we have been saved, through faith, and this is not our own doing but the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast. Yet Stott is careful with the place of works: we are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which are the fruit of salvation, not its root.
content_detail:
Stott regards Ephesians 2:1-10 as a compact summary of the whole gospel, and he follows its movement from ruin to rescue. Paul begins with a devastating diagnosis of the human condition apart from Christ. We were dead in our trespasses and sins, and Stott stresses that this is spiritual death, a real inability and unresponsiveness toward God, not mere weakness or sickness. He notes the three enemies Paul names as the powers that held us captive: the world, whose course we followed; the flesh, whose passions and desires we obeyed; and the devil, the spirit now at work in the sons of disobedience. The verdict is that we were by nature children of wrath, under God's righteous displeasure by our very condition, not merely by occasional lapses.

Into this hopeless situation breaks Paul's great adversative, and Stott makes much of the two words but God. Everything turns on the divine initiative. God, being rich in mercy, out of the great love with which he loved us, acted while we were still dead. Stott draws out the three verbs by which Paul describes what God did in union with Christ: he made us alive together with Christ, raised us up with him, and seated us with him in the heavenly places. As Christ was raised and enthroned, so those joined to him share his resurrection life and exaltation even now. The motive throughout is grace, that in the coming ages God might show the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us.

Stott then expounds the classic statement of 2:8-9 with characteristic precision. For by grace you have been saved through faith. He identifies grace as the source and faith as the means, and insists that neither leaves any room for human boasting. Salvation is not our own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works. Stott is careful to say that even faith is not a meritorious contribution but the empty hand that receives; the whole of salvation, from beginning to end, is of God, precisely so that no one may boast.

Finally Stott addresses the place of good works, which Paul brings in at 2:10 without any contradiction of what he has just said. We are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand that we should walk in them. Stott resolves the apparent tension carefully: we are not saved by good works, but we are saved for them. Good works are not the ground of salvation but its goal and evidence, the fruit that grace inevitably produces. So the passage excludes both the pride that would earn salvation and the complacency that would live without obedience.

source_work: Stott on Ephesians
title: One New Humanity: The Dividing Wall Broken Down
content_summary: Stott sees here the theme that gives his exposition its title, the church as God's new society. Once the Gentiles were far off, without Christ, without hope and without God in the world, separated from Israel by the law and by deep hostility. But now in Christ Jesus those who were far off have been brought near by his blood. Stott stresses that Christ himself is our peace, who has made the two one and broken down the dividing wall of hostility between Jew and Gentile. By abolishing in his flesh the law of commandments, Christ created in himself one new humanity in place of the two, making peace, and reconciled both to God in one body through the cross. Stott draws the double reconciliation together: the cross reconciles us to God and to one another, forming a single new people, a holy temple where God dwells by his Spirit.
content_detail:
Stott treats this passage as the heart of the letter's teaching on the church, and he lets it define what he calls God's new society. Paul tells the Gentile readers to remember what they once were, and Stott draws out the bleak catalogue of their former condition: separated from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world. He notes the deep religious and racial division that ran through the ancient world, symbolized by the temple barrier that shut Gentiles out of the inner courts.

Against this Stott sets Paul's second great but now in 2:13. Those who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ. The instrument of reconciliation is the cross, and Stott stresses that both dimensions of estrangement are healed there. Paul declares that Christ himself is our peace, and Stott lingers on that personal statement: peace is not merely something Christ made but something Christ is, and to have him is to have peace both with God and with one another.

Stott then expounds the central affirmation that Christ has made the two groups one and has broken down the dividing wall of hostility. He explains that the barrier was the law with its commandments, which both condemned sinners and fenced Israel off from the nations. By abolishing this in his flesh, that is, by his death, Christ removed both the enmity between the two peoples and the enmity between them and God. Stott is careful with Paul's striking phrase in 2:15 that Christ's purpose was to create in himself one new man, or one new humanity, in place of the two, thus making peace. He underlines the newness of it: the result is not merely Gentiles absorbed into Judaism, nor Jews and Gentiles kept politely apart, but a single new race, a third entity, brought into being by the cross.

Stott then follows Paul's insistence that this horizontal reconciliation rests on a vertical one. Christ reconciled both to God in one body through the cross, thereby killing the hostility, and through him both now have access in one Spirit to the Father. Stott draws the conclusion Paul builds toward: the Gentiles are no longer strangers and aliens but fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ as the cornerstone. The whole structure grows into a holy temple in the Lord, a dwelling place for God by the Spirit. For Stott this is the glory of the new society: a reconciled community, Jew and Gentile made one, in which God himself now lives.

source_work: Stott on Ephesians
title: The Mystery Revealed: Gentiles Fellow Heirs in Christ
content_summary: Stott expounds Paul's account of the mystery entrusted to him, a truth once hidden but now revealed by the Spirit to God's apostles and prophets. Stott explains that in Paul's usage a mystery is not something mysterious and obscure but a secret purpose of God now openly disclosed. The content of this mystery is that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel. Stott stresses how revolutionary this was: not merely that Gentiles could be saved, but that they are incorporated on equal terms into one body with believing Jews. He notes Paul's sense of privilege in being made a minister of this gospel, and the grand purpose Paul assigns to it, that through the church the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known even to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places.
content_detail:
Stott presents this chapter as Paul's reflection on his own commission and on the astonishing truth he was called to proclaim. Paul describes himself as a prisoner for the sake of the Gentiles and speaks of the stewardship of God's grace given to him for them. At the centre stands what Paul repeatedly calls the mystery, and Stott is careful to define the word, since it can mislead. In the New Testament a mystery is not a truth that remains puzzling but a secret long hidden in the mind of God and now, in Christ, fully revealed. It was made known to Paul by revelation and disclosed to God's holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit.

Stott then states the content of the mystery as Paul gives it in 3:6: that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel. He draws out the force of the three compound words Paul coins, each emphasizing togetherness. The Gentiles are not second-class dependants or associate members; they are joint heirs of the same inheritance, joint members of the same body, and joint sharers in the same promise. Stott stresses how radical this was against the background of centuries of separation. The Old Testament had foreseen the blessing of the nations, but the full equality of Jew and Gentile in a single body was the new thing now revealed, and it is realized in the church.

Stott notes the deep humility with which Paul speaks of his part in this. He calls himself the very least of all the saints, yet to him this grace was given, to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ and to bring to light the administration of this mystery. Stott observes that Paul regards his ministry not as an achievement but as a gift of grace, and his sufferings for the Gentiles as their glory rather than their shame.

Finally Stott expounds the breathtaking purpose Paul assigns to the church in 3:10, that through the church the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places. He explains that the very existence of the church, a reconciled community of Jews and Gentiles made one in Christ, is itself a public demonstration to the unseen powers of the wisdom of God. God's eternal purpose, accomplished in Christ, is displayed on the stage of history through this new humanity. For Stott this lifts the doctrine of the church to a cosmic level: the reconciled people of God are the visible proof of God's manifold wisdom before the whole created order.

source_work: Stott on Ephesians
title: The Worthy Walk: Unity, the Gifts, and the New Self
content_summary: Stott marks Ephesians 4 as the turn from what God has done to how we must live, from the doctrine of the new society to its practical calling. Paul appeals to us to walk worthily of our calling, and Stott shows that this worthy walk begins with unity: eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, grounded in the sevenfold oneness of one body, one Spirit, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God. Yet unity is not uniformity, for the ascended Christ has given diverse gifts, apostles, prophets, evangelists, and pastors and teachers, to equip the saints for ministry and to build up the body until all attain to mature unity and the measure of the fullness of Christ. Stott then draws out the ethical demand: to put off the old self, corrupt and deceived, to be renewed in mind, and to put on the new self, created after God in righteousness and holiness.
content_detail:
Stott regards the beginning of chapter four as the great hinge of the letter, where doctrine passes into duty. The first three chapters have unfolded what God has done in creating one new humanity; now Paul appeals to his readers to walk in a manner worthy of their calling. Stott stresses that Christian conduct is always a response to Christian privilege; the indicative of grace grounds the imperative of obedience.

The first mark of the worthy walk, Stott observes, is unity. Paul urges believers to bear with one another in love and to be eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. Stott is careful here: this unity is not something we create but something the Spirit has already given, which we are called to guard and express. He points to the sevenfold basis Paul lays down, one body and one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, and shows how the whole is rooted in the oneness of the triune God.

Yet Stott insists that this unity is not a drab uniformity, for the same passage celebrates diversity. The ascended Christ, having led captivity captive, gave gifts to his people, and Paul lists them as gifted persons: apostles, prophets, evangelists, and pastors and teachers. Stott draws out the crucial purpose clause of 4:12: these ministers equip the saints for the work of ministry, so that the whole body, not merely a clerical few, builds itself up. The goal is corporate maturity, that we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to mature manhood and the fullness of Christ. Stott notes that this maturity includes doctrinal stability and growth in truth and love, until the body grows up into Christ its head.

Stott then turns to the ethical demand of 4:17-24, where Paul contrasts the old life of the Gentiles with the new life in Christ. The readers are no longer to walk as they once did, in the futility of their minds and the hardness of their hearts. Using the vivid imagery of changing clothes, Paul calls them to put off the old self, which belongs to their former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires, to be renewed in the spirit of their minds, and to put on the new self, created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness. Stott stresses the central place of the mind and the pattern of decisive renunciation and renewal: the old self is discarded, the new self deliberately put on. Holiness is not merely improving the old life but living out a new creation.

source_work: Stott on Ephesians
title: Walk in Love and Light, and Be Filled with the Spirit
content_summary: Stott expounds Paul's call to walk in love and light as the pattern of the new life. We are to be imitators of God as beloved children and to walk in love, and Stott points to the supreme model Paul gives: as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God. Christian love is cross-shaped, self-giving love. Then Paul turns to light: once we were darkness, but now we are light in the Lord, and we are to walk as children of light, having nothing to do with the unfruitful works of darkness but exposing them. Stott draws out the climactic command of 5:18, not to be drunk with wine but to be filled with the Spirit, contrasting the false stimulant with the true. The Spirit-filled life overflows in worship, thanksgiving, and mutual submission.
content_detail:
Stott continues to follow Paul's series of exhortations about the Christian walk, now gathered under the images of love and light. The section opens with the lofty summons to be imitators of God as beloved children. Stott notes the boldness of the command; it is grounded in the fact that we are God's dear children, and children naturally resemble and imitate their father. The specific likeness in view is love, and Paul at once supplies the pattern in 5:2: we are to walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God. Stott stresses that Christian love is defined by the cross; it is not sentiment but sacrifice, the self-giving that seeks the good of others at cost to oneself, modelled on Christ's own self-oblation.

Paul sets this walk of love against the sexual immorality, impurity, and greed that have no place among the saints, and Stott observes that such sins are incompatible with both love and the coming inheritance. This leads into the second image, that of light. Once you were darkness, Paul says, but now you are light in the Lord; walk as children of light. Stott draws out the completeness of the change: believers are not merely enlightened but are themselves light, and their conduct is to match their nature. The fruit of light is found in all that is good and right and true, and Paul calls them to take no part in the unfruitful works of darkness but rather to expose them, since light by its nature drives out darkness and makes things visible.

Stott then reaches the climactic command of the section in 5:18, and treats it as central to the whole passage: do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit. He draws out the deliberate contrast. Drunkenness is a false and destructive attempt to find release and stimulation; the fullness of the Spirit is the true and life-giving alternative. Stott notes that the command is in the present tense and addressed to all, so that being filled with the Spirit is not a once-for-all crisis reserved for a few but a continuous experience meant for every Christian, to go on being filled. He points to the results Paul lists, which flow from the same sentence: addressing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody to the Lord from the heart, giving thanks always for everything, and submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ. For Stott the Spirit-filled life is not chiefly about ecstatic experience but about a transformed common life marked by worship, gratitude, and humble mutual submission.

source_work: Stott on Ephesians
title: Marriage as the Picture of Christ and the Church
content_summary: Stott expounds Paul's teaching on marriage, which he sets within the wider principle of 5:21, submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ. Stott stresses that Christian marriage is patterned on the relationship between Christ and the church. Husbands are called to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, a costly, sacrificial, sanctifying love that seeks the beloved's highest good. Wives are called to respect and submit to their husbands as the church submits to Christ. Stott is careful to define headship not as domination but as loving responsibility modelled on Christ's self-sacrifice. He notes that Paul finally lifts the veil: the profound mystery of two becoming one flesh refers ultimately to Christ and the church, so that every true marriage is a living parable of the gospel union between the Saviour and his people.
content_detail:
Stott approaches this passage carefully, aware both of its importance and of the controversy surrounding it. He insists that the whole section on household relationships is governed by the heading in 5:21, be subject to one another out of reverence for Christ, so that mutual submission is the atmosphere in which the particular duties are set. Within that framework Paul addresses wives and husbands, and Stott reads the passage as elevating marriage by grounding it in the relationship between Christ and his church.

Stott takes up the call to wives first, to submit to their own husbands as to the Lord, since the husband is the head of the wife as Christ is the head of the church. He is at pains to strip the word head of any notion of tyranny or the wife's inferiority. Headship in the New Testament, he argues, is defined by the model of Christ, and Christ's headship over the church is expressed not in self-assertion but in self-sacrifice. So whatever submission means, it is the free response of respect within a relationship of love, not servile subjection, and it is offered as to the Lord.

The greater weight of Paul's charge, Stott observes, falls on husbands, who are commanded to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her. Stott dwells on the extraordinary standard this sets. The husband's love is to be sacrificial, like Christ's self-giving on the cross; it is to be purifying, seeking the wife's holiness as Christ sanctifies and cleanses the church; and it is to be caring, nourishing and cherishing her as a man cares for his own body. Stott notes that a husband who loves like this will pose no threat to his wife, and that such love is the true meaning of headship. Far from licensing male domination, Paul's teaching binds the husband to the most demanding love imaginable.

Finally Stott draws out the deepest point of the passage, that Paul is not merely using Christ and the church to illustrate marriage but is revealing that marriage itself was designed to illustrate Christ and the church. Quoting the creation ordinance that a man shall leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh, Paul declares this a profound mystery, and says that he is speaking about Christ and the church. Stott takes this to mean that the one-flesh union of husband and wife is a God-given parable of the saving union between Christ and his redeemed people. So Christian marriage is lifted to its highest dignity: every faithful, loving, self-giving marriage becomes a visible sign of the gospel itself.

source_work: Stott on Ephesians
title: The Armour of God and the Unseen Spiritual War
content_summary: Stott expounds the letter's closing summons to be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might, putting on the whole armour of God to stand against the schemes of the devil. Stott takes the reality of the spiritual conflict seriously: our struggle is not against flesh and blood, against human enemies, but against the rulers, the authorities, the cosmic powers of this present darkness, and the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places. Because the enemy is supernatural, the resources must be divine, and Stott works through the pieces of armour God supplies, the belt of truth, the breastplate of righteousness, the shoes of the gospel of peace, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit which is the word of God, all sustained by constant prayer. The Christian's calling is to stand firm in a strength that is not his own.
content_detail:
Stott treats the final major section of Ephesians as the fitting climax of a letter about God's new society, for the new humanity created by grace lives in a world contested by hostile spiritual powers. Paul's opening command, to be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might, sets the tone that Stott underlines throughout: the strength required is not the Christian's own but the Lord's.

Stott gives careful attention to Paul's analysis of the enemy in 6:11-12. Believers are to put on the whole armour of God so as to stand against the schemes of the devil, and Stott takes the devil's reality and craft seriously, refusing both the scepticism that dismisses him and the sensationalism that is preoccupied with him. Paul insists that our struggle is not against flesh and blood; Stott stresses that our real adversaries are not the human beings who oppose us but the unseen powers behind them, described as rulers, authorities, cosmic powers of this present darkness, and spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places. The conflict is supernatural, organized, and formidable.

Because the foe is spiritual, the armour must be spiritual too, and it is God's own armour, supplied by him. He works through the pieces Paul names, drawn from the equipment of a Roman soldier but filled with Christian meaning. The belt of truth speaks of integrity and the truth of the gospel; the breastplate of righteousness of a righteous life and standing; the shoes of the readiness given by the gospel of peace; the shield of faith with which the flaming darts of the evil one are quenched; the helmet of salvation; and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, the one offensive weapon in the list. Stott observes that most of the armour is defensive, fitting the repeated command simply to stand and to stand firm; the Christian's task is to hold the ground Christ has already won, not to gain a victory still in doubt.

Stott closes by noting that Paul does not regard the armour as complete without prayer. Praying at all times in the Spirit, with perseverance, is the atmosphere in which the whole armour is worn and the battle fought. He points out that Paul asks even for prayer for himself, that words may be given him to make known the mystery of the gospel boldly. For Stott the message of the passage is realistic and reassuring at once: the Christian faces a genuine and powerful spiritual enemy, but is armed by God and called simply to stand firm, strong in the Lord, and dependent through prayer on a strength that is his own.

source_work: Stott on Galatians
title: No Other Gospel: The Finality of the Apostolic Message
content_summary: Stott shows that Paul opens not with his customary thanksgiving but with astonishment and alarm, because the Galatians are deserting the God who called them and turning to a different gospel. Stott stresses that Paul's point is that there is really no other gospel at all; the rival message of the Judaizers, which adds circumcision and law-keeping to faith in Christ, is not an alternative version of the good news but a perversion that destroys it. So grave is the matter that Paul pronounces a solemn curse on anyone, even himself or an angel from heaven, who should preach a gospel other than the one they received. Stott presses the seriousness: the gospel is not human opinion open to revision but the fixed, God-given truth of salvation by grace, and to tamper with it is to imperil souls.
content_detail:
Stott draws attention to the abruptness of the letter's opening. Every other Pauline letter begins with thanksgiving, but here Paul is too disturbed to give thanks. He is astonished, and the tense suggests the defection is happening even as he writes: the Galatians are in the act of turning away. Stott is careful about the object of their desertion; Paul says they are deserting not merely a doctrine but the God who called them by the grace of Christ. To abandon the gospel of grace is to abandon the God of grace.

The heart of the passage is Paul's insistence that the message troubling the churches is not a legitimate variant of the gospel. Stott explains the situation: false teachers, commonly called Judaizers, were insisting that Gentile converts must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses in order to be true Christians, adding law-works to faith as a condition of acceptance with God. Paul will not allow this to be described as another gospel, because there is no other. Any message that adds human works to the finished work of Christ is not a different good news but a contradiction of the only good news, and Stott underlines that such an addition does not enrich the gospel but overthrows it.

Stott gives full weight to the double curse of 1:8-9. Paul says that if he himself, or even an angel from heaven, should preach a gospel contrary to the one the Galatians received, let him be accursed, and he repeats it for emphasis. Stott reads this not as intemperate anger but as a measure of what is at stake. Because the gospel is the way of salvation, to corrupt it is to endanger the eternal welfare of those who believe it; a false gospel cannot save. Moreover, Stott notes, Paul subordinates even apostolic and angelic authority to the gospel itself: the message is not validated by the messenger, but the messenger is judged by the message. The gospel is God's, received by revelation and not of human origin, and therefore it is fixed and final. No church, no apostle, no angel has the authority to change it. For Stott this establishes the theme of the whole letter: the defence of the one true gospel of justification by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone.

source_work: Stott on Galatians
title: Justified by Faith in Christ, Not by Works of the Law
content_summary: Stott reaches the doctrinal heart of the letter in Paul's statement that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ. Stott defines justification as a legal term: it is God's act of declaring a sinner righteous, of accepting and acquitting the guilty, not of making them morally good. The great question the verse settles is on what basis God accepts us, and Paul's answer is emphatic and exclusive. It is not by works of the law, not by anything we do, but through faith in Christ. Stott notes that Paul says this even of himself and Peter, Jews by birth who knew the law, yet who believed in Christ precisely in order to be justified by faith and not by works, since by works of the law no one will be justified.
content_detail:
Stott sees these verses, arising from Paul's confrontation with Peter at Antioch, as the doctrinal centre of Galatians, the clearest single statement of the truth the whole letter defends. Peter, under pressure from certain men, had withdrawn from table fellowship with Gentile believers, and Paul saw that his conduct was not in step with the truth of the gospel. The principle Paul draws out in response is justification by faith alone.

Stott is careful to define his terms, because the word justify is easily misunderstood. He insists that it is a legal or forensic term, drawn from the law court, and that its opposite is condemnation. To justify is not to make a person righteous in character but to declare a person righteous in status, to accept and acquit them before God. The doctrine of justification therefore answers the most fundamental of all questions: how can guilty sinners be accepted by a holy God?

Paul's answer, Stott stresses, is framed both negatively and positively, and the two must be held together. Negatively, no one is justified by works of the law. Stott takes this to mean not merely the ceremonial law but law-keeping as such; nothing we do can be the ground of our acceptance, because our best works are stained and our record is one of failure. Positively, justification is through faith in Jesus Christ. Faith, Stott repeats throughout the letter, is not itself a work or a merit but the receiving of what Christ has done; it is the empty hand that takes God's gift.

Stott underlines the force of Paul's argument that even he and Peter, Jews by birth and not Gentile sinners, had come to believe in Christ for this very reason, that they might be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law. If lifelong keepers of the law needed to be justified by faith, how much more everyone else. And Paul clinches it by echoing the psalmist: by works of the law no human being will be justified. Stott presses the exclusiveness of the word faith here; the moment works are added as a ground of acceptance, grace is nullified and Christ died for nothing. The whole gospel stands or falls on this single point, that we are justified by faith in Christ and not by our own works.

source_work: Stott on Galatians
title: Crucified with Christ: Christ Lives in Me
content_summary: Stott expounds this famous verse as Paul's testimony to the personal reality of union with Christ. To be justified by faith is to be joined to Christ, and Paul describes that union in the language of death and new life: I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. Stott is careful to say that the self is not annihilated; Paul goes on to speak of the life he now lives in the body. Rather, the old self, the person under law and condemnation, has died with Christ, and a new life has begun, indwelt and animated by Christ himself. This new life is lived by faith in the Son of God, and Stott dwells on the personal note of its ground: Christ loved me and gave himself for me.
content_detail:
Stott regards Galatians 2:20 as one of the most personal and profound verses Paul ever wrote, and he treats it as the experiential counterpart to the doctrine just stated. Justification by faith is not a cold transaction; it brings the believer into living union with Christ. Paul expresses that union first in terms of death: I have been crucified with Christ. Stott connects this with the broader New Testament teaching that in Christ's death the believer died, so that the old life under law and under sin's condemnation was brought to an end. The believer is not merely a spectator of the cross but a participant in it.

Stott then handles the striking paradox of the verse, that it is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. He is anxious to guard against a mystical misreading in which the human personality is dissolved. Paul does not mean that he has ceased to be himself, for he immediately speaks of the life he now lives in the flesh, in the body, as a continuing personal existence. What has died is the old self, the person Paul was under the law, trying to establish his own righteousness; what now lives is a self renewed and possessed by Christ. Stott summarizes it as a change of centre and of master: the ego has been dethroned and Christ enthroned, so that Christ's indwelling life becomes the animating principle of the believer's own.

Stott lays weight on the means by which this new life is sustained. Paul says the life he now lives he lives by faith in the Son of God. Faith is therefore not only the way we are first justified but the daily principle of the new life; the Christian lives, moment by moment, by trusting and drawing upon Christ. And Stott lingers over the deeply personal ground Paul gives for this faith, that the Son of God loved me and gave himself for me. He observes how Paul makes the universal truth of the atonement intensely individual, appropriating for himself what Christ did for all. The love that gave itself on the cross is not merely love for the world in general but love for me in particular. For Stott this is the secret of Christian living: a life lived out of union with a Christ who died in our place and now lives within us, received and sustained by a faith that rests on his personal love.

source_work: Stott on Galatians
title: Christ Became a Curse for Us: The Blessing of Abraham
content_summary: Stott expounds Paul's argument that all who rely on works of the law are under a curse, since the law pronounces its curse on everyone who fails to keep it perfectly, and no one does. The good news is that Christ redeemed us from that curse by becoming a curse for us, for it is written that anyone hung on a tree is cursed. Stott reads this as plain substitution: on the cross Christ bore the curse we had earned, standing in our place under the judgment of God. The purpose was that the blessing promised to Abraham might come to the Gentiles in Christ, and that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith. Stott stresses that the curse and the blessing are exchanged at the cross: Christ takes our curse so that we may receive Abraham's blessing.
content_detail:
Stott follows Paul's tightly argued case that the law can only condemn those who look to it for justification. The reasoning begins with a stark alternative: those who rely on works of the law are under a curse, because Scripture itself pronounces a curse on everyone who does not continue in all things written in the law to do them. Stott presses the word all: the law demands not partial but perfect and perpetual obedience, and since no one renders it, the law can bring the law-reliant only condemnation. Paul reinforces this with Habakkuk's principle that the righteous shall live by faith, showing that law and faith operate on opposite principles; the law says do and live, but faith receives what God gives.

Against this dark background Stott sets the gospel of 3:13. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us. Stott takes redeemed in its full sense of purchasing release at a price, and he reads the verse as one of the clearest statements of substitutionary atonement in Paul. The curse that the law pronounced on us, our due penalty for breaking it, Christ took upon himself. Paul grounds this in the words of Deuteronomy that everyone hung on a tree is under God's curse; Stott explains that the manner of Jesus' death, crucifixion, publicly marked him out as bearing a curse, and that this curse was not his own but ours. He stood in our place, under the judgment we deserved, so that we might go free.

Stott then draws out the double purpose Paul states in 3:14. The first is that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles. The blessing God had promised to Abraham, that in him all nations would be blessed, is nothing less than justification and acceptance with God, and it now flows out to the nations, not through law or circumcision, but through Christ. The second purpose is that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith. Stott notes how the two verses effect a great exchange: Christ takes our curse, and we receive Abraham's blessing and the gift of the Spirit. He stresses that all of this comes through faith and not through works, so that the argument returns to the letter's central theme. The cross is the place where curse and blessing change hands.

source_work: Stott on Galatians
title: The Law as Guardian Until Christ Came
content_summary: Stott addresses the question Paul's argument provokes: if we are justified by faith and not by law, why was the law given at all? Paul answers that the law was added because of transgressions, to expose and even to increase the awareness of sin, and that it was temporary, in force until the promised offspring, Christ, should come. Stott expounds the image of the law as a paidagogos, the household guardian or custodian who supervised a child until the age of maturity. The law was not the way of salvation but a temporary custodian that shut us up under sin and led us to Christ, so that we might be justified by faith. Now that faith has come, Stott stresses, we are no longer under this guardian; the law's supervisory role has ended, and in Christ we have reached our maturity as sons.
content_detail:
Stott recognizes that Paul's exaltation of the promise over the law raises an obvious objection: if the law cannot justify and came four hundred and thirty years after the promise to Abraham, does it have any purpose, and does it perhaps conflict with the promise? Paul's answer is a firm no; the law and the promise do not compete but play different roles in God's single plan. The law was not given to justify but for other ends, and Stott sets out the two Paul emphasizes.

First, the law was added because of transgressions. Stott explains that the law's function was to reveal sin, to define it, and even to provoke and multiply it, turning wrongdoing into conscious transgression against a known command. Far from making people righteous, the law exposed their unrighteousness and made their guilt plain, so that Scripture consigned everything under sin. Second, the law was temporary, given until the offspring should come to whom the promise referred, that is, Christ. It was an interim measure with a built-in expiry, always pointing beyond itself to the fulfilment in Christ.

The heart of Stott's exposition is Paul's image in 3:24 of the law as a paidagogos, which he is careful to explain, since the modern word schoolmaster or tutor can mislead. In the Greco-Roman household the paidagogos was not the teacher but a trusted slave who had charge of a boy in his minority, escorting him to school, supervising his conduct, and exercising a strict, temporary discipline until the child came of age. Stott applies this to the law's role in the history of salvation and in personal experience alike: the law was our custodian, keeping us under restraint and under condemnation, but its very severity drove us to seek the freedom that is in Christ. So the law was our guardian until Christ, that we might be justified by faith.

Stott then presses Paul's decisive conclusion in 3:25: now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian. With the coming of Christ the custodial role of the law has ended, not because the law was bad but because its purpose has been served and the age of maturity has arrived. Stott is careful to say this does not abolish the moral law as a standard, but it does end the law as a way of acceptance and as a regime of tutelage. In Christ, believers have grown up into the full status of sons, and this leads directly into the next great theme of adoption and freedom.

source_work: Stott on Galatians
title: From Slaves to Sons: Adoption, the Spirit, and Freedom
content_summary: Stott expounds the transition Paul describes from slavery under the law to the freedom of sons. In the fullness of time God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons. Stott stresses the deliberate double sending: God sent his Son to secure our status as sons, and then sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying 'Abba, Father,' to assure us of it. So we are no longer slaves but sons, and if sons, then heirs. On this basis Paul issues the great charge of 5:1: it was for freedom that Christ set us free, so stand firm and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery. Stott sees Christian liberty as the birthright of the adopted, to be guarded against every attempt to re-impose the law.
content_detail:
Stott reads Galatians 4 as the climax of Paul's argument about the law, moving from the legal category of justification to the family category of adoption. Paul illustrates the change with the picture of an heir who, while still a child, is no different in practice from a slave, being under guardians and trustees until the time set by his father. So it was with God's people under the law; they were in a state of minority and bondage. But the situation has been transformed by a decisive divine act.

Stott gives careful attention to the great statement of 4:4-5, that when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons. He notes the marks of the incarnation compressed here: the Son's pre-existence implied in his being sent, his true humanity in being born of a woman, and his placement under the law that he might redeem those enslaved by it. The purpose of this redemption is adoption, the granting of full filial status to those who were slaves. Stott stresses that adoption is not the same as regeneration; it is the legal bestowal of the standing and privileges of sons upon those brought into God's family.

Stott then highlights the second sending in 4:6. Because we are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, Abba, Father.
