He observes the trinitarian shape of salvation here: the Father sends the Son to give us the status of sons, and then sends the Spirit of the Son to assure us of it. The cry Abba is the Spirit's witness within, so that sonship is not only a legal fact but a felt reality. The conclusion Paul draws is triumphant: so you are no longer a slave but a son, and if a son, then an heir through God.

Stott then carries this straight into 5:1, the hinge between the doctrinal and practical halves of the letter. For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm, therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery. Stott presents Christian freedom as the birthright of the adopted son, freedom from the law as a way of acceptance, from its curse and its bondage. And he stresses the urgency of Paul's command to stand firm: this liberty is precious and precarious, constantly threatened by the false teachers who would re-impose circumcision and law-keeping. To return to the law after being freed by Christ is to exchange sonship for slavery all over again, and Paul will not allow it.

source_work: Stott on Galatians
title: The Spirit Against the Flesh, and the Fruit of the Spirit
content_summary: Stott shows how Paul guards Christian freedom from being misused as license. Freedom is not an excuse for the flesh but the opportunity to serve one another in love and to walk by the Spirit. The believer is caught in a real conflict, for the flesh desires what is against the Spirit and the Spirit what is against the flesh, and the two are opposed. Stott sets Paul's two lists side by side: the works of the flesh, the ugly and self-centred products of fallen nature, and the fruit of the Spirit, the beautiful cluster of Christ-like graces beginning with love. Stott stresses that this fruit is not self-generated but grown by the Spirit in those who walk by him, and he underlines Paul's summons to keep in step with the Spirit, since those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.
content_detail:
Stott presents this section as Paul's answer to a natural fear: if Christians are free from the law, what is to restrain them from sin? Paul's reply is that Christian liberty is not lawlessness but life in the Spirit. Freedom is not to be used as an opportunity for the flesh; rather, through love believers are to serve one another, and indeed the whole law is fulfilled in the command to love your neighbour as yourself. Stott notes the irony that the very love the law required is produced not by the law but by the Spirit in those set free from it.

The governing command of the passage, Stott observes, is to walk by the Spirit, with the promise that those who do so will not gratify the desires of the flesh. He then expounds the reality of the Christian's inner conflict in 5:17: the flesh, our fallen self-centred nature, and the Spirit are locked in opposition, each desiring what is contrary to the other, so that the believer cannot simply do as he pleases. Stott is realistic about this warfare: the Christian life is a genuine and lifelong struggle. Yet the outcome is not in doubt for those who walk by the Spirit, and Stott points out that being led by the Spirit is itself evidence of being free from the law's condemnation.

Stott then works through the two contrasting lists Paul draws up. The works of the flesh are many and varied, ranging over sexual sin, false religion, social discord, and excess; Stott notes that they are called works, the busy output of unaided human nature, and that they are largely destructive of community as well as of the self. Over against them stands the fruit of the Spirit, and Stott dwells on the deliberate change of number: not works but fruit, singular, a single ripening cluster grown by the Spirit rather than manufactured by effort. He notes that the list begins with love and unfolds into joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control, and that these graces together form a portrait of the character of Christ himself, reproduced in the believer by the Spirit.

Stott closes with Paul's summary in 5:24-25. Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires; the decisive break has been made. Therefore, since we live by the Spirit, we are also to keep in step with the Spirit, walking in line with him day by day. For Stott the message is that holiness is neither law-keeping nor self-effort but the fruit of a Spirit-directed life, in which freedom expresses itself not in self-indulgence but in the character and love of Christ.

source_work: Stott on Galatians
title: Boasting Only in the Cross, and the New Creation
content_summary: Stott shows how Paul, taking up the pen himself, sums up the whole letter by contrasting two kinds of religion. The false teachers want to boast in the flesh, compelling circumcision to make a good outward showing and to avoid persecution for the cross. Paul, by contrast, will boast in nothing except the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to him and he to the world. Stott stresses that the cross is the ground of the Christian's whole confidence and the death of all self-glory. What matters, Paul concludes, is neither circumcision nor uncircumcision but a new creation. Stott reads this as the letter's final verdict: external religious marks count for nothing, and everything depends on the inward transformation God works, so that the believer is a new creation in Christ.
content_detail:
Stott notes that Paul takes the pen from his secretary to write the closing paragraph in his own large letters, a sign of the personal urgency with which he presses home the letter's message. In these final verses Paul sets two rival religions side by side and lays bare their motives, and Stott draws the contrast sharply because it gathers up everything the letter has argued.

On one side are the Judaizers. Stott exposes the motives Paul attributes to them: they want to make a good showing in the flesh, to point to the outward mark of circumcision as evidence of religious success, and they press it on the Galatians in order to avoid being persecuted for the cross of Christ. Their religion is external, self-advertising, and cowardly, concerned with human approval and human boasting. Stott observes Paul's cutting point that they do not even keep the law themselves; their interest is not obedience but the credit of having circumcised converts to boast about.

Over against this Paul sets his own confession in 6:14, which Stott treats as one of the noblest statements in the letter: far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ. Stott stresses the totality of it. The cross, an instrument of shame and the symbol of everything the world despised, has become the Christian's only ground of boasting, because there alone is salvation found. And the cross has effected a mutual crucifixion: through it the world has been crucified to Paul, and Paul to the world. Stott explains that the values, approval, and standards of the world are now dead to the man who glories in the cross, and he is dead to them; the cross has severed the old allegiance and cut the nerve of self-glory.

Stott then draws out Paul's final verdict in 6:15, which he sees as the summary of the whole epistle: neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation. External religious marks, the very things over which the whole controversy raged, are declared to be of no account. What matters is that God makes a person new, a new creation in Christ. Stott underlines that this is the ultimate issue: not ritual, not law-keeping, not the flesh, but the inward, transforming work of God. Upon all who walk by this rule Paul pronounces peace and mercy, and calls them the Israel of God, the true people of God defined not by circumcision but by faith and new birth. So the letter that began by defending the one true gospel ends by locating everything in the cross and the new creation it brings.

source_work: Stott on Romans
title: The Gospel and the Righteousness of God Revealed
content_summary: Stott reads Romans 1:16-17 as the text written over the door of the whole letter. Paul is not ashamed of the gospel because it is not a philosophy to admire but God's own saving power for everyone who believes, Jew first and also Greek. The core of the good news is 'the righteousness of God,' which Stott refuses to flatten to a single idea: it names God's own righteous character, his saving activity that sets things right, and above all the righteous standing God confers on people who have none of their own. Because guilty sinners possess no righteousness, the gospel announces one that comes from God, received by faith and never earned. The phrase 'from faith to faith' underlines that faith alone is the channel from start to finish, and Habakkuk's promise clinches it: the one justified by faith shall live.
content_detail:
Stott treats these two verses as the thesis statement that governs everything that follows. Paul's declaration that he is unashamed answers a Greco-Roman world that despised a crucified Jewish Messiah as foolishness and weakness; the gospel needs no apology because it is the very power of God, his dynamis at work to rescue. Its reach is universal, embracing everyone who believes, yet it preserves an order of privilege and responsibility in the phrase 'to the Jew first and also to the Greek,' honouring Israel's historical priority without turning it into a claim of merit.

The hinge of the passage is the expression 'the righteousness of God.' Stott resists narrowing it to one meaning. It designates God's own righteous character; it describes his righteous initiative in acting to save; and, decisively for Paul's argument, it points to the righteous status God grants to those who deserve condemnation. Since human beings have no righteousness to plead, the gospel offers a righteousness that originates in God and is credited to the believer. This is why salvation is by grace: what the law demands and we cannot supply, God provides as a gift.

Stott takes the compact phrase 'from faith to faith' to stress that faith is the sole means of receiving this righteousness, from the first moment to the last, excluding works of law at every stage. Paul seals the point by quoting Habakkuk 2:4, that the righteous shall live by faith. Stott shows how the two great words of that quotation, faith and life, map the structure of the letter: the righteousness received by faith dominates the early chapters, and the new life that flows from it fills chapters five through eight. So the introduction already frames the entire message as God's initiative received by trust, unmasks self-salvation as the great rival, and sets justification by faith as the banner Paul will defend against every objection.

source_work: Stott on Romans
title: The Whole World Guilty: Wrath Revealed and No One Righteous
content_summary: Before the good news can land, Stott shows that Paul establishes the bad news: the wrath of God is being revealed against all human ungodliness. Stott insists this wrath is not a capricious temper or petty rage but God's steady, holy, personal hostility to evil, expressed in his handing sinners over to the consequences of their chosen rebellion. Paul's argument moves in stages. The pagan world suppresses the truth it knows and is given up to idolatry and its fruits. The moralist who judges others condemns himself by doing the same things. The religious Jew, entrusted with the law, breaks it. So Paul closes every mouth: all alike are under sin, and all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God. Stott presses this universal verdict because only those who see they are lost will receive a righteousness they cannot earn.
content_detail:
Stott handles this long section as Paul's carefully constructed case for the prosecution, designed to leave the whole human race without excuse. The opening word about God's wrath being revealed is crucial for him. Stott is at pains to strip the concept of everything unworthy of God: this is not sudden loss of temper or arbitrary vengeance, but the constant and principled reaction of a holy God against everything that violates his character. He notes that its present operation appears partly in the threefold refrain that God 'gave them up,' surrendering people to the very desires and disorders they preferred.

Paul's indictment advances against three groups. First the Gentile world: possessing genuine knowledge of God through creation and conscience, they suppress that truth, refuse to honour or thank him, and exchange his glory for images, spiralling into moral chaos. Second the self-righteous critic, whether pagan moralist or observant Jew, who passes judgment on others while practising the same sins; Stott stresses that the act of judging proves the judge knows the standard and so deepens his own guilt. Third the Jew who boasts in the law and in circumcision yet dishonours God by breaking the law, so that outward privilege without obedience saves no one.

Stott shows how Paul draws the strands together at 3:9, declaring Jew and Greek alike to be 'under sin,' and drives the point home with a catena of Scripture proving that no one is righteous. The summary verdict at 3:23, that all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, is for Stott the level ground on which the gospel is preached: sin is universal, and so is the failure to reach God's intended glory. He underlines that the law's role here is diagnostic, not curative; through it comes the knowledge of sin, closing every mouth and holding the world accountable to God. Only people who accept this verdict will welcome a righteousness that is entirely God's gift.

source_work: Stott on Romans
title: But Now: Justification by Grace Through Faith
content_summary: Stott calls 3:21 one of the great turning points of Scripture: the little phrase 'but now' pivots from the darkness of universal guilt to the dawn of grace. The righteousness of God, long witnessed by the law and the prophets, has now been manifested apart from law, for all who believe, without distinction. Justification, Stott stresses, is a legal verdict, not a moral transformation; God the Judge declares the guilty to be in the right, not because they have become good but because he credits them with a righteousness they lack. This acquittal is undeserved, given freely by his grace, and grounded entirely in the redemption accomplished in Christ Jesus. So the same gospel that condemns human boasting also excludes it, because justification is received as a gift and rests on Christ's work, never on our own.
content_detail:
For Stott the transition at 3:21 is the hinge of the letter. Having proved that no one can be justified by works of the law, Paul announces that a righteousness from God has now been disclosed on a completely different basis, apart from law-keeping, yet not disconnected from the Old Testament, since the law and the prophets bore witness to it in advance. This righteousness is available to all who believe, and Stott emphasizes the great leveller in 3:22-23: there is no distinction, because all have sinned, and therefore all who are justified are justified the same way.

Stott is careful to define justification precisely. It is a word borrowed from the law court, the opposite of condemnation. To justify is not to make righteous in character but to declare righteous in status, to pronounce a favourable verdict. He guards this from two misunderstandings: it is neither a legal fiction, since it rests on the real and objective work of Christ, nor a reward for improvement, since God justifies the ungodly. The paradox that a righteous Judge can declare the guilty righteous is resolved only by the cross.

Paul piles up three metaphors to display the fullness of what God has done, and Stott draws them out. Justification is the language of the law court, addressing our guilt. Redemption, the payment of a price to secure release, addresses our bondage. And propitiation, which Stott will expound further, addresses God's wrath. Together they show salvation as a many-sided rescue. Above all, Stott insists on the freeness of it: we are justified 'freely by his grace,' a gift with no price tag we could meet, flowing from God's undeserved favour. And it is grounded 'through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus,' so that the whole ground of our acceptance lies outside us, in what Christ has done. This is why boasting is forever excluded: a gift can only be received, and a verdict of acquittal purchased by another leaves the acquitted with nothing to claim as their own.

source_work: Stott on Romans
title: Propitiation in His Blood: God Satisfying God
content_summary: Stott mounts a vigorous defence of 'propitiation' as the right rendering of the term Paul uses for what God set forth in Christ, over against those who reduce it to mere 'expiation' of sin. He argues that the biblical wrath of God is real and personal, and therefore must be dealt with, but he removes every pagan overtone. In heathen religion an angry deity is placated by a nervous worshipper's bribe. In the gospel it is the wronged God himself who provides, at his own cost, the propitiation that turns his wrath away, offering his own Son. So God is at once the one who propitiates and the one propitiated, both the subject and the object of the atonement. The cross therefore vindicates God's justice, showing him to be both just and the justifier of those who believe.
content_detail:
This verse carries some of Stott's most careful theological work, and his exposition turns on the meaning of the disputed word. He acknowledges the objection, associated with C. H. Dodd, that 'propitiation' imports crude pagan notions and that the term should mean only 'expiation,' the wiping away of sin rather than the appeasing of anger. Stott answers that the wrath of God is a solid biblical reality, established already in chapter one, and that a wrath which is real cannot simply be ignored; it must be dealt with. Expiation of sin and propitiation of wrath are therefore two sides of one act.

What Stott labours to establish is that biblical propitiation is utterly unlike its pagan counterfeit at three points. First, the cause of the wrath is not injured pride or arbitrary offence but God's righteous reaction against real evil. Second, the author of the propitiation is not the anxious sinner trying to buy off an unpredictable deity, but God himself; Paul says God 'set forth' Christ, so the initiative is entirely divine. Third, the offering is not a bribe from human hands but the gift of God's own Son, indeed of himself in his Son. Stott presses the wonder of this: the same God who must be propitiated provides the propitiation, so that he is both subject and object of the atoning act. This preserves both the seriousness of sin and the freeness of grace.

Stott then draws out Paul's stated purpose in 3:25-26: the cross demonstrates the righteousness of God. God had passed over former sins in his forbearance, and this delay raised a question about his justice. At the cross that question is answered, for there sin is judged even as the sinner is spared. So the atonement vindicates God's own character, showing that he is not indifferent to evil. The result is the great statement Stott loves to underline: God is shown to be both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus. Divine justice and divine mercy meet, without either being compromised, in the propitiation Christ made in his blood.

source_work: Stott on Romans
title: Abraham Justified by Faith, Not by Works
content_summary: Stott shows that in Romans 4 Paul proves justification by faith from Scripture itself, taking Abraham as the decisive test case, since the Jew revered him as the model of righteousness. Genesis says Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness. Stott stresses that this crediting was reckoned, not earned: if Abraham had been justified by works he would have something to boast about, but the text says he simply believed and was counted righteous. Moreover Abraham was justified before he was circumcised and centuries before the law, so neither ritual nor law-keeping was the ground. Faith, Stott insists, is not a meritorious achievement that earns a reward; it is the empty hand that receives a gift, the trust of the ungodly in the God who justifies. So Abraham is the father of all who believe.
content_detail:
Stott reads chapter four as Paul's scriptural proof, answering the imagined objection that justification by faith is a novelty. Paul anchors it in the very first patriarch, quoting the pivotal sentence of Genesis 15:6, that Abraham believed God and it was credited to him as righteousness. Stott fastens on the verb 'credited' or 'reckoned,' a term drawn from commerce and accounting. If a man works, his wages are counted as a debt owed to him, something earned. But Abraham's righteousness was not wages; it was reckoned to him as a gift while he was still, in Paul's startling phrase, ungodly. God justifies the ungodly, and faith is simply the trust that takes him at his word.

Stott then follows Paul's two supporting arguments. The first concerns timing: Abraham was declared righteous in Genesis 15, but he was not circumcised until Genesis 17, years later. Therefore his justification could not depend on circumcision; the sign came afterward as a seal of a righteousness he already had by faith. This makes him father of both believing Gentiles, who are uncircumcised, and believing Jews who share his faith. The second argument concerns the law: the promise came to Abraham some four centuries before Moses, so it could not rest on law-keeping either. Law and promise operate on different principles, and Paul will not let them be confused.

Throughout, Stott is concerned to protect faith from being misread as a new kind of work. Faith has no merit in itself; its whole value lies in its object. Stott pictures it as the empty hand stretched out to receive what God freely gives, or as trust that honours God by taking him at his promise. Abraham's faith was strong precisely because it rested not on his own circumstances, an aged body and a barren wife, but on the power and faithfulness of God who gives life to the dead and calls into existence things that do not exist. Stott closes the chapter with Paul's application: these words were written not for Abraham alone but for us, who will be counted righteous if we believe in the God who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead.

source_work: Stott on Romans
title: Peace with God and the Hope That Does Not Disappoint
content_summary: Stott marks the shift at chapter five from how we are justified to what justification secures. The first fruit is peace with God, which Stott insists is objective before it is subjective: not first a feeling of tranquillity but a new relationship in which the war is over and hostility is ended. Through Christ we also have standing access into grace and a settled hope of sharing God's glory. Stott notes how this hope holds even in suffering, since trials produce endurance, character, and a hope that will not put us to shame, because God's love has been poured into our hearts by the Spirit. The ground of it all is that Christ died for us while we were still sinners and enemies; if God reconciled us at such cost, Stott argues, he will surely save us to the end.
content_detail:
Stott sees Romans 5 opening a new movement in the letter. Having established justification by faith, Paul now unfolds its blessings, and Stott lists them as they cascade from the opening 'therefore.' The first and foundational blessing is peace with God. Stott is emphatic that this is not primarily an inward serenity but an objective change of status: the sinner who was under wrath and at enmity with God is now at peace with him, the hostility removed from God's side by the cross and from ours by faith. Feelings of peace may follow, but they rest on this accomplished reconciliation, not the reverse.

From this flow further privileges. Through Christ believers have obtained access, like being ushered into a royal presence, and they now stand in grace as their permanent position rather than their occasional visitor. And they rejoice in the hope of the glory of God, the very glory they had forfeited by sin now restored as their sure destiny. Stott highlights the confidence of this hope: it is not wishful thinking but well-founded expectation.

Stott then follows Paul into the paradox of rejoicing in sufferings. Rather than contradicting Christian hope, tribulation actually serves it, setting in motion a chain that runs from endurance to proven character to hope. This hope does not disappoint or shame us, and Stott points to the reason Paul gives: God has already poured his love into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, so we have present experiential proof of a love that guarantees the future.

Finally Stott draws out Paul's argument from the greater to the lesser in 5:6-11. The measure of God's love is that Christ died for us not when we were attractive or deserving but while we were still weak, ungodly, sinners, even enemies. Human love might just rise to dying for a good person; God's love reached us at our worst. Stott presses the logic: if God did the harder thing, reconciling his enemies through the death of his Son, he will certainly do the easier thing, saving his reconciled friends through Christ's risen life. So justification issues in an unbreakable security, and the believer can boast in God himself.

source_work: Stott on Romans
title: The Two Humanities: Adam and Christ
content_summary: Stott expounds this dense passage as the contrast between two representative men, each the head of a humanity. Adam's single act of disobedience brought sin, condemnation, and death upon all who are 'in him,' because he acted not merely as an individual but as the head of the race. Over against him stands Christ, whose single act of obedience brings righteousness, justification, and life to all who are 'in him.' Stott stresses that the two heads are parallel but not equal: Paul repeatedly says 'much more,' because grace overflows sin and the gift outstrips the trespass. This corporate framework, Stott notes, is the key to the whole gospel: just as we were condemned through no achievement of our own, in Adam, so we are justified through no achievement of our own, in Christ. Solidarity with a representative head, not personal performance, decides our destiny.
content_detail:
Stott regards this paragraph as one of the most important and most compressed in the letter, laying the theological foundation for everything Paul has said about justification. Its logic is corporate rather than individualistic. Paul sets two men side by side, Adam and Christ, and treats each as a representative figure whose one act determined the destiny of the many joined to him. Stott calls them the two heads of the two humanities, and he insists that grasping this solidarity is essential; without it Paul's gospel collapses into a scheme of private merit.

On the one side, Adam's single trespass introduced sin into the world and death through sin, and death spread to all because all are implicated in his fall. Stott handles the difficult question of how Adam's sin affects his posterity by pointing to the representative principle already at work in Scripture: as head of the race Adam acted for all, so that his condemnation became theirs. This is a solemn reality, but Stott notes it is the very principle that makes salvation possible.

For on the other side stands the last Adam. Christ's single act of obedience, his righteous life crowned by his obedient death, becomes the ground of justification and life for all who belong to him. Just as we did nothing to earn our condemnation in Adam, so we do nothing to earn our acquittal in Christ; both come through incorporation into a representative head. Stott finds in this the deepest answer to the charge that justification by faith is unjust: it rests on the same solidarity by which we all fell.

Stott gives special weight to Paul's insistent 'much more.' The parallel between the two men is real but not symmetrical, for grace is not merely equal to sin but vastly greater. The trespass brought condemnation from one sin; the gift brought justification from many trespasses. Where sin increased, grace superabounded. So the reign of death through Adam is answered and overthrown by the reign of grace through righteousness, leading to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord. Stott thus reads 5:18-19 as the hinge on which the two humanities turn: one man's disobedience made the many sinners, one man's obedience will make the many righteous.

source_work: Stott on Romans
title: Dead to Sin, Alive to God: Union with Christ
content_summary: Stott shows how Paul answers the slander that grace encourages sin. The reply is not more rules but a fact: those united to Christ have died to sin and cannot go on living in it. Baptism dramatizes this union, joining us to Christ in his death, burial, and resurrection, so that our old self was crucified with him and a decisively new life has begun. Stott draws out the pattern of indicative and imperative. First Paul states what is true: we died to sin's dominion and are alive to God in Christ. Then he commands us to reckon it so and to live accordingly, refusing to let sin reign and offering ourselves to God. Stott clarifies that this is not sinless perfection but a decisive break with sin's mastery; we obey not to become God's but because in Christ we already are.
content_detail:
Stott introduces Romans 6 as Paul's response to a logical objection to free grace: if we are justified apart from works, and if grace abounds where sin abounds, why not sin freely so that grace may abound the more? Paul's horrified 'by no means' rests on a truth about the believer's identity. We died to sin; how can we still live in it? Stott insists the argument turns on a fact of union with Christ, not on a fear of punishment.

Baptism, Stott explains, is the visible sign and seal of this union. To be baptized into Christ is to be baptized into his death, so that we were buried with him and raised with him to walk in newness of life. Stott is careful to say that our old self, the person we were in Adam, was crucified with Christ, so that the body ruled by sin might be rendered powerless and we should no longer be enslaved to sin. A death has occurred; a new master has taken over; the old tyranny is broken in principle.

Stott then teaches the crucial distinction between the indicative and the imperative, which he regards as the key to New Testament holiness. Paul first states the fact, that we have died to sin and are alive to God in Christ Jesus. Then, and only then, he issues the command, telling us to consider or reckon ourselves to be exactly that. Stott stresses that this reckoning is not make-believe; it is faith's grasp of a reality already accomplished. Because it is true that we died with Christ, we are to count on it and act on it.

The practical outworking follows in the imperatives Stott highlights. We are not to let sin reign in our mortal bodies, and we are to offer ourselves and our members to God as instruments of righteousness. He is careful about the limits of the claim: Paul does not teach that the believer is now incapable of sin, but that sin's reign is ended, its dominion overthrown, so that the Christian is genuinely free to serve a new Lord. Grace, far from licensing sin, is the very power that liberates from it, and the fruit of this new servitude is sanctification and, at the last, eternal life, the free gift of God in Christ Jesus.

source_work: Stott on Romans
title: The Law and the Cry of the Divided Self
content_summary: Stott takes up Paul's defence of the law and his portrait of inner conflict. The law is holy, righteous, and good; the trouble lies not in the law but in sin, which uses the commandment to expose and provoke evil. Then comes the famous struggle of the person who wills the good yet cannot perform it, in whom nothing good dwells so far as the flesh is concerned, until he cries out for deliverance from this body of death. Stott reads the 'wretched man' as a regenerate person, describing the real and painful conflict a Christian knows when facing God's law in his own strength, apart from the fuller experience of the Spirit set out in chapter eight. The anguished cry is answered at once: thanks be to God through Jesus Christ, whose Spirit is the way out of the impasse.
content_detail:
Stott approaches Romans 7 as Paul's careful vindication of the law against the suspicion that, since we are not justified or sanctified by it, the law itself must be evil. Paul recoils from that conclusion. The law is holy, and the commandment is holy, righteous, and good. The fault lies entirely with sin, which seizes the commandment as a base of operations, using even the prohibition to arouse the very desire it forbids, so that the commandment meant for life proves to be an occasion of death. Thus the law is not sin but the instrument that unmasks sin and shows its true character.

The heart of the chapter, and its most debated part, is the vivid first-person account of moral defeat. The speaker delights in God's law in his inmost self yet finds another principle at work in his members; he wills the good but does not do it, and does the evil he hates. Stott acknowledges the long debate over the identity of this 'I,' but he argues that the language fits a regenerate person: an unbeliever does not, as a rule, delight in the law of God or wage this inward war against sin. Stott's considered reading is that Paul describes a genuine believer, though a believer contemplating God's holy standard and his own inability, in his own strength and under the aspect of the law, rather than a believer living in the full power of the Spirit.

Stott is careful to keep this in proportion. Romans 7 is not the whole Christian life but one true dimension of it, the experience of conflict and frustration when the flesh is confronted by the law's demand. He does not read it as counselling despair but as exposing the limits of the law even in the life of the redeemed: the law can command holiness but cannot supply it. That is why the chapter ends where it does, with the wretched cry, who will rescue me from this body of death, and the immediate answer, thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord. Stott sees this as the deliberate bridge to chapter eight, where the answer is unfolded: what the law was powerless to do, God has done through his Son and by his Spirit. The struggle of Romans 7 is real, but it is not the last word.

source_work: Stott on Romans
title: Life in the Spirit: No Condemnation, No Separation
content_summary: Stott regards Romans 8 as the summit of the letter, moving from the struggle of chapter seven to triumphant assurance. It opens with the ringing declaration that there is now no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus, because in Christ the law of the Spirit of life has set us free. Stott traces the chapter's argument: the Spirit indwells, leads, and assures believers as adopted children who cry 'Abba, Father,' and by the Spirit we put to death the deeds of the body. The chapter climbs to its close in unbreakable security. Even suffering cannot thwart God, who works all things together for the good of those who love him and moves them through an unbroken chain toward glory. Stott lets Paul's final challenge stand: nothing in all creation, neither death nor life nor any power, can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
content_detail:
Stott presents Romans 8 as the answer to the cry of Romans 7 and the crown of Paul's exposition of salvation. The chapter begins with the verdict of no condemnation, which Stott grounds not in our improvement but in our union with Christ and the liberating work of the Spirit. What the law could not do, weakened as it was by our sinful flesh, God did by sending his own Son as a sin offering and condemning sin in the flesh, so that the law's righteous requirement might be fulfilled in those who walk by the Spirit rather than the flesh.

Stott then follows the great theme of life in the Spirit. The Spirit is the mark of belonging to Christ, the source of life and peace, and the power of holiness. Here Stott places the imperative of 8:13: if by the Spirit we put to death the deeds of the body, we will live. He stresses that this mortification is neither self-salvation nor passivity, but the Spirit-empowered, deliberate slaying of sin that is the daily business of the Christian. The same Spirit is also the Spirit of adoption, assuring us that we are God's children and heirs, and even our sufferings and groanings are taken up as the Spirit intercedes for us according to God's will.

From this Stott moves to the chapter's soaring conclusion, which he divides into two great assurances. The first is the assurance of God's purpose in 8:28-30: God works all things together for the good of those who love him, and this good is defined by an unbreakable chain that runs from foreknowledge and predestination through calling and justification to final glorification. Stott notes that Paul speaks of glorification in the past tense, so certain is it in the purpose of God. The second is the assurance of God's love in 8:31-39. Paul flings out a series of unanswerable questions: if God is for us, who can be against us; if he gave his own Son, will he not give us all things; who can accuse or condemn those God has justified and Christ has died for. Then comes the triumphant climax that Stott loves, the confident conviction that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor to come, nor any power in all creation, can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord. In Christ, security is total.

source_work: Stott on Romans
title: God's Sovereign Mercy, Israel, and the Depth of His Wisdom
content_summary: Stott treats these chapters not as a detour but as integral to the letter, addressing the agonizing question of Israel's unbelief and the faithfulness of God. Stott holds together two truths Paul refuses to separate: God's sovereign freedom in mercy, seen in his word that he will have mercy on whom he will have mercy, and human responsibility, since salvation comes to everyone who confesses Jesus as Lord and believes God raised him from the dead. Israel stumbled by pursuing righteousness through works rather than faith, yet Stott follows Paul in insisting their fall is neither total nor final: a remnant believes now, and God's purpose reaches out to include the Gentiles and finally to show mercy to all. The whole meditation ends not in a neat system but in worship, before the unsearchable depth of God's wisdom and knowledge.
content_detail:
Stott insists these chapters belong to the argument of Romans and are not an awkward appendix. The gospel Paul has proclaimed raises a sharp problem: if it is God's saving power for the Jew first, why have so many Jews rejected it, and does their unbelief mean God's promises have failed? Paul's answer occupies chapters nine through eleven, and Stott reads it as a sustained defence of God's faithfulness and freedom.

In chapter nine Stott lets the emphasis fall on divine sovereignty. God's word has not failed, because not all Israel by physical descent are the true Israel; election runs by promise, not by blood, as the choice of Isaac over Ishmael and Jacob over Esau shows. When God declares that he will have mercy on whom he has mercy and compassion on whom he has compassion, Stott takes this as Paul's plain assertion of God's sovereign liberty in salvation, a freedom the creature has no standing to contest, since the potter has rights over the clay. Yet Stott is equally careful not to let this cancel human responsibility.

For in chapter ten the emphasis shifts to Israel's accountability and to human faith. Israel stumbled because they sought to establish their own righteousness by works and refused to submit to the righteousness that comes from God by faith. Over against this Paul sets the accessibility of the gospel: the word is near, in the mouth and heart, so that if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. Stott underlines that this promise is open to everyone, without distinction, and that faith comes by hearing the word of Christ, which is why the gospel must be preached.

Chapter eleven then holds out hope. Israel's rejection is neither complete, since there is a believing remnant, nor final, since their fall has opened salvation to the Gentiles and God is able to graft the natural branches back in. Stott follows Paul's vision of a wide mercy in which God has consigned all to disobedience precisely that he may have mercy on all. Significantly, Stott observes, Paul does not resolve the tension between sovereignty and responsibility into a tidy formula. He ends instead in doxology, adoring the unsearchable depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God, whose judgments are beyond tracing out. For Stott this is where sound theology always leads: to worship.

source_work: Stott on Romans
title: The Living Sacrifice and the Renewed Mind
content_summary: Stott marks the great 'therefore' of 12:1 as the turn from doctrine to duty, from the mercies of God to the life of gratitude they demand. In view of all God has done, Paul appeals to us to offer our bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, which Stott calls our reasonable and spiritual worship. Christian worship, he stresses, is not confined to a service but is the offering of the whole self and the whole of ordinary life to God. Then comes the double command that shapes the transformed life: do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind. Stott presses the contrast between pressure from without and renewal from within, and notes the goal: a renewed mind that can discern and prove God's good, pleasing, and perfect will.
content_detail:
Stott regards Romans 12:1 as one of the pivotal verses of the letter, the point at which Paul turns from the exposition of the gospel to its ethical outworking. The little word 'therefore' is loaded: everything Paul now asks rests on everything God has already done. Christian conduct is never a way of earning God's favour but always the grateful response to mercy already received. Stott stresses that the appeal is grounded in the mercies of God, the whole sweep of grace unfolded in chapters one through eleven.

The appeal itself uses the language of the altar. Paul urges believers to present their bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God. Stott draws out the paradox of a living sacrifice: unlike the dead victims of the old cultus, the Christian offering is a life laid on the altar and kept there, a continuous self-giving. He notes the significance of 'bodies,' insisting that biblical worship is not an escape into the spiritual but the consecration of the physical and practical, the members and faculties through which we live in the world. This, Paul says, is our reasonable or spiritual worship, and Stott takes it to mean the intelligent, wholehearted service that is the only fitting response to grace.

Stott then expounds the twin commands of 12:2 as the negative and positive of Christian transformation. Negatively, we are not to be conformed to this world, squeezed into the mould of a godless age with its values and assumptions. Positively, we are to be transformed, and Stott is careful to note that the change is inward and continuous, effected by the renewing of the mind. He gives real weight to the mind here: Christian transformation is not achieved by external pressure or mere willpower but by a renewed way of thinking, a mind reshaped by the truth of the gospel. The world moulds from outside; the Spirit renews from within.

Finally Stott points to the stated purpose of this renewal: that we may test and approve what God's will is, his good, pleasing, and perfect will. A renewed mind is a discerning mind, able to recognize and delight in the will of God in the concrete choices of daily life. So the transformed Christian is not given a rulebook for every situation but a renewed mind that can weigh and prove what pleases God. For Stott, these two verses form the hinge of Christian ethics: consecration of the whole self, and the renewal of the mind that alone makes obedience discerning.

source_work: Stott on Romans
title: Love, the State, and the Fulfilment of the Law
content_summary: Stott expounds Paul's teaching on the Christian's relation to the governing authorities and to neighbours. Every person is to be subject to the authorities, because there is no authority except from God, and rulers are God's servants for order and justice. Stott is careful to keep this from becoming a blank endorsement of tyranny: submission is required because the state is a divine institution with a God-given function, but the authority is delegated and accountable, and obedience to God remains supreme when the two collide. Alongside civic duty Paul sets the debt of love: we are to owe no one anything except to love one another, for love does no harm to a neighbour and so fulfils the law. Stott shows that the commandments against adultery, murder, theft, and coveting are all summed up in the single command to love your neighbour as yourself.
content_detail:
Stott treats Romans 13 as Paul's instruction on the believer's public responsibilities, first toward the state and then toward the neighbour. On the first, Paul lays down the principle that every person should submit to the governing authorities, and Stott identifies the ground carefully: there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by him. Government as such is a divine ordinance, given for the restraint of evil and the maintenance of order, so the ruler is described as God's servant, an agent of his justice, who does not bear the sword in vain.

Stott is anxious that this not be misread as absolute or uncritical obedience. He points out that Paul is stating the general purpose and legitimacy of the state, not sanctioning every act of every regime. The authority is delegated and therefore accountable to the God from whom it derives; the ruler is meant to commend good and punish evil, and when a government reverses that function it acts against its own divine warrant. Stott holds, with the wider witness of Scripture, that where obedience to the state would mean disobedience to God, the Christian must obey God rather than human authority. Within those limits, however, submission, the payment of taxes, and the giving of respect and honour are Christian duties, not merely prudent policies.

Stott then turns to the second sphere, the debt of love in 13:8-10. Paul tells us to owe no one anything, except the one debt that can never be discharged, the ongoing obligation to love one another. Stott draws out the point that love is here presented as the fulfilment of the law: the specific commandments against adultery, murder, theft, and coveting are all gathered up and summed in the single rule to love your neighbour as yourself. Love does no harm to a neighbour, and so, far from abolishing the moral law, it accomplishes its deepest intent. Stott stresses that Christian love is not a vague sentiment but the concrete refusal to injure and the active pursuit of a neighbour's good, and that it therefore honours in the heart what the commandments spelled out in prohibition. He closes by noting Paul's urgency: knowing the time, that salvation is nearer than when we first believed, believers are to wake from sleep, cast off the works of darkness, and put on the Lord Jesus Christ, living now in the light of the coming day.

source_work: Stott on the Sermon on the Mount
title: The Beatitudes: The Character of the Counter-Culture
content_summary: Stott reads the Beatitudes not as eight separate personality types but as one balanced portrait of every citizen of God's kingdom. The 'blessing' is God's own approval, not a warm feeling, and it rests on qualities the world despises. To be 'poor in spirit' (5:3) is to confess spiritual bankruptcy -- that we have nothing to offer God and must receive everything as grace; this is where the kingdom begins. To 'hunger and thirst for righteousness' (5:6) is to crave both personal holiness and social justice with the appetite of the starving. To be 'pure in heart' (5:8) is to be single-minded and transparent, free of the duplicity that corrodes religion. Together they describe a people utterly unlike the self-confident, self-satisfied world around them -- the essence of what Stott calls the Christian counter-culture.
content_detail:
Stott treats Matthew 5:3-12 as the introduction to the whole Sermon: a description of the people over whom God reigns, given before any of their conduct is spelled out. 'Blessed' is not a subjective feeling of happiness but an objective declaration -- God pronouncing these people approved and in the right. The striking thing, Stott stresses, is the sheer contrariness of the list: nearly every quality Jesus congratulates is one the surrounding culture pities or scorns.

To be 'poor in spirit' (5:3) is not to be financially destitute but to acknowledge our spiritual destitution -- that before God we are bankrupt, with no merit to plead and nothing to bring. Stott makes this the doorway to the kingdom, because only those who know they have nothing will receive the kingdom as a gift; it is the exact opposite of the self-reliance the world prizes. Mourning (5:4) follows naturally: a sorrow first over one's own sin, then over the world's.

To 'hunger and thirst for righteousness' (5:6) is to desire it with the raw urgency of the starving and parched. Characteristically, Stott refuses to narrow 'righteousness': it embraces righteousness of standing (justification), righteousness of character (holiness), and righteousness in society (justice). The disciple craves all three and is promised satisfaction.

To be 'pure in heart' (5:8) is to be single-minded and sincere -- undivided in devotion and free of the mixed motives and hypocrisy that infect religion. The promise, that they 'shall see God,' is the highest imaginable, reserved for the transparent.

Read together, Stott argues, the Beatitudes are not a menu of optional temperaments but a composite portrait of the one kingdom character to which every disciple is called, and the values by which that community stands over against both the godless world and merely nominal religion. This is what he means by a Christian counter-culture: a people whose beatitude is defined not by what they achieve but by what, in poverty of spirit, they receive.

source_work: Stott on the Sermon on the Mount
title: Salt and Light: The Christian Influence on Society
content_summary: Stott takes salt and light as the two ways the counter-culture affects the world. Salt (5:13) is a preservative that hinders decay; light (5:16) positively illumines. The images assume a fundamental difference: society is dark and rotting, and Christians are to arrest its corruption and dispel its darkness precisely by being unlike it. Salt is useless once it loses its saltiness, and a lamp pointless when hidden -- so the church influences the world only so long as it keeps its distinctive character and stays visible. Stott presses the balance: Christian good works must be public enough to be seen ('let your light shine before men'), yet aimed not at self-advertisement but at glory redirected to the Father. Withdrawal into a holy huddle and worldly assimilation are the twin failures the metaphors rule out.
content_detail:
In Matthew 5:13-16 Stott sees Jesus defining the disciples' relation to the wider world through two everyday metaphors. Salt and light are both useful, but they work in opposite directions: salt works negatively, checking decay, while light works positively, dispelling darkness. Both images carry a sober assumption about society -- that left to itself it tends toward rottenness and darkness. The Christian's task is not to imitate this decay but to counteract it.

Stott insists that the effectiveness of both depends on the Christian being distinct. Salt does its work only by remaining salt; if it loses its saltiness it is worthless, fit only to be thrown out and trodden underfoot. A lamp, likewise, is meant to be set on a stand, not hidden under a bowl; a concealed light is a contradiction in terms. The lesson he draws is pointed: the church affects the world only so far as it refuses to become like the world. Assimilation destroys influence as surely as saltless salt or a hidden lamp is useless.

At the same time, Stott resists any retreat into invisibility. The command is that our light should 'shine before others,' so that they may 'see your good works.' Christian influence is therefore not merely private and inward; it is meant to be seen -- a matter of visible good deeds in the public arena, consistent with Stott's lifelong insistence on the church's social responsibility. The safeguard against vanity is the last clause: the aim is that people, seeing the works, should 'glorify your Father in heaven,' not admire the doer. Good works are to be public in their visibility yet God-ward in their motive.

So the two images together map a whole posture toward society: neither escapist withdrawal nor comfortable conformity, but penetration -- a distinctive, visible people whose difference preserves and illumines the community they are set within, and whose goodness points beyond itself to God.

source_work: Stott on the Sermon on the Mount
title: A Greater Righteousness: Christ Fulfils the Law, Not Abolishes It
content_summary: Against any notion that grace cancels God's moral demand, Stott expounds Jesus' insistence that he came not to abolish the Law and the Prophets but to fulfil them (5:17). The Old Testament is not repealed; it is brought to its intended completion in Christ and his teaching. From this follows the Sermon's programmatic verse: unless the disciples' righteousness surpasses that of the scribes and Pharisees, they will never enter the kingdom (5:20). Stott is careful to define the surplus qualitatively, not quantitatively -- not more rules more scrupulously kept, but a deeper, inward righteousness of the heart that the Pharisees' external religion never reached. The antitheses that follow illustrate exactly this: Jesus does not relax the commandments but radicalizes them, driving them past outward conformity to inward reality.
content_detail:
Matthew 5:17-20 functions for Stott as the hinge between the Beatitudes and the specific ethical teaching that follows, and as a decisive statement about the disciple's relation to the Old Testament. Jesus flatly denies any intention to abolish the Law and the Prophets; he has come to 'fulfil' them. Stott unpacks 'fulfil' broadly: Jesus brings the law to its intended completion by obeying it, by driving it to its full and deep meaning, and by embodying the reality to which its types and prophecies pointed. The Scriptures are not discarded but honoured and consummated in him.

The permanence of God's moral standard is underscored by the saying that not the smallest letter or stroke will pass from the law until all is accomplished (5:18). Stott uses this to warn against antinomianism -- the assumption that Christian liberty means freedom from God's righteous demands. The kingdom does not lower the ethical bar; it raises it.

Hence verse 20, which Stott treats as programmatic for the rest of chapter 5: the disciples' righteousness must exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees, or they will not enter the kingdom at all. The crucial question is how it exceeds. Stott argues the difference is one of kind, not merely of degree. Pharisaic righteousness was external, concerned with the outward act and the letter of regulation, and it was fatally shallow because it left the heart untouched. The greater righteousness Jesus requires reaches inward to motive, desire, and attitude; it is a matter of the heart before it is a matter of the hand.

Stott thus positions the Sermon between two errors it equally rejects: the pharisaism that reduces righteousness to external performance, and the antinomianism that dispenses with righteousness altogether. The antitheses of 5:21 onward are, on his reading, six worked examples of this same principle -- Jesus taking commandments the tradition had shrunk to outward observance and restoring their full, heart-searching depth.

source_work: Stott on the Sermon on the Mount
title: Murder and Adultery in the Heart: Righteousness Made Inward
content_summary: In the first two antitheses Stott shows Jesus taking the commandments against murder and adultery and pressing them back to their root in the heart. The contrast ('you have heard... but I say') is not between Jesus and Moses, but between Jesus and the scribal tradition that had shrunk God's law to external acts. Unjust anger and the contemptuous word already breach the sixth commandment (5:22); the lustful look already breaches the seventh (5:28). Sin is thus located in attitude and imagination, not merely in deed, so no one can claim innocence on the ground of outward respectability. The drastic sayings about the eye and the hand (5:29-30) are Stott's vivid case for ruthless self-discipline: whatever feeds sin must be dealt with decisively, though the surgery he intends is moral, not literal.
content_detail:
Stott reads the six 'antitheses' as Jesus' own illustrations of the greater righteousness of 5:20, and he is emphatic on one point of interpretation: the formula 'You have heard that it was said... but I say to you' does not pit Jesus against Moses. Jesus is not correcting the Old Testament; he is correcting the scribal misinterpretations of it that had reduced God's commandments to a matter of external observance. His quarrel is with the tradition, not with the text.

In the first antithesis Jesus reaches behind the act of murder to the anger and contempt that fuel it. To nurse unjust anger against a brother, or to spit out the contemptuous insult, already places a person under judgment (5:22), because it is the same murderous disposition that the sixth commandment forbids. Stott notes the corollary Jesus draws: reconciliation takes priority even over worship, so that one should leave the gift at the altar and first be reconciled (5:24). The command is not merely to avoid killing but to pursue peace.

In the second antithesis Jesus reaches behind the act of adultery to the lustful look and the cultivated fantasy: to look at another 'with lustful intent' is already to commit adultery in the heart (5:28). Sin is thus traced to the imagination and the will, not confined to the body's deed. This is precisely the inwardness that makes the disciple's righteousness exceed the Pharisees'.

The hard sayings about tearing out the eye and cutting off the hand (5:29-30) follow as Jesus' call to drastic action. Stott is clear that Jesus is not commanding literal mutilation but demanding a ruthless moral discipline -- a readiness to renounce whatever occasions sin, however precious it feels, because the stakes are the whole self. Taken together, the two antitheses show that the kingdom's righteousness is a matter of the heart's disposition, exposing sin where mere respectability had concealed it and refusing the comfort of a merely external innocence.

source_work: Stott on the Sermon on the Mount
title: Non-Retaliation and Love of Enemies: The Measure Is the Father
content_summary: Stott reads the last two antitheses as the summit of the Sermon's counter-culture. Jesus forbids personal retaliation (5:39) -- not the abolition of justice or the courts, but the renunciation of private revenge and a readiness to absorb insult and go the second mile. He then demolishes the 'love neighbour, hate enemy' formula the tradition had built, commanding love even of enemies and prayer for persecutors (5:44). The ground is theological, not sentimental: God sends sun and rain on just and unjust alike, and his children are to reflect that indiscriminate generosity. To love only those who love us is merely to match the tax collectors; the disciple is called to a love without boundary, summed up in the call to be 'perfect' -- that is, all-embracing in love -- as the heavenly Father is (5:48).
content_detail:
The fifth and sixth antitheses, Stott argues, carry the Sermon's ethic to its most demanding and most distinctive point. In the matter of retaliation, Jesus cites the 'eye for eye' principle (5:38). Stott observes that this lex talionis was originally a merciful limit on vengeance and a rule for the courts, restricting punishment to fit the crime. The scribes had twisted it into a licence for personal revenge. Jesus forbids that private retaliation altogether. The four vivid illustrations -- turning the other cheek, surrendering the cloak as well as the tunic, going the second mile, giving to the one who asks -- are not, on Stott's reading, a naive abolition of law, order, or justice, but a portrait of a heart so free of vindictiveness that it will rather suffer wrong and overflow in generosity than insist on its rights.

The climax is the command to love enemies and pray for persecutors (5:44). Stott stresses that the tradition's addition, 'and hate your enemy,' appears nowhere in the law; Jesus strips it away and extends neighbour-love to its widest possible reach. The motive he gives is imitation of God: the Father 'makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust.' Since God's generosity is indiscriminate, his children's love must be too. To love only those who love us, Jesus points out, is no achievement at all -- even tax collectors and pagans manage that. The distinctive mark of the kingdom is love that reaches the undeserving and the hostile.

Stott interprets the concluding command, 'be perfect as your heavenly Father is perfect' (5:48), not as a demand for flawless sinlessness but, in context, as a summons to the completeness and maturity of love -- a love as all-embracing as God's own. Here, he says, is the height of the Christian counter-culture: a community whose love has no natural boundary because it mirrors the character of the Father himself.

source_work: Stott on the Sermon on the Mount
title: Devotion for God's Eyes: Giving, Praying, Fasting, and the Lord's Prayer
content_summary: Turning from conduct toward others to devotion toward God, Stott shows Jesus attacking the great religious temptation: performing piety to be admired. Giving, prayer, and fasting are each to be done in secret, 'seen' only by the Father who sees in secret (6:6), because an audience of one is the death of hypocrisy and the birth of sincerity. Christian prayer avoids both the ostentation of the hypocrite and the mechanical babbling of the pagan; God already knows our needs, so prayer is the trusting approach of children, not the manipulation of a reluctant deity. In the Lord's Prayer (6:9) Stott finds the model of right priorities: God's name, kingdom, and will come first, and only then our bread, forgiveness, and deliverance -- the whole ordered by the intimate address 'Our Father.'
content_detail:
Having dealt with the disciple's righteousness toward other people, Stott notes that in Matthew 6 Jesus turns to the disciple's righteousness toward God -- the realm of religious devotion. The governing warning is against practising piety 'to be seen by others.' Jesus takes the three classic acts of Jewish devotion -- almsgiving, prayer, and fasting -- and in each case exposes the same danger and prescribes the same remedy. The hypocrites parade their giving, praying, and fasting for a human audience, and Stott presses Jesus' verdict: they have their reward in full, the applause they sought and nothing more. The disciple, by contrast, is to give, pray, and fast in secret, before the Father 'who sees in secret' (6:6). The point is not that piety must be invisible for its own sake but that its true audience is God alone; when we no longer perform for people, sincerity becomes possible.

Stott then distinguishes Christian prayer from two counterfeits. It is unlike the hypocrite's prayer, which is really self-display; and it is unlike the pagan's 'empty phrases,' the heaping up of words as though God must be worn down or informed. Since the Father already knows our needs before we ask, prayer is not the manipulation of a reluctant deity but the confident approach of children to a Father who delights to give.

Against that backdrop Stott expounds the Lord's Prayer (6:9-13) as the model of rightly ordered prayer. It opens with the relationship, 'Our Father in heaven' -- intimacy and reverence held together. Its first three petitions are God-centred: that his name be hallowed, his kingdom come, his will be done. Only then do the human petitions follow -- daily bread, forgiveness, and deliverance from evil. Stott draws out the sequence as a lesson in priorities: God's glory and cause come before our needs. He also highlights the sobering reciprocity attached to forgiveness (6:12, 6:14-15) -- those who will not forgive others cannot expect to be forgiven, because an unforgiving spirit shows that grace has not truly been received. Throughout, the Fatherhood of God frames the whole: devotion is the family life of God's children, lived for his eyes.

source_work: Stott on the Sermon on the Mount
title: God or Mammon: Undivided Loyalty and Freedom from Anxiety
content_summary: Stott presents the choice of two masters as unavoidable: 'You cannot serve God and mammon' (6:24). Money is not neutral once it becomes a rival god; the heart follows its treasure, so the disciple lays up treasure in heaven rather than on earth. From this settled loyalty flows freedom from anxiety. Stott stresses that Jesus does not commend carelessness but forbids corrosive worry, and does so by appeal to the Father's providence: if God feeds the birds and clothes the grass, his children need not be paralyzed by fear over food and clothing. Worry is, at bottom, a failure of faith and a pagan preoccupation. The positive command reorders everything -- 'seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness' (6:33) -- and the necessities will be supplied as by-products of that single-minded pursuit.
content_detail:
In Matthew 6:19-34 Stott sees Jesus addressing the disciple's relation to material possessions, and he treats the passage as a unity built around one decisive either/or. The heart, Jesus says, follows its treasure: where you store your wealth, there your affections will settle (6:21). So the disciple is to lay up treasure in heaven rather than on earth, choosing durable, eternal riches over perishable ones. Between these two lies no neutral ground. 'No one can serve two masters... You cannot serve God and mammon' (6:24). Stott underlines that mammon -- money and material security -- is not a harmless servant but a would-be rival god, demanding a devotion that belongs to God alone. Loyalty must be single and undivided.

From this settled loyalty Stott derives the passage's second theme: freedom from anxiety. He is careful to say that Jesus is not commending an irresponsible carelessness about work or provision; he is forbidding the corroding worry that betrays a lack of trust. Jesus argues from the lesser to the greater: God feeds the birds, who neither sow nor reap, and clothes the wild flowers, which are here today and gone tomorrow -- how much more will he provide for his own children? To be consumed with anxiety over food, drink, and clothing is, Jesus says, to behave like the pagans who do not know the Father; it is, in effect, practical unbelief.

The cure Stott highlights is not merely the removal of worry but its replacement by a new and overriding ambition: 'Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you' (6:33). The disciple who makes God's rule and God's righteousness the first priority discovers that the necessities of life are supplied as by-products of that single-minded pursuit. Anxiety and the divided heart are thus answered by the same remedy -- a wholehearted, trusting orientation toward God, which Stott presents as another facet of the counter-culture: a community freed from the money-worship and the fretful insecurity that drive the surrounding world.

source_work: Stott on the Sermon on the Mount
title: Do Not Judge: Against the Censorious Spirit
content_summary: Stott is careful not to let 'Judge not' (7:1) be misread as a ban on all moral discernment -- the same passage warns against dogs and swine, and false prophets follow soon after, both of which require judgment. What Jesus forbids is the censorious, fault-finding spirit that presumes to play God over others while excusing itself. The comedy of the speck and the plank (7:3-5) exposes the hypocrite who fusses over a splinter in a brother's eye while a great beam juts from his own; self-examination must come first, and only then is the disciple fit to help remove the brother's speck. Stott thus holds together two truths the world keeps splitting apart: Christians are to be neither harsh, presumptuous critics nor undiscerning sentimentalists, but humble, clear-sighted people who judge themselves before assessing anyone else.
content_detail:
Stott approaches 'Judge not, that you be not judged' (7:1) by first clearing away a common misreading. The verse cannot be an absolute prohibition of all evaluation, for two reasons drawn from its immediate context. In verse 6 Jesus tells his disciples not to give what is holy to 'dogs' or to throw pearls before 'swine,' which requires a discriminating judgment about people; and a few verses later he commands them to beware of false prophets and to test them 'by their fruits' (7:15-20), which is impossible without discernment. So Jesus is not forbidding the exercise of a critical faculty as such.

What he forbids, Stott argues, is being censorious -- the harsh, fault-finding, condemning spirit that sets itself up as judge over others. This is a usurpation of God's prerogative, for God alone is the true Judge, and it is invariably marked by a double standard: severe toward others, indulgent toward oneself. Jesus warns that the measure we use will be measured back to us (7:2); the censorious invite the very judgment they hand out.

The famous illustration of the speck and the plank (7:3-5) drives the point home with deliberate absurdity. The critic obsesses over a tiny splinter in his brother's eye while a whole plank protrudes from his own -- and is so blinded by it that he cannot even see straight to perform the delicate operation he presumes to offer. Stott notes that Jesus does not forbid helping a brother remove the speck; he insists only on the right order. First deal drastically with the plank in your own eye -- that is, honest and humbling self-examination and self-judgment -- and then you will 'see clearly' to help your brother.

Stott thus refuses both extremes. The disciple is not to be a harsh, hypocritical critic, nor a flabby sentimentalist who has abandoned all moral discrimination. The kingdom character is humility that judges itself first, joined to a clear-sighted love that can then help others -- discernment purged of the censoriousness that so easily counterfeits it.

source_work: Stott on the Sermon on the Mount
title: The Sermon's Great Divide: Two Ways, Two Trees, Two Builders
content_summary: Stott reads the Sermon's ending as a series of stark either/ors that press for decision. There are two gates and two ways (7:13-14): the broad road that many travel to destruction, and the narrow one, hard to find, that leads to life. There are two kinds of teacher, to be tested by their fruit, since not everyone who says 'Lord, Lord' will enter, but only the one who does the Father's will (7:21) -- profession without obedience is worthless and self-deceiving. And there are two builders (7:24): the wise who hears Jesus' words and does them, founded on rock, and the foolish who hears and does nothing, built on sand. When the storm comes the difference between hearing and doing proves total. The counter-culture, Stott concludes, is entered only by a deliberate, obedient commitment.
content_detail:
Stott treats Matthew 7:13-27 as the deliberate conclusion of the whole Sermon, in which Jesus stops describing the kingdom life and demands a response to it. The rhetoric turns to a series of sharp alternatives, each pressing the hearer to choose.

First come the two ways (7:13-14). There is a wide gate opening onto an easy, spacious road that 'many' travel, and it ends in destruction; and there is a narrow gate opening onto a hard road that 'few' find, and it leads to life. Stott notes the deliberate discomfort of this: the popular, crowded path is not thereby the safe one, and entering the kingdom requires a definite decision to turn aside onto the harder, less-travelled road.

Second come the two kinds of teacher (7:15-20), the false prophets who come in sheep's clothing but are inwardly ravenous wolves. They are to be recognized 'by their fruits,' since a tree is known by what it produces. Stott stresses that Jesus expects his disciples to discriminate -- an echo of the discernment presupposed earlier -- rather than to be naive about those who mislead.

Third, and closely joined, is the warning that profession is not the same as reality (7:21-23). Not everyone who says 'Lord, Lord' will enter the kingdom, but only the one 'who does the will of my Father.' Stott presses the sobering scene of those who claim impressive works in Jesus' name yet hear, 'I never knew you.' Words, orthodoxy, even apparent power are no substitute for obedience and a real relationship with Christ.

Finally come the two builders (7:24-27), which Stott sees as gathering up the whole. The wise builder hears Jesus' words 'and does them,' and so builds on rock; the foolish builder hears the same words and does nothing, building on sand. Both face the same storm, but only the house on rock stands. The decisive line runs between hearing and doing. So the Sermon ends, Stott concludes, not with admiration but with a summons: the counter-culture is entered and sustained only by those who translate Christ's teaching into obedient action.

source_work: Stott on the cross and the atonement
title: The Centrality of the Cross: Why Jesus Focused on His Death
content_summary: What sets Christianity apart from the other great religions, Stott observes, is the prominence it gives to the death of its founder rather than to his teaching or example alone. Jesus did not stumble into martyrdom; he moved toward Jerusalem with deliberate purpose, repeatedly telling his disciples that the Son of Man must suffer and die, and naming his crucifixion 'the hour' for which he had come. The Last Supper, instituted on the night of betrayal, fixes his death — not his birth or miracles — at the center of Christian memory, and the church took the cross, an instrument of Roman execution, as its emblem. Stott argues that this focus is not morbid but faithful: Jesus himself treated his death as the purpose of his coming, so any account of him that sidelines the cross has already misread him.
content_detail:
Stott opens the book by asking why Christians should ever have chosen a gibbet as the symbol of their faith. Crucifixion was so degrading that Roman citizens were normally exempt from it and polite society avoided naming it; yet the early church made the cross its badge. The reason, he argues, lies in Jesus' own self-understanding. The Gospels present a man who moved toward his death rather than away from it. From Caesarea Philippi onward the passion predictions recur: the Son of Man 'must' suffer, be rejected, be killed, and rise (Mrk.8.31) — a divine necessity, not an accident of politics. Luke marks the turning point when Jesus 'set his face' to go to Jerusalem (Luk.9.51), knowing what awaited him. In John's Gospel Jesus speaks repeatedly of 'the hour,' troubled yet resolved: 'for this purpose I have come to this hour' (Jhn.12.27).

Stott notes that Jesus deliberately timed and interpreted his death. At the Last Supper he took bread and wine and identified them with his body given and his blood poured out, commanding that this — his death — be remembered until he comes. He gave the church a rite centered not on his birth or his teaching but on his dying. Paul inherited the same emphasis, resolving to know nothing among the Corinthians 'except Jesus Christ and him crucified' (1Co.2.2), and the book of Revelation places a slain Lamb at the throne of heaven (Rev.5.6).

For Stott the conclusion is unavoidable: the cross is not one Christian doctrine among many but the heart of the gospel and the interpretive key to Jesus' whole mission. To understand Christ, one must begin where he himself placed the emphasis — at his death. This sets the agenda for the rest of the book, which asks not merely that Jesus died, but why, and what his death achieved.

source_work: Stott on the cross and the atonement
title: The Problem of Forgiveness: The Gravity of Sin and the Majesty of God
content_summary: Why is forgiveness a problem at all? Stott insists that the glib assumption 'God will forgive because that is his job' trivializes both sin and God. Two realities make pardon costly: the seriousness of human sin and the majesty of the God against whom it is committed. Sin is not a trifle but rebellion against the Creator, and its wages are death. God, for his part, is not indulgent but holy; his very nature reacts against evil, and Scripture refuses to picture him waving wrongdoing aside. The same self-revelation that calls him 'forgiving iniquity' adds that he 'will by no means clear the guilty' (Exo.34.7). Stott argues that any doctrine of atonement must reckon with this double truth. Cheap forgiveness would compromise God's righteousness; the cross exists because God's holy love found a way to pardon without ceasing to be just.
content_detail:
Stott devotes the pivotal middle section of the book to what he calls the problem of forgiveness, arguing that we feel no need of the cross until we grasp how grave our situation is. Modern people, he notes, assume forgiveness is easy for God — but this assumption depends on shrinking both terms of the equation. First, we minimize sin. Scripture, however, treats sin as rebellion, a defiance of the Creator's rightful authority; all have sinned and fall short of God's glory (Rom.3.23), and sin is culpable rejection of God rather than mere weakness or immaturity.

Second, we domesticate God, reducing his holiness to sentimental benevolence. Stott recovers the biblical vision of a God whose purity cannot look upon evil with indifference (Hab.1.13) and whose own gracious self-disclosure to Moses holds two things together: he forgives iniquity, transgression and sin, and yet 'will by no means clear the guilty' (Exo.34.7). Here is the tension at the heart of atonement. God cannot simply overlook sin without denying his own righteous character, for that would make him complicit in evil and undermine the moral order of his universe.

Stott's phrase for the two poles is memorable: the gravity of sin and 'the majesty of God.'
