source_work: Lennox on Genesis 1 — creation and science
title: Humanity Made in the Image of God (Genesis 1:26-27)
content_summary: Genesis 1:26-27 is, for Lennox, the charter of human dignity. Alone among the creatures, humankind is made 'in the image of God,' male and female alike, and given a place of responsible dominion over the created order. Lennox reads this as a decisive answer to every reductionism that would treat human beings as nothing but animals, machines or accidental arrangements of matter. To bear God's image is to be a person capable of relationship, reason, moral responsibility and stewardship, a creature who reflects, however imperfectly, the character of the Creator. This confers a worth that does not depend on utility, ability or status, and grounds the equal dignity of every human being. The verse thus underwrites both the value of the individual and the vocation of humanity to care for the world on God's behalf.
content_detail:
Lennox draws attention to the solemn deliberation that precedes the creation of humankind, 'let us make man in our image,' which sets it apart from the preceding acts of creation and signals that something distinctive is happening. The image is conferred on humanity as such: 'male and female he created them,' so that the dignity in view belongs equally to men and women, not to one sex or class.

To be made in God's image, on Lennox's reading, is not primarily about physical form but about capacities and calling that mirror the Creator: rationality, moral awareness, the ability to love and to relate, and a delegated authority to rule and steward the earth. The dominion granted in verse 26 is therefore not licence to exploit but a trust to be exercised responsibly, under God and on his behalf.

Much of the force Lennox finds here is apologetic, but he keeps it anchored to the text. If human beings are the image-bearers Genesis says they are, then the reductive account that describes them as merely complex biochemistry, or as survival machines programmed by their genes, fails to reckon with what they most deeply are. The worth of a person cannot then be measured by usefulness, intelligence, health or productivity; it rests on a status conferred by God at creation and shared by all.

Lennox also sees in this verse the foundation of a coherent ethic. Human rights, the obligation to treat others as ends rather than means, and the special gravity of taking human life all follow naturally if humans bear the divine image, and are left hanging if they do not. In a culture tempted either to inflate humanity into its own god or to deflate it into an accident, Genesis 1:26-27 holds the balance: creatures, yet crowned with a God-given dignity and responsibility that nothing in the natural order can account for on its own.

source_work: Lennox on Genesis 1 — creation and science
title: Creation Pronounced Very Good: Goodness and Rational Order (Genesis 1:31)
content_summary: Genesis closes its account of the six days by pronouncing the whole 'very good' (Gen 1:31), and Lennox makes much of this verdict. The world is not an illusion, not evil, and not a chaotic accident, but a good and ordered cosmos that its Maker delights in. The repeated refrain that each stage is 'good,' rising to 'very good' at the end, presents creation as coherent, purposeful and fundamentally positive. Lennox connects this goodness and order to the very possibility of science: a rational, intelligible universe is what one would expect from a rational Creator, and the ordered structure of Genesis 1, separating and then filling day by day, mirrors that intelligibility. The goodness of the original creation also sets the stage for everything that follows, including the problem of evil, since the world as God made it began good.
content_detail:
Lennox notes the deliberate rhythm of the chapter: at successive stages God sees that what he has made is good, and at the climax, surveying the whole, he pronounces it 'very good.' This is a value judgment placed in the mouth of the Creator himself, and it shapes the biblical attitude to the material world. Matter is not a prison or an illusion to be escaped, as in various ancient and modern philosophies; it is God's good handiwork, to be received with gratitude and cared for.

Equally important for Lennox is the order the chapter displays. The six days move in a patterned way from formless emptiness toward structure and fullness: realms are separated, light from darkness, waters above from waters below, sea from land, and then populated with lights, creatures and finally humankind. This is not chaos slowly stumbling into shape but the work of a mind, producing a cosmos, an ordered whole, rather than a disordered heap.

Here Lennox links Genesis to a theme he presses elsewhere: the rational intelligibility of the universe. Science proceeds on the conviction that the world is orderly and can be understood, and Lennox argues that such intelligibility is exactly what one would expect if a rational God made the world by his word. The goodness and order of Genesis 1 thus underwrite, rather than compete with, the scientific enterprise.

Finally, the 'very good' verdict has theological weight for what comes next. Because the world began good, evil and suffering are intruders rather than original features of creation; they enter a good world and spoil it, which is why the biblical story can speak of redemption and of a restored creation. Lennox is careful to keep this tied to the text: the goodness pronounced in Genesis 1:31 is the baseline against which the later disruption of the fall, and the hope of renewal, are to be understood.

source_work: Lennox on Genesis 1 — creation and science
title: Creation Through the Word and the Son (John 1:1, 1:3; Colossians 1:16)
content_summary: Lennox insists that Genesis must be read in the light of the New Testament, which identifies the God who spoke creation into being as the eternal Word. John opens his Gospel by echoing Genesis, 'in the beginning,' and declares that the Word was with God and was God, and that 'all things were made by him' (John 1:1, 1:3). Paul says the same of Christ: 'by him were all things created,' in heaven and on earth (Col 1:16). For Lennox this means the personal Word who created is the very one who became flesh in Jesus. Creation is therefore Christ-centred: the universe was made through him and for him, and the rational order that makes the cosmos intelligible has its source in a personal Logos rather than in impersonal law or blind chance.
content_detail:
Lennox reads John 1 as a deliberate theological commentary on Genesis 1. John's opening words consciously repeat 'in the beginning,' and where Genesis says 'and God said,' John names the one who speaks: the Word, who was with God and was God, and through whom all things came into being. Nothing that exists came to be apart from him. For Lennox this identifies the creative speech of Genesis with a personal agent, the Logos, and so answers the question of what, or rather who, lies behind the ordered universe.

Paul's language in Colossians 1:16 reinforces the point: all things, visible and invisible, in heaven and on earth, were created through Christ and for him, and in him they hold together. Creation is thus not only from God and through the Word but also toward a purpose centred on Christ. The universe has a goal, not merely an origin.

Lennox draws two conclusions he cares about deeply. First, the ultimate explanation of the cosmos is personal. If the Word is the agent of creation, then mind and meaning are not late by-products of matter but are woven into the foundations of reality; the world is the expression of a rational, purposeful person. This, he argues, makes far better sense of the universe's intelligibility, and of the existence of rational, meaning-seeking creatures within it, than an account that begins with the impersonal.

Second, the Creator is not remote. The Word through whom the worlds were made is the one who entered his own creation and became flesh. Lennox sees this as the deepest answer to human questions about God's care: the God who made everything is not a distant first cause but has come near in Christ. Genesis and the Gospel thus belong together. The God who begins the Bible as Creator is revealed at its centre as the incarnate Word who upholds and redeems what he has made.

source_work: Lennox on Genesis 1 — creation and science
title: By Faith We Understand: Reasoned Trust in the Creator (Hebrews 11:3)
content_summary: Hebrews 11:3, 'through faith we understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God,' gives Lennox his account of how creation is known. He is at pains to correct the caricature that faith is belief without evidence, or belief against evidence. Biblical faith, he argues, is a reasoned trust that leads to understanding, not a leap in the dark; the verse pointedly links faith with understanding. To grasp that the universe was made by God's word, and that the visible came from what is invisible, is an insight of faith that is nonetheless rational and illuminating. Far from being the enemy of thought, faith here opens the mind to the true origin of things. Lennox thus reads Hebrews 11:3 as a charter for the harmony of faith and reason and for creation out of nothing.
content_detail:
Lennox fastens on the wording of Hebrews 11:3: it is by faith that we understand. Faith and understanding are not set against each other here; faith is the means by which a genuine understanding is reached. This lets him challenge the widespread modern assumption, which he attributes especially to certain popularisers of atheism, that faith by definition means believing where there is no evidence. On the contrary, he argues, the faith the Bible commends is trust grounded in evidence and testimony, more like the well-placed confidence we extend to a trustworthy person than like credulity.

The content of this understanding is striking: the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that what is seen was not made out of things that are visible. Lennox reads this as an early and clear statement of creation out of nothing. The visible order does not derive from some prior visible stuff but from the invisible God and his word; the material rests on the immaterial, the physical on the personal.

He connects this to his broader case that faith and reason are allies rather than enemies. The same word of God that framed the worlds is the word that faith trusts, and the intelligibility of those worlds is part of the evidence that invites such trust. To perceive design, order and contingency in the universe and to conclude that it was made is not irrational; it is, Lennox contends, the reasonable response to what is there.

He is careful, however, not to reduce this to mere inference. Hebrews speaks of understanding that comes through faith, a knowing that engages the whole person in trust toward God, not only the intellect assembling an argument. The origin of the universe, on this account, is finally grasped not by unaided calculation but by faith that is itself reasonable, a faith that receives the testimony that God spoke, and in receiving it comes to understand where everything came from.
